1014-the-lure-of-the-dim-trails:
B. M. Bower wrote this western about the lure of the dim trails, opening with a search for the western tone. Reeve-Howard, an artist of dry-point etchings, asks a friend why he worries that a mere pastime fails to pay, since he does not depend on the work for a living. The friend, a writer, seeks a truer West.

Bower follows the pair through ranch country, where art, work, and romance test their ideas of the frontier. Her prose is warm and knowledgeable, with the West as both a place and a dream. The book suits readers who like westerns about the West itself, and about those who chase its fading trails.
10202-maria-mitchell-life-letters-and-jo:
Phebe Mitchell Kendall compiled this life of her relative Maria Mitchell in 1896, from letters, journals, and family papers. Mitchell, a Nantucket astronomer, won fame in 1847 by finding a comet, and later taught at Vassar. The book follows her from a Quaker home and library work to wide scientific honor.

Chapters trace her comet sweeps, her tools, her tours south, and her views on slavery, seen on trips to New Orleans and Charleston. Letters show her humor, faith, and care for young women in science. Readers get a warm, detailed portrait of America's first famous woman astronomer.
10453-a-practical-physiology-a-text-book:
Albert F. Blaisdell, a physician and author of school health books, wrote this practical physiology text for higher schools. Blaisdell aims to give high school, normal school, and academy pupils the main facts of physiology and hygiene in a form they can use. The book stresses daily living over mere facts.

Each organ's structure comes before its function, so students can see how parts work together. Laws of health, exercise, food, and cleanliness then follow from those facts. Readers get a clear, old-style school manual of the human body, useful for history of science teaching.
10737-book-about-animals:
A Book About Animals, published at Concord, New Hampshire, by Rufus Merrill in 1850, taught children about beasts with pictures and plain text. The elephant leads, described as the biggest of land animals, five times as big as an ox, yet harmless, fond of cake from a pocket and of carrying riders. The orangutan follows, with long arms and reddish hair.

Each animal gets a short, clear account of size, habits, and home, made for young readers. The book's simple style and illustrations mark it as an early American natural history for children. Modern readers get a quaint, earnest introduction to the animal kingdom as the 1850s knew it.
10796-the-story-of-the-two-bulls:
The Story of the Two Bulls, published in New York by Daniel Burgess in 1856 with original engravings, is a verse tale for children. Deacon R., neither the worst nor the best of men, owns broad acres and prizes his cattle above all. His brindle cow won at the county fair, and old Bonny Gray, a noble steed, was famous at the race.

Above all, the spotted bull fills the deacon's mind, straight-backed and broad-breasted, perfect of his kind. The verses follow pride, rivalry, and a lesson about boasting. Young readers get a rhymed farm fable, simple and moral, in the style of mid-century children's books.
1081-dead-souls:
Pavel Chichikov, a smooth-talking clerk with a scheme, tours provincial Russia buying up serfs who have died since the last census but still count on paper. With these "dead souls" as collateral, he hopes to borrow, marry, and rise. Nikolai Gogol follows him through a gallery of greedy, lazy, and absurd landowners.

Each estate visit turns into a comic duel of haggling, and each host grows stranger than the last. Gogol's prose swings from satire to lyrical praise of Russia's roads and troikas. The novel, left unfinished at his death, stands as Russia's great comic epic and a portrait of a whole society.
10935-the-wonderful-adventures-of-nils:
Selma Lagerlof wrote this Swedish classic about Nils, a lazy fourteen-year-old boy who teases animals and shirks work. After angering an elf, Nils shrinks to thumb size and joins a flock of wild geese flying the length of Sweden, led by Akka from Kebnekaise. Velma Swanston Howard translated the book, with some geography trimmed at the author's approval.

Each chapter pairs adventure with place: Glimminge Castle, the crane dance at Kullaberg, Karlskrona, Oland, Stockholm, and Lapland, with legends and animal tales along the way. Nils learns kindness, courage, and responsibility by helping geese, eagles, and people. Written to teach Swedish geography, the story became a beloved children's book far beyond Sweden.
11014-christmas-in-legend-and-story-a-bo:
Elva S. Smith of Carnegie Library, Pittsburgh, and Alice I. Hazeltine of St. Louis Public Library compiled this 1915 Christmas anthology for boys and girls. Illustrated from famous paintings, it gathers carols, legends, and stories: Luke's shepherds, Milton's peaceful night, Longfellow's three kings, Eugene Field's kings of Cologne, and Selma Lagerlof's flight into Egypt.

Later pieces include St. Francis at Greccio, Good King Wenceslas, the legend of St. Christopher, and tales of Christmas roses and a little gray lamb. The editors mix scripture, poetry, and folk legend, so children meet both the Nativity story and the customs around it. The collection works as a family read-aloud book for the Christmas season.
11150-gems-gathered-in-haste-a-new-year-:
This New Year's gift for Sunday schools, signed by a friend with the initials T. B. F. , gathers short pieces written in haste for four schools. The editor opens with a story of July 3 in a year of the 1830s. Perseverance, who insisted a motto could be made prettier that very day.

Mr. Perseverance nails two sticks together, begs show-bills from a bookstore for letter patterns, buys gold paper and gum-arabic, and has a lady cut and gum the motto on ribbon. Later gems include verses on tidy girls, dog-eared books, and order in school and home, plus the heroine of Pillau, a Prussian woman of remarkable intrepidity. The book offers Sunday-school children moral tales and verses for the new year.
12225-tales-of-lonely-trails:
Zane Grey published Tales of Lonely Trails in 1922, a book of true outdoor adventures from his travels in the American West. Grey, famous for Riders of the Purple Sage, here writes as a hunter and camper rather than a novelist.

Chapters cover Nonnezoshe, Colorado trails, roping lions in the Grand Canyon, Tonto Basin, and Death Valley, with photographs of Grey after two months in the wilds and of Monument Valley. Grey describes forested ridges smelling of sheep, Mexican herders flocks, and country where cattle ranged too tame for his taste. The book mixes hunting yarn with landscape praise. It shows Grey love of empty country, and the limits of his era sporting eye.
12253-wholesale-price-list-of-newspapers:
This wholesale price list comes from a magazine subscription agency of many years ago, preserved as a cross section of American periodicals for the general public and for professions. The transcriber notes that the offers are no longer available and most titles are no longer published.

The forty-page octavo booklet lists newspapers and magazines with club offers. Leslie and Harper Bazar cost three dollars, with the Journal of Education three dollars seventy-five, and with World Work four dollars twenty-five. The list shows what Americans read before radio: farm papers, women magazines, religious weeklies, and trade journals. As a document, it is a price map of print culture, useful to historians of reading and advertising.
12526-boy-scouts-in-northern-wilds-or-th:
Major Archibald Lee Fletcher's 1913 boys' book sends Boy Scouts into northern wilds, from a camp on Moose River to a signal from the hills. Chapters promise a little brass god, a cabin in the swamp, a cave of two bears and a trapper's treachery. Two hungry bears, a half-breed, a face at the window and a pillar of fire follow.

Scout craft drives the plot: tricks, signals, tracking and camp discipline save boys in tight places. Fletcher, author of several Boy Scout tales, writes in a brisk, outdoor style for young readers. The book belongs to the early scouting craze, teaching resourcefulness through adventure, with the northern forest as both playground and test.
13126-the-king-s-daughter-and-other-stor:
Published in 1910 as Sabbath readings for the home circle, this collection promises that every story holds an important lesson. Its contents run from The King's Daughter and The Old Brown House to school tales, stories on lying, courtesy, and confiding in mother. The title picture shows a prison and a young girl who is a king's daughter.

One story has a mother teach a girl to seek worth in character, not in riches or rank. Another follows Flora, who kneels to pray after stealing an orange, and long remembers her shame. A third tells of a ragged boy feared by small creatures near an old empty house. The tales are plain, moral, and meant for reading aloud on Sundays.
1313-over-the-sliprails:
Henry Lawson gathers Australian stories of men over the sliprails, the rough bars that let riders pass between paddocks: shearers, drovers, and swagmen on the track, telling yarns and facing hard times. The tales are plain, funny, and often sad.

Lawson writes the bush without romance, and his people endure drought, drink, and debt with humor and mateship. The book is a companion to his other bush volumes. It suits readers who like spare, true tales of working Australia. Lawson's bush tales endure as spare, true stories of working Australia.
13404-tom-tufton-s-travels:
Evelyn Everett-Green's historical adventure opens with the death of Squire Tufton of Gablehurst and his only son Tom left to make his way. Tom goes out into London, falls in with Lord Claud, learns fencing, and is drawn toward the court and camp of the great Duke Marlborough.

Later chapters carry him to peril, to the monks of St. Bernard, back to London, and onto the king's highway with despatches too secret for paper. Swordplay, loyalty, and a young man's choice between ease and duty drive the plot. Everett-Green writes a boy's-eye view of an age of soldiers, courtiers, and dangerous roads, with home always waiting behind the journey.
13706-socialism-and-american-ideals:
William Starr Myers, a Princeton professor of politics, published this short work in 1919. It argues that socialism clashes with American ideals of equality of opportunity, democracy, and religion. Myers traces socialist thought to materialism and asks why it appealed to foreign-born workers. He then cites cases where socialist schemes failed in practice.

The book belongs to the debate that followed the Russian Revolution and wartime unrest. Myers defends private effort, competition, and faith as foundations of American life. His tone is academic, not polemical, and he quotes British and American writers at length. Readers today can use it as a period statement of anti-socialist argument. Its value lies in its clarity and its moment.
13767-edward-macdowell-his-work-and-idea:
Elizabeth Fry Page wrote this short study of Edward MacDowell, the American composer. It surveys his work and ideals, with poetical interpretations of his music by the author. Pieces discussed include A. D. 1620, To a Wild Rose, To a Water Lily, and In Deep Woods. Page dedicates the book to the founder of the MacDowell Club of Nashville.

Page quotes MacDowell's view that music means harmony, harmony means love, and love means God. She notes Wagner's influence on the young American, heard in many passages. The study praises MacDowell's gift for short, singing piano pieces. It suits music lovers meeting MacDowell for the first time. The volume also preserves early American musical criticism.
14188-fifty-two-story-talks-to-boys-and-:
Rev. Howard J. Chidley wrote fifty-two story talks for boys and girls, one for each week of the year, published in 1914. Titles promise variety: a Bible riddle, closed gates, hiring a coachman, the fiercest thing in the Bible, habits, courtesy, and little foxes. A sermon for the boys, tire trouble, and watching for idle boys keep the tone practical and friendly.

Nature stories carry the morals. An eagle above Storm King mountain on the Hudson dodges hunters by flying so high that bullets merely kiss his plumage and fall back. A fable then pits sun against north wind: bluster fails, while steady heat makes a traveler remove hat and coat of his own accord. Gentleness, Chidley argues, wins where force fails. Parents and teachers found here a year's worth of short talks, each with a story first and a lesson second.
14679-stray-thoughts-for-girls:
L. H. M. Soulsby addresses girls at what she calls the awkward age, in short essays meant to be read, kept and returned to. Manners, conversation, planning and friendship sit beside pieces on mothers and daughters, holidays, Sunday observance and first love.

The tone is warm but firm. Soulsby values honesty, kindness, self-command and a sense of humour about one's own faults, and she treats plainness, awkwardness and high spirits as matters of character rather than shame. Quotations and small anecdotes carry the teaching. The volume now reads as a candid window on Edwardian advice for young women, earnest in its morals and humane in its detail.
14744-different-girls:
Harper's Novelettes gathers short stories about young women at turning points in their lives, edited by William Dean Howells and Henry Mills Alden. Contributors include Richard Le Gallienne, Elizabeth Jordan, Alice Brown and Octave Thanet, each taking a different heroine and a different kind of choice.

One story follows Margaret, the last sister still at home after her five sisters have married and left. Others centre on a sister, a bride, a girl on a bicycle and a young woman seeking a prize fund. Romance, family duty, pride and fresh independence recur, but every tale keeps its own tone, setting and ending.
14841-life-of-lord-byron-vol-6-with-his-:
Thomas Moore's life of Lord Byron, volume six, covers letters and journals from February 1823 to Byron's death in April 1824, with notices of his life and an appendix. A letter from Genoa to Moore in February 1823 opens the run, written as Byron prepared for his last journey.

Parliamentary speeches, reviews of Wordsworth and of Gell's Greece, fragments and letters to John Murray on Pope and Bowles fill the appendix. Together they show a poet still arguing, joking and planning in his final year. Moore's edition, first issued in the 1850s, remains a standard source for Byron's late voice: brilliant, restless and already aware of his own legend.
14890-the-hunters-of-the-hills:
Joseph A. Altsheler's 1916 story of the great French and Indian War follows three friends: Robert Lennox, a lad of unknown origin, Tayoga, a young Onondaga warrior, and David Willet, a hunter. Brilliant French officer Raymond Louis de St. Luc and other French officers stand against them.

St. Luc, the tomahawk, an intelligent canoe, a Mohawk chief, two Frenchmen and New France open the tale, with guests of the enemy, an inn, a meeting and Bigot's ball. Hunter and bravo, bowmen, Champlain, the vale of Onondaga and a great test follow. Altsheler writes frontier war as comradeship and woodcraft, where loyalty across cultures matters as much as battles.
15149-the-palace-beautiful-a-story-for-g:
Meade's story for girls follows three sisters named for flowers. Primrose was born in a March springtime, Jasmine in a brilliant Italian summer, and Daisy in an English cottage as the family fortunes fell. Their father, a captain in India, dies before he can come home, and the girls face trouble together.

Chapters trace their first month of hardship, efforts to earn a living, a move to London, and the dream of a palace beautiful built from work and hope. Meade writes with warmth for young readers, praising pluck and sisterly love. The book offers Victorian girls' fiction at its most earnest and kind.
15209-clear-crystals:
Clara Beede's 1946 poetry book, printed at Cleveland, gathers devotional and reflective verse, with a dedication to Olney, Russell, William, Ellwood, and all soldier boys. A list of her other torchbearer books fronts the volume, from Brown Plumes to Golden Leaves. Mother's Prayer opens the spirit of the set.

Poems give thanks for a new day, pray for rest, light, and duty, and ask blessing on dear ones and on soldiers far from home. Beede writes in plain, prayerful lines, without irony or show. Readers who like mid-century devotional verse will find the book sincere, gentle, and rooted in wartime home feeling.
15282-uncle-wiggily-s-travels:
Howard Garis's 1913 Uncle Wiggily book sends the old rabbit gentleman traveling, with pictures by Louis Wisa. The bedtime series offers thirty-one stories per volume, one for each night of the month, in cloth binding for reading aloud. Rabbit, squirrel, duck, and dog cousins fill the set.

Uncle Wiggily, with his crutch and kind heart, meets animal friends, dodges foxes and wolves, and helps small creatures along the way. Garis writes in a warm, simple style for little folks. The book remains a cozy classic of animal bedtime tales. His travels mix jokes, rescues, and gentle lessons in every chapter.
15351-h-g-wells:
J. D. Beresford published this short critical study of H. G. Wells in 1915, when Wells was already famous. Beresford reads Wells as a writer with a plain, normal way of seeing, and uses that idea as a key to his work. The book is an essay in criticism, not a life story, and it closes with lists of Wells's books in Britain and America.

Four chapters carry the argument. One takes up the early scientific romances, one the novels of social life, and one the books on sociology and reform. Beresford asks what holds such unlike books together, and finds the answer in Wells's direct gaze at ordinary life and at the future. For a reader new to Wells, it maps his output before the First World War in clear, short chapters.
15419-letters-to-a-daughter-and-a-little:
Helen Ekin Starrett published this advice book in Chicago in 1886, pairing nine letters to a daughter with a short sermon to schoolgirls. The letters speak in a mother's voice to a young woman leaving home, and each takes one part of conduct: manners, self-control, aims in life, habits, talk, friends, tact, culture, and faith.

Starrett's rule is simple: good manners grow out of good behavior, and the power to win friends rests on character more than wealth. She urges plain habits, kind speech, wise choice of company, and steady religious duty. The closing sermon turns the same counsel to girls still at school. As a record of late Victorian ideals for young women, it is direct, earnest, and full of practical detail.
15547-the-life-of-robert-louis-stevenson:
Jacqueline M. Overton wrote this life of Robert Louis Stevenson for boys and girls, published in New York in 1933 by Charles Scribner's Sons. It is dedicated to the boys at the Yorkville Library. It is also dedicated to all other boys who love to tramp and camp and seek adventure. Overton hopes to make them better friends with a man who loved these things. A frontispiece shows Stevenson from a photograph by Lloyd Osbourne.

Nine chapters follow lighthouse builders, Stevenson's boyhood, the lantern bearer, Edinburgh days, amateur emigrant, Scotland again, a second visit to America, the South Seas, and Vailima. Pictures show his birthplace, Colinton Manse, Swanston Cottage, Edinburgh Castle, the Treasure Island map, and his tomb on Væa Mountain. Overton writes a clear, admiring life for young readers, centered on adventure and the making of a storyteller.
15595-vocational-guidance-for-girls:
Marguerite Stockman Dickson wrote this vocational guidance book for girls. It belongs to a series edited by J. Adams Puffer. Companion works cover the teacher as counselor and guidance for the professions. Its contents divide into present-day ideals of womanhood and guiding girls toward that ideal, with a foreword and fourteen chapters.

Part one treats woman's place in society, the ideal home, establishing a home, and running its domestic machinery. Part two covers education, training the little child, and housekeeping mechanics. It treats the girl's inner life and adolescence, and her work in detail. That work runs from classification of occupations to vocations shaped by training and homemaking. Marriage closes the book. The volume shows early vocational guidance at work: practical, domestic in focus, and earnest about fitting girls for life and labor.
15858-the-social-emergency-studies-in-se:
A set of studies in sex hygiene and morals, edited by William Trufant Foster, president of Reed College. Houghton Mifflin issued the book in 1914, with an introduction by Charles W. Eliot, president emeritus of Harvard. Foster also led the Pacific Coast Federation for Sex Hygiene. The book treats a subject then called the social emergency.

Eliot's introduction frames the studies, and Foster's own essay on the emergency leads. Later papers treat schools, health, and the moral dangers facing youth. The tone is earnest and reforming, aimed at parents, teachers, and pastors. The volume shows Progressive-era America facing sex frankly for the first time: science, morals, and public health joined.
15892-the-education-of-catholic-girls:
A study of girls' schooling by Janet Erskine Stuart, on the education of Catholic girls. Stuart, a leading Catholic educator, argues that faith should shape the whole curriculum, not sit beside it. Chapters move from religion and character through philosophy and the realities of life. Lessons, play, and manners each find a place.

Mathematics, natural science, and nature study join English, modern languages, history, and art in her plan. A chapter on the higher education of women closes the argument. Stuart writes for headmistresses, teachers, and parents. The book still speaks to Catholic schools: form character first, and learning will follow in its train.
16184-his-life-a-complete-story-in-the-w:
William E. Barton, Theodore G. Soares, and Sydney Strong prepared His Life as a complete story of Jesus in the words of the four gospels, using the American Standard Revised Bible. Hope Publishing of Chicago and New York sold it cheaply for wide use. Paper covers cost fifteen cents, and ten copies cost twelve and a half cents each. Larger lots cost ten cents each, with a de luxe leather presentation edition at seventy cents.

By weaving Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John into one narrative, the editors give readers the gospel story straight, without added comment. A companion volume on the disciples and their letters followed in the same styles. Churches, schools, and families used it as a plain, affordable life of Christ.
1632-a-book-of-scoundrels:
Charles Whibley's Book of Scoundrels, reprinted from the National Observer, the New Review, the Pall Mall Gazette. Macmillan's Magazine, offers lives of rogues from Captain Hind to Moll Cutpurse and Jonathan Wild. An introduction on Greek foolishness frames chapters that treat crime as a kind of art.

Whibley writes with wit and learning, admiring his scoundrels' daring while noting their ends. The book is a gallery of highwaymen, thieves, and impostors. It is a delightful period work for readers who enjoy rogues' lives told with style and a touch of irony.
16329-the-other-girls:
Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney's The Other Girls, listed among her Houghton Mifflin books at one dollar twenty-five, speaks to young women learning to wait and to help. Its preface pictures Life as an old mother warning girls not to touch the pie until it is cut, saying wait until you are helped. As individuals, Whitney adds, we may not have things until help comes, a lesson in patience and dependence.

The book that follows turns that moral into stories of girls at work, at home, and among friends, in Whitney's earnest, domestic style. Her neighborhood tales and homespun yarns made her a favorite guide for American girls. Readers who like Victorian advice wrapped in fiction will find a kind, thoughtful volume.
16548-life-of-lord-byron-vol-3-with-his-:
Thomas Moore's third volume of Byron's life covers February 1814 to April 1817 in letters and journals, with notices of the poet's life between them. A journal entry for February 18, 1814 finds Byron back in London to a press uproar over stanzas on Princess Charlotte, with talk of a motion in the House. Hobhouse's return and the news of Buonaparte fill the same pages.

Moore lets Byron speak for himself, and the voice is witty, restless, and candid. The volume catches the poet between fame and exile, still the talk of London. Readers of Byron will find here the raw matter of his legend, in his own hand.
16549-life-of-lord-byron-vol-4-with-his-:
Thomas Moore's fourth volume of Byron's life covers April 1817 to October 1820 in letters and journals. Letter 272, from Venice in April 1817, tells Murray of a slow fever now gone, with nocturnal burnings and morning sweats, cured, Byron jokes, by neither medicine nor doctor. Rome waits in a few days, though Byron warns his plans change often.

Moore's notices link the letters into a life abroad: Venice, Rome, and the years of exile's height. Byron's voice stays witty, restless, and frank. Readers following the poet will find this volume the heart of his Italian years, in his own vivid words.
16570-life-of-lord-byron-vol-2-with-his-:
Thomas Moore's second volume of Byron's life covers July 1811 to January 1814, from the poet's return from the Continent to the eve of his fame's height. Moore pauses first to weigh how two years of travel shaped Byron's mind, after a youth spent among scenes fit to plant poetic feeling. Letters and journals then carry the story home.

The volume catches Byron young, restless, and newly famous, with the pilgrim's travels still fresh in his verse. Moore's notices link the letters into a life. Readers following Byron's arc will find this volume the bridge between the wanderer and the London lion.
16609-life-of-lord-byron-vol-5-with-his-:
Thomas Moore put together this fifth volume of his life of Lord Byron, issued by John Murray in London in 1854. It prints Byron's letters and journals from October 1820 to November 1822, with Moore's own notes on his life. The letters go to friends in Paris, Ravenna, and London, and touch on verse, travel, and Italian politics.

Moore lets Byron speak in his own sharp, restless voice, then steps in to set the scene. Readers hear a poet at work and at odds with those who watch him, keen on shooting, on verse in French dress, and on his own memoir. The volume works as both life story and letter book for the middle years of Byron's exile.
17288-herzegovina-or-omer-pacha-and-the-:
Lieutenant G. Arbuthnot's 1862 Herzegovina, or Omer Pacha and the Christian Rebels, adds a brief account of Servia's social, political, and financial condition. Arbuthnot, an artillery officer and fellow of the Royal Geographical Society, traveled a few short months in a land whose language he knew slightly. He writes only what met his own notice, joined to the views of the few who studied these countries. Chapters follow Zara, Sebenico, Spalatro, Ragusa, and the road to Mostar.

His preface owns the limits of a brief visit, yet claims plain, simple description over grand theory. The book suits readers of Balkan history and Victorian travel. As a period account, it shows the Ottoman frontier through British eyes, and should be read with its age and standpoint in mind.
17354-cave-regions-of-the-ozarks-and-bla:
Luella Agnes Owen, a member of the French Society of Speleology and a fellow of the American Geographical Society, published this study of caves in Cincinnati in 1898. Owen writes as a cave scholar, not a casual tourist, and her book covers the cave country of the Ozarks and the Black Hills. Pictures accompany the text, as in other Gutenberg editions of the work.

Readers follow explorations underground, learning how caves form, what lives in them, and how explorers map their passages. The book joins travel writing to natural science, with the author's learned standing behind every chapter. It still appeals to cavers, geologists, and readers who like wild places described by someone who went down into them.
17684-life-of-lord-byron-vol-1-with-his-:
Thomas Moore wrote this life of Lord Byron, with his letters and journals, in a six-volume series. This first volume opens the series, with links to the other five volumes given in the transcription. Moore, Byron's friend and literary executor, writes from close knowledge and from Byron's own papers.

Readers get the founding Byron biography, rich in letters and journals, and shaped by a poet's hand. The book suits Byron readers and biographers, as the life against which later lives are measured. Its first volume sets the pattern for the whole series.
18438-explanation-of-catholic-morals:
Rev. John H. Stapleton wrote this concise, reasoned, and popular exposition of Catholic morals, published by Benzinger Brothers in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago, with copyright in 1904. The book carries the approval of the censor and of Archbishop John M. Farley of New York. Stapleton opens by distinguishing morals from dogma: dogma directs belief, morals shape lives, and both together form the worship owed to God.

Chapters treat believing and doing, the moral agent, conscience, laxity and scruples, the law of God and its breach, sin, and how to count sins. Capital sins follow in order: pride, covetousness, lust, anger, gluttony, drink, envy, and sloth. Later chapters return to belief, its grounds in reason, grace, and will. Readers get Catholic moral teaching in plain form: short chapters, clear order, and guidance for conscience.
18504-sex-in-education-or-a-fair-chance-:
Edward H. Clarke, a Boston doctor and former Harvard teacher, first gave this essay as a talk to the New England Women's Club. Printed in 1875, it asks how schooling for girls should take account of health and the body. Its five parts cover an opening case, the body, cases from practice, mixed schooling, and the way schools worked in Europe.

Clarke feared that heavy study at certain ages strained young women's health, and he urged schools to ease that strain. His claims sparked wide dispute at the time and still draw debate now. The book remains a key source for the history of women's schooling and of medical ideas about girls.
18525-on-the-trail-an-outdoor-book-for-g:
Lina Beard and Adelia Belle Beard wrote this outdoor guide for girls, published at New York in 1915. It answers what the authors saw as a new demand: girls wanted real woodcraft, not books that treated them as fearful of insects and snakes. Chapters cover trailing, woodcraft, camping, trail clothes, handcraft, wild food, knots, and care for hurts.

Later chapters add cameras on the trail, life on and in the water, and camp games and Sunday fun. The Beards, who drew the pictures themselves, write in a brisk, can-do tone. The book stands as a landmark in girls' outdoor writing of its era.
1858-plain-tales-from-the-hills:
Hill stations, heat, gossip, and rank decide fates in these early stories of Anglo-Indian life, from Lispeth to the watches of the night. The tales are set among soldiers, civil servants, and their wives in hill stations, where heat, gossip, and rank decide fates.

Kipling writes with a young man's confidence and a reporter's eye, and the stories move fast: a marriage arranged, a reputation lost, a conversion attempted. The collection made his name, and it remains the sharpest introduction to his India. A world of verandahs, telegraph offices, and people trying to live by codes that keep breaking under them.
18656-the-tale-of-pony-twinkleheels:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote this Slumber-Town Tale in 1921, with pictures by Harry L. Smith. Its hero, Twinkleheels, is a small pony only half as big as a horse, so his tiny feet must move twice as fast to keep pace. Farmer Green likes to say it is spirit, not size, that counts, and old dog Spot soon learns the pony is no mere toy after one trip to the village.

Chapters follow fun in the pasture, tricks, a race with Ebenezer, a stuck drift, the blacksmith's shop, new shoes, and a circus rider turn. Johnnie Green rides him and drives him in a red-wheeled buggy. Bailey tells it all with warmth and humor for young readers.
18712-levels-of-living-essays-on-everyda:
Henry Frederick Cope gathered these short essays on everyday ideals into a 1908 volume from Fleming H. Revell. They first ran in the Chicago Sunday Tribune as A Sermon for To-day, with brief sentence sermons beside them, and reached readers through a group of great dailies.

Cope writes of higher levels, unseen allies, the sovereignty of service, the right to happiness, and the curriculum of character, then of faith, money, worry, and the everyday heaven. Each piece aims at the art of daily living in the light of eternal life, in short chapters a busy reader can take up singly. The book's plain, hopeful counsel suits anyone seeking steadier footing for ordinary days.
18779-physiology-and-hygiene-for-seconda:
Francis M. Walters wrote this school text on physiology and hygiene for D. C. Heath, first copyrighted in 1909. It studies the body from three sides at once: anatomy for structure, physiology for the use of parts, and hygiene for care and management.

Hygiene, the book says, is personal for one's own body, domestic for the family, and public for the community. All rest on one law of harmony: "the mode of living must harmonize with the plan of the body." Health means supplying what the body's nature requires and avoiding what injures it. The text aims to train accurate observation and sound reasoning along with useful knowledge.
19001-all-aboard-a-story-for-girls:
Fannie E. Newberry wrote this 1898 story for girls about a voyage abroad. Faith and Hope, two sisters, pack their bags in a rush of nerves and laughter, say farewell to their home, and set sail for new scenes. The book follows them from leave-taking to life on board ship.

Their stops include the Bay of Biscay, towns in Portugal, and Gibraltar, with kite flying, gossip, and small mishaps along the way. Each chapter mixes travel sights with lessons in pluck, kindness, and good manners. Young readers get a cheerful voyage tale, full of sisterly talk and foreign colour.
19007-danger-signals:
John A. Hill and Jasper Ewing Brady wrote this 1902 book of true railroad tales about train dispatchers and engineers. It praises men with nerves of steel who held their posts through wreck, fire, and storm. Each story is short, vivid, and told as a first-hand memory.

One tale follows an engineer testing a new engine and a new fuel, with a young fireman hired through a sister's plea. Others turn on split-second choices at signals and switches. Readers get stirring accounts of courage on the rails, where a calm head could save a train full of lives.
19089-a-pagan-of-the-hills:
Charles Neville Buck wrote this 1919 novel set in the Appalachian hills. It follows mountain folk, timber deals, and a young man named Bud whose drinking brings shame and danger to his neighbours. Aaron McGivins, an older mountain man, tries to steer Bud home before trouble grows.

Log trading, family pride, and rough talk shape the plot, while Brent, an outsider, watches the clash between old ways and new business. Whiskey, threats, and stubborn honour drive the scenes. Readers get a mountain tale of pride, pity, and the hard pull between freedom and duty.
19360-six-to-sixteen-a-story-for-girls:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote this story for girls, Six to Sixteen, published by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge and dedicated to Eleanor Lloyd. Ewing warns that it paints no model girl or model education, and calls the tale fragmentary. The heroine grows from six to sixteen in a northern home.

Girls sit in a large, airy, spotless kitchen with stone floor, yellow walls, scrubbed tables, and a huge blazing fire, covering table and floor with books and belongings. Keziah the cook stones the floor and moulds the hearth. Young readers get a warm, domestic coming-of-age tale of family, books, and home life.
19701-health-work-in-the-public-schools:
Health Work in the Public Schools argues that schools must guard children's bodies too. Its key tool is medical inspection of pupils. The book says educator and physician should join hands in the school. Their shared aim is health strong enough for children to use free schooling well. Inspection, in its words, safeguards children from disease.

School health work was a young field when this guide appeared. Reformers saw crowded classrooms spreading sickness fast. A doctor's eye in school could catch what teachers missed. The book lays out that case in plain, hopeful terms. It also promises healthier, happier, more vigorous children. Modern school nursing grew from arguments exactly like these.
19850-the-human-side-of-animals:
Royal Dixon wrote The Human Side of Animals in 1918. It argues that animals show traits we call human. One odd claim stars the porcupine and the hedgehog. After shaking down berries or grapes, they roll in them. Then they hurry home with food stuck to their quills. Dixon reports such tales with warm sympathy for animal minds.

Popular natural history then loved animal intelligence stories. Dixon collected anecdotes of memory, affection, and cunning. Science has since tested many such claims hard. Some of Dixon's travelers' tales will not survive testing. The book still shows the era's animal feeling. It helped build public kindness toward wildlife.
19896-queer-stories-for-boys-and-girls:
Queer Stories for Boys and Girls gathers Edward Abbott Parry's odd tales. Parry explains this is their first fair book issue. Earlier editions fell into the hands of freebooters, he complains. He had to pay a round sum for the plates to free his tales. Queer here means strange and whimsical, not anything else. The stories mix nonsense, fairies, and upside-down logic.

Parry was a judge who wrote children's fantasy on the side. His tales play with words, animals, and polite absurdity. Piracy of popular books was a real author's grievance then. His preface's anger is part of the period record. The stories themselves stay light on their feet. Young readers got wit without a single sermon.
20081-a-houseful-of-girls:
Sarah Tytler wrote A Houseful of Girls, a novel of a home full of young women. The book notes a strange, quick bond among girls on the edge of womanhood. They catch looks and whispers meant to pass over their heads. Blushes, shrugs, and quick glances spread through the group at once.

Tytler writes of sisters, friends, and the small storms of a full house. Each girl reads the others with sharp, shared instinct. The tale turns on youth, love, and family strain. Readers get a warm, keen look at girlhood as one writer of the era saw it.
20260-daybreak-a-story-for-girls:
Florence A. Sitwell wrote Daybreak, a story for girls with a gentle, devout tone. A woman reads Milton's Ode on the Morning of Christ's Nativity. She lays the book aside only as small feet gather at her door. Clear, passionless voices then blend in a Christmas hymn outside.

That calm scene sets the mood for a tale of girls and faith. Daybreak, as a title, promises new light after doubt or sorrow. Sitwell writes of home, school, and inner growth with quiet care. Young readers get a soft, uplifting story in the Victorian girls' tradition.
20424-a-son-of-the-hills:
A Son of the Hills, published in 1913, is a novel of the American hill country. Its people trace their roots back to the days of the Revolution. The book insists that the hill folk of that age were of the best stock in the land.

All who could serve their country then, the story says, did it nobly and well. Some signed the Declaration of Independence and then went home with dignity to their hills. The novel builds its tale of love and hardship on that proud heritage, and on the stubborn ways of families who answer to no one.
20475-the-two-admirals:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote The Two Admirals as a sea novel of the age of sail. Two old admirals, friends and rivals, command fleets in wartime. Cooper had served in the navy himself, and his battle scenes rest on hard knowledge of ships and seamanship.

He explains that a fleet's power is bound by its slowest ship. The efficiency of a fleet, he writes, is confined to the rate of sailing of its dullest member. Winds and currents rule every plan an admiral makes. The novel pairs that stern sea craft with a story of honor between two aging commanders.
20499-afloat-or-adventures-on-watery-tra:
Afloat, or Adventures on Watery Trails, published in 1917, is a boys' outdoor adventure. A group of friends finds a couple of weeks of vacation still ahead of them. Toby speaks for the rest: it would be a shame to let the good old summer dribble away.

One more whack at the woods and the open air is what they want. The boys take to boats and trails, camping and fishing as they go. The book belongs to the row of summer adventure stories that taught city boys to prize canoes, campfires, and self-reliance.
20557-ontario-teachers-manuals-household:
This Ontario teachers' manual aims to bring household science into rural schools across the province. Household science covered cooking, sewing, health, and the running of a home. The manual was issued to encourage its introduction and further its progress.

The need was large. The manual counts 903 urban schools against 5,697 rural schools in Ontario. Rural pupils made up nearly forty-six percent of the school population. Lessons therefore had to suit one-room schools and farm homes. The manual shows how governments of the day tried to carry modern home training into the countryside.
20633-winsome-winnie-and-other-new-nonse:
Stephen Leacock's Winsome Winnie and Other New Nonsense Novels parodies the popular fiction of his day. Leacock, the Canadian humorist, wrote each short novel as a burlesque of a familiar type. Sob stories, sea tales, and society novels all get the treatment.

The contents list alone raises a laugh. Has Anybody Here Seen Kelly? stands beside Show Me the Man Who Wore Those Boots. The Kidnapped Plumber is billed as a tale of the new timberland. Broken Barriers offers red love on a blue island. Leacock's nonsense novels remain models of the parody form.
20775-the-annals-of-the-cakchiquels:
The Annals of the Cakchiquels record the past of a Maya people of highland Guatemala. The translator worked straight from the source text, owning his own errors. He thanks the late Abbe Brasseur, a famed student of native America, for a prior draft.

Kings, wars, migrations, and rites unfold in the Cakchiquel's own telling. Few native histories from the colonial age survive in such full form. Daniel Brinton, who brought this text to English readers, prized such sources. The annals let a conquered people speak of their own past in their own order and voice.
20918-auld-licht-idylls:
Hens roost on kitchen rafters among staves and fishing rods in Auld Licht Idylls. J. M. Barrie's 1896 sketches show a thrift-driven home that took hens indoors. Meal times strew the hearth with feathers, yet the birds give little true trouble.

The Auld Lichts, a strict Scots church sect, fill Barrie's tales of Thrums life. Elders, weavers, and widows move through sketches warm with wry pity. Barrie drew on his mother's tales of old Kirriemuir for this world. The book made his early fame and still shows how deftly he mixed humour and pathos in small-town Scots life.
20963-grandmother-dear-a-book-for-boys-a:
Three children stand mute, each hiding a view on the matter at hand in Grandmother Dear. Mrs. Molesworth opens her book for boys and girls on that shy deadlock. Each waits to learn the others' minds before risking a word.

Molesworth, a queen of Victorian children's tales, centres a wise, loved grandmother here. Home trials, small faults, and mended ways fill her gentle plot. Her tales taught by example, with talk as true as life. Grandmother Dear shows her art at its best: no shouting morals, just a home whose love slowly sets young hearts right.
21109-big-game-a-story-for-girls:
Margot's brother Ron wants to be a poet, but their father insists he should take a proper job in the family firm. In Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's story for girls, Margot schemes to get Ron's poems published and change their father's mind. She learns that a poetry magazine editor holidays at a remote Scottish Highlands hotel.

She books them into the same hotel, whose landlady dislikes women guests. Fishing trips and a long walk in bad weather follow, and Margot catches pneumonia after getting Ron near the editor. Back in London the truth about her own admirer surprises her, and one of Ron's poems does reach print.
21120-the-fortunes-of-the-farrells:
Old Bernard Farrell is immensely rich, long unseen by his family, and suddenly in need of care. Visiting relatives take him in for a few days. He proposes that his nephews and nieces come stay with him in turn, so he can judge who should inherit most of his wealth.

Mrs George de Horne Vaizey gathers the young people at his house, where he proves an unpleasant host. He has made a secret early will in case of accident, and the guests burn to read it. Someone does peek at his desk, and Farrell demands the truth at his bedside. Vaizey keeps the answer back for the end.
21121-a-houseful-of-girls:
Six big girls live in a big house on a long road. The road runs out of London into Hertfordshire, in Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's Edwardian novel. Christabel, the youngest, keeps a picture of John Gilpin on her wall because his famous ride passed down that road. Each sister meets life in her own way.

Engagements made and broken set the sisters reacting differently to the same news, which is the book's chief pleasure. Friends and suitors move through the houseful of girls as they grow up. Vaizey, also known as Jessie Mansergh, writes family talk and sisterly loyalty with an easy, amused touch throughout.
21213-new-ideals-in-rural-schools:
George Herbert Betts, a professor of psychology at Cornell College in Iowa, wrote this 1913 volume in the Riverside Educational Monographs series. Rural schools, he argues, face the same problem as any school: giving the community the largest return on its investment with the least waste. He calls schools great education factories working on raw material.

Four chapters treat the rural school's problem, its social organisation, its curriculum, and its teaching. Betts wants country schools fitted to farm life rather than copied from city models. The book belongs to the country life movement that tried to keep rural communities strong through better schooling.
21223-the-carbonels:
Summer 1822 opens Charlotte M. Yonge's novel in a shabby garden. A lawyer in a green coat delivers his verdict on the Uphill people: a bad lot, good for nothing and ungrateful. The Carbonel family has just arrived to live among them. Military dress, white dresses, and a tall old gig set the period.

Yonge follows the Carbonels as newcomers in a country parish where opinion is already fixed against their poorer neighbours. The story tests that first harsh judgement against daily knowledge of the people condemned. Village talk, church life, and family duty fill the chapters. It is quieter than her historical tales, and firmly rooted in place.
21229-thistle-and-rose-a-story-for-girls:
Anna is fifteen, motherless, and about to travel alone for the first time in Amy Walton's story for girls. Her father must go abroad on business, so Anna goes to Dornton while he is away. She looks forward to meeting relatives there, including a grandfather long estranged from her father.

The old man lives quietly with no servants and works as organist at Dornton church. He is known as a fine music teacher, above all of the violin. Anna's stay opens the way between father and grandfather. Walton keeps the tale short and warm, with music, first journeys, and family healing at its heart.
21447-the-three-admirals:
Old friends rise to the top of the navy in W. H. G. Kingston's The Three Admirals. The book closes a set of four that begins with The Three Midshipmen. It shows life in the Royal Navy of the 1860s, as the three men reach flag rank.

The corvette Dragon, once led by their friend Jack Rogers, crosses the wide Pacific in one strand. She sails from Japan toward Esquimalt harbour on Vancouver's Island with dispatches. The three admirals also visit the grave of Admiral Triton on the Isle of Wight. Service, travel, and loyalty tie this long last volume together.
21608-the-dawn-of-reason-or-mental-trait:
James Weir, a doctor of medicine, argues that animals think in The Dawn of Reason, published in 1899. His full title adds Mental Traits in the Lower Animals. Weir dedicated the book to his father, no scientist, who yet followed the work with keen interest.

Chapters begin with conscious and unconscious mind, traced from jellyfish upward. The senses of touch, taste, and smell in low animals come next. Weir ties body, form, and mind into one chain of growth. His cases of clever beasts test where instinct ends and reason starts, a live question in the age after Darwin.
21666-uncle-rutherford-s-nieces-a-story-:
Joanna H. Mathews writes for girls in Uncle Rutherford's Nieces, copyrighted in 1888. A rustic seat, built by the devoted Jim, tips unless its riders balance exactly. The nieces' small dog lies at their feet as the tale opens.

Chapters promise an arithmetical puzzle, a cablegram, and food for the gods. A morning bugle, Uncle Rutherford's prize, and two peanut sellers follow. Mathews, author of the Bessie Books, fills the tale with home fun and small trials. Stokes of New York published it with original pictures, dedicated to a boy named Herbert Hunt on his birthday.
2180-in-a-hollow-of-the-hills:
A group of men on a mountain ridge talk nervously about a strange light they saw below, half joking and half afraid. Bret Harte places this tale in the California hills, where miners and wanderers live rough and rumors travel fast. The hollow beneath them holds something none of them can quite explain.

The talk turns to faces glimpsed in the dark and to the uneasy feeling that the hills keep secrets. Harte mixes rough humor with a chill of the unknown, letting the landscape do much of the storytelling. The result is a short, atmospheric piece about fear, talk, and the wild country at night.
21835-the-jew-and-american-ideals:
Anti-Semitism in America is John Spargo's target in this 1921 Harper book, written by a socialist thinker who knew the radical world from inside. Spargo begins with his own story. Five years earlier he was invited to join a rich manufacturer's plan to end the war by Christmas. His chapters then take up the alleged great Jewish conspiracy and the mystery of the Protocols.

He asks whether socialism is a Jewish plot, studies Jewish socialists and Bolshevism, and calls anti-Semitism itself a vicious force. The close pleads for the cooperation of Christian and Jew in American life. Spargo writes as a debater with documents in hand. The book is a notable early American answer to a rising poison.
21857-joyce-s-investments-a-story-for-gi:
A young heiress puts her money to work for a factory village in Joyce's Investments, a story for girls by Fannie E. Newberry, published in 1899. Joyce Lavillotte is not yet twenty-two, but she has been motherless long and knows her own mind. The factory may be the manager's province, she tells the lawyer, but the village shall be hers. Her investments are people.

Chapters follow her among the cottages, into a social house she builds, and through sorrow, a lock-up visit, and a railroad wedding. The motto on the title page praises woman's genius of charity. Newberry writes reform as a girl's adventure. Joyce's bright eyes and firm will carry a serious plan: wealth spent on neighbors, face to face.
21876-mary-louise-and-the-liberty-girls:
American girls organize for war work in Mary Louise and the Liberty Girls, by Edith Van Dyne, published in 1918. Van Dyne's preface says the tale means to show what large tasks girls can do when spurred by patriotism. Liberty Girls, she urges, can form in every city and hamlet, useful in peace as in war. Charity toward all and malice toward none is her second message.

Mary Louise takes command at a mass meeting, opens a Liberty Shop, and hunts a traitor through hints, explosions, and a black satchel. Josie, the detective's daughter, brings the professional touch. Edith Van Dyne was a pen name of L. Frank Baum, the Oz author. The book is wartime series fiction with a patriotic heart and a mystery plot.
21973-anecdotes-of-the-habits-and-instin:
Animal cleverness is collected story by story in Mrs. R. Lee's Anecdotes of the Habits and Instinct of Animals, published at London in 1852. Lee, formerly Mrs. Bowdich, had written on Africa and Australia and a memoir of Cuvier. In her preface she says the material crowded in beyond all her plans. Much was new, or stamped true by friends who drew on private stores. Harrison Weir drew the pictures, a monkey painter among them.

Dry details of science and classification are laid aside, she promises, though a loose order is kept. Dogs, elephants, birds, and beasts of every kind act out their natures in short tales. The book belongs to the age when natural history was taught by anecdote. Its charm is its faith that animals have characters worth watching.
22164-a-modern-tomboy-a-story-for-girls:
Mrs. L. T. Meade, one of the most prolific girls' writers of her age, published A Modern Tomboy as a story for girls. It opens with a new school: Mrs. Merriman and Lucy stand ready to receive their pupils. Talk runs on the new girls, and one name charms everyone in advance. "Phyllis Flower" sounds too sweet, Lucy declares, and she knows she will fall in love with its owner.

The tomboy of the title upsets the school's smooth ways. Meade builds her tales on character, discipline, and girls learning to judge each other fairly. Hundreds of her books filled school prize lists. This one shows her formula at its most characteristic.
22309-an-american-robinson-crusoe-for-am:
An American Robinson Crusoe retells the famous castaway story for American boys and girls. The catalog notes it as an adaptation, with added incidents. Its preface explains why the old tale was reshaped for schools.

The adapter drew on many years of work with the story in early grades. The book was made for use in elementary classrooms. Its aim was to teach how human progress begins and grows. A lone survivor building a life from nothing made that lesson vivid. Generations of children met Crusoe this way, in a version sized and shaped for young readers.
22363-the-country-of-the-neutrals:
The Country of the Neutrals traces a region from Champlain to Talbot, per its subtitle. Old map notes anchor much of the account. One marks where the Neutral Nation formerly stood.

West of Burlington Bay, a map calls the land good. On the Niagara River, it warns the current can hardly be ascended. At the river's mouth, Native reports put Niagara Falls above two hundred feet. Lake Ontario's south side is drawn, the writer says, pretty accurately. Such scraps rebuild a lost geography of the lakes. Readers get early Canada and New York border country through maps, names, and memory.
22396-king-arthur-s-knights-the-tales-re:
Henry Gilbert retold King Arthur's Knights for boys and girls. The tales open with King Uther Pendragon dying in London. He lies in his Roman palace, long sick with a wasting disease.

Uther gnaws his beard with wrath at his own weakness. Meanwhile, pagan Saxons ravage the broad lands of Britain. They leave smoking ruin, broken towns, and desolated villages behind. Mothers lie dead beside their children on the hearths. Churches stand pillaged and desecrated across the land. From that darkness, Arthur's story rises for young readers. Gilbert gives children the Round Table legends with their danger and wonder kept strong.
22561-tame-animals:
Tame Animals is a simple natural history book for young readers. It explains the farm and household animals children knew best. Cows come first in its plain, useful account of stock.

Cows are very useful to mankind, the book begins directly. They supply milk from which butter and cheese are made. Their young ones are called calves, young readers are told. The flesh of calves is veal, it adds without flinching. A good cow gives about fifteen or more quarts daily. Much depends on the quality of pasture she feeds upon. Such facts made the book a small farm primer. It teaches animal names, products, and care together.
22599-the-hindu-arabic-numerals:
David Eugene Smith wrote The Hindu-Arabic Numerals, a history of the number signs the world now uses. The catalog record gives no year. Smith, a noted historian of mathematics, traces how the digits traveled from India through the Arab world into European counting houses and classrooms.

The sample dives into scholarly detail, comparing letter sounds across alphabets as part of tracing how symbols and names moved between languages. Such care marks the whole book: inscriptions, manuscripts, and merchant practice all get weighed. Smith shows that a system now taken for granted was once a foreign novelty that spread slowly. Readers of math history will find a compact, learned account of our everyday numbers.
22699-pipefuls:
Christopher Morley wrote Pipefuls, a 1920 collection of his light essays, named for the pipe a reader might smoke through them. Morley, bookseller, novelist, and beloved columnist, made a career of small subjects treated with warmth. The contents list reads like a stroll through his city, from Manhattan anatomy to Brooklyn Bridge and a long lunch.

Other pieces hunt houses, ride a Fifth Avenue bus, confess the feelings of a human globule, and revisit Long Island. Morley writes as a friend talking across a desk, learned but never heavy. Pipefuls belongs to the golden age of the newspaper column, when an essay could be about nothing but a Sunday morning. It still charms readers who like their prose companionable.
2277-condensed-novels:
Bret Harte's Condensed Novels parodies the leading novelists of his day by retelling their kinds of stories in a few pages each. A Dickensian orphan, a sensation heroine, a sea yarn, and a frontier romance all appear in miniature, with each author's habits lovingly exaggerated. The book made Harte's name as a humorist before his California tales did.

The parodies work because Harte admired his targets even as he teased them, catching their rhythms and pet phrases. Read today, the volume doubles as a tour of Victorian popular fiction. It is best sampled in small doses, one burlesque at a time.
22961-nell-of-shorne-mills:
Charles Garvice sets Nell of Shorne Mills ringing with music and temper. Someone is picking out Old Folks at Home on one string, and it is intolerable, one character bursts out, while he tries to check a wretched book. Put it down, Dick, he threatens, or I will come over and smash both of you.

Garvice was among the best-selling romance writers of his age, and Nell's story follows his proven pattern. A mill village, a heroine of spirit, crossed love, and hidden circumstances fill the chapters. His dialogue snaps, his settings glow, and his plots forgive almost everyone by the end. Modern readers meet here the popular novel in its Edwardian Sunday-best, built to be borrowed, devoured, and passed along.
23301-each-man-kills:
Each Man Kills is a tale touched by the supernatural. Its narrator admits to unease about the district Maria is bound for. That country is the realm of gypsies and fortune tellers, and the birthplace of many strange legends, which makes him watchful on her behalf.

Maria, he adds, claimed to be strongly psychic. She had foretold one or two things that were probably coincidence, such as the death of their parents. Even so, those hits made an impression on him, and he is hardly a believer. Readers get a story poised between doubt and dread, where prophecy refuses to stay a parlour trick.
23312-the-education-of-american-girls:
Anna C. Brackett edited this series of essays on the education of American girls, opening with Plato's image of huntsmen surrounding justice lest it slip away. The essays argue that girls deserve schooling as serious as boys', and debate what that schooling should be.

Writers weigh health, study, and the claims of home and public life, at a moment when women's colleges were new and contested. The volume remains a key source for the history of women's education in America. The essays debate health, study, and home against public life claims. One essay warns a girl to keep faith and love till the true knight appears, rather than settle for dreary belief.
23565-red-tape-and-pigeon-hole-generals:
A citizen soldier wrote this eighteen sixty four account of red tape and pigeon hole generals, as seen from the ranks during a campaign in the Army of the Potomac. Carleton of New York printed it. The preface opens with Greek fire said to have shattered Calhoun's statue in Charleston, a sign of loyal wrath against armed treason and its sly allies.

From the ranks, the author watches generals filed away like papers, orders tangled in red tape, and brave men wasted by staff folly. The book speaks plainly, with a soldier's anger and humour, against the gap between headquarters and the field. Readers of Civil War history will find a rare, ground level voice, bitter about blunders yet loyal to the cause, and full of the small truths that official reports leave out.
23755-birds-of-the-indian-hills:
Douglas Dewar published Birds of the Indian Hills in 1915, as a companion to the bird volumes of The Fauna of British India. Much of the book had first appeared as articles in the Pioneer, the Madras Mail, the Englishman, and other papers, and Dewar thanks their editors for leave to republish.

Part One treats the birds of the Himalayas, from the habitat of Himalayan birds to the common birds of the western and eastern ranges. Later parts cover the Nilgiris and the Palni Hills, with chapters on tits at work, the Pekin-robin, black bulbuls, and the great Himalayan barbet. It is a field companion for birdwatchers in British India, written by a keen observer.
24077-textiles-for-commercial-industrial:
William H. Dooley, principal of the Lowell Industrial School in Massachusetts, wrote this textbook for students in commercial, industrial, and domestic arts schools. It also served workers in the wholesale and retail dry-goods, wool, cotton, and dressmaking trades. The revised edition, published by D. C. Heath and copyrighted in 1910, 1912, and 1914, added experiments for classroom use.

Early chapters sort fibers by origin: animal fibers such as wool, silk, and mohair; plant fibers such as cotton, flax, jute, and hemp; and mineral and remade materials. Later material covers the structure and grading of wool, sheep shearing, shipping fleeces, and the value of the wool trade. Readers learn how raw fiber is judged and prepared before it ever becomes cloth.
24263-a-hundred-anecdotes-of-animals:
Percy J. Billinghurst drew the pictures for this book of animal anecdotes, published by John Lane at the Bodley Head in London and New York in 1901. It gathers one hundred short true tales, arranged alphabetically, from Are Beasts Mere Machines and An Ass Cast Away through the Bear and Child, the Calculating Crow, and the Canine Sheep-Stealer.

Later entries include the Cat and Crows, a Conversing Parrot, the Dog of Montargis, and the Dolphin. Elephant Rope Dancing, a Faithful Companion, a Grateful Lioness, the Heroism of a Hen, and Immovable Fidelity follow. Each anecdote is brief and meant to show animal sense, courage, or affection. Readers get a charming old book of beasts, made for young naturalists.
24671-making-a-garden-of-perennials:
Published as one of the House and Garden Making Books, this short handbook shows the home-maker how to make a garden of perennials, plants that return year after year. It belongs to a series of little illustrated volumes on country and suburban home features, covering rose gardens, lawns, tennis courts, and fireplaces.

Text, pictures, and diagrams explain how to choose, plant, and tend perennials for lasting beds and borders. The book is practical rather than grand, written for amateurs with a modest garden. Gardeners today will enjoy it as a clear, old-fashioned guide, and as a picture of how Americans gardened a century ago.
2475-the-circus-boys-across-the-continen:
The Circus Boys cross the continent in this volume, winning new laurels as their show travels from coast to coast. Edgar B. P. Darlington follows the young performers through big cities and small towns, with new acts, new friends, and the grind of the road. The continent itself becomes part of the spectacle.

The book's travelogue energy keeps the series fresh, as the boys grow in skill and confidence. Young readers will enjoy the tour. It is a solid, cheerful installment. The cross-country tour takes the show through mountain passes and prairie towns.
24826-hildegarde-s-holiday-a-story-for-g:
Laura E. Richards published Hildegarde's Holiday in 1891, the second book of her Hildegarde series. Hildegarde, a lively girl heroine, spends a holiday among new friends and country scenes, with the series' usual mix of fun, kindness, and small trials. The volume went through many printings, a mark of its long favor with girl readers.

Richards writes in a warm, old-fashioned voice, and one holiday episode tells of a poor wandering woman, called the Queen, who finds care and work spinning and trimming a house with flowers. The book suits young readers who like gentle stories of friendship, home, and helping others.
25017-a-son-of-the-immortals:
Louis Tracy's 1909 romance, published by Edward J. Clode with illustrations by Howard Chandler Christy, follows Joan and Alec through fortune tellers, the Orient Express, and a White City toward a storm over a Danubian kingdom. Chapter titles trace the arc: Joan goes into society, becomes the victim of circumstances, decides, and flees, while Felix surmounts difficulties and a broken treaty looms. The frontispiece shows Alec carrying his fair burden to cheers from a crowd.

Midway, Joan learns that Prince and Princess Michael Delgrado travel the same road, and that Alec truly belongs to his mother, for all her weak chin and air of resignation. Dismayed, she asks Felix why he brought her there, and he answers that their lives run in grooves, furrows converging on the Danube like ships foredoomed to collision. The novel mixes Ruritanian adventure with society romance.
25055-the-odes-of-casimire-translated-by:
The Odes of Casimire presents the Latin odes of Mathias Casimir Sarbiewski, a seventeenth-century Polish Jesuit poet, in the English version made by G. Hils in 1646. The Augustan Reprint Society reissued that translation in 1953 with an introduction by Maren-Sofie Roestvig, printing Latin and English side by side.

Sarbiewski, often called the Polish Horace, writes short lyrics on virtue, fame, envy, fortune, and the quiet life. Hils renders them in the vigorous, slightly rough English of the Civil War era. The volume serves both as poetry and as a record of how an earlier age heard a celebrated continental Latin poet.
25308-eugenics-and-other-evils:
G. K. Chesterton's Eugenics and Other Evils, published by Cassell in 1922, attacks the eugenics movement with wit and moral anger. Chesterton notes that most of his preliminary notes were written before the war, when eugenic babies sprawled across illustrated papers and Shaw praised breeding men like cart-horses.

He argues that eugenics treats human beings as livestock and asks citizens to give their bodies for an experiment whose end even the experimenter does not know. A closing summary calls the whole theory false. Chesterton's essays remain a classic defense of human dignity against scientific planning.
25428-anecdotes-of-animals:
Anecdotes of Animals, published by McLoughlin Brothers of New York with pictures by Percy J. Billinghurst, collects short true stories of beasts. Its alphabetical contents run from amusing mimics and animal concerts to faithful companions, grateful lions, and dogs that steal sheep.

Tales include the Dog of Montargis, an elephant's revenge and rope dancing, mice as sailors, and a monkey versus a snake. A horse and a greyhound race four miles head to head, the mare winning by a head, while a watch dog foils a thief in Cellini's shop. The book suits young naturalists and animal lovers alike.
25568-domesticated-animals:
Nathaniel Southgate Shaler, dean of Harvard's Lawrence Scientific School, writes this illustrated study of domesticated animals and their relation to man and his advance in civilisation. Scribner published it in 1908 with a 1895 copyright. An African elephant fronts the book.

Chapters treat the dog first, from ancestry and early uses through shepherd dogs and breeding evils. Shaler compares dog emotions with man's, and dogs with cats for intelligence and place beside man. The horse chapter follows the dog, judging value by strength and service. Shaler asks how taming changed both animals and people, and what future development each species might show under human care.
25630-dorothy-s-travels:
Evelyn Raymond writes Dorothy's Travels, published in New York in 1908 with pictures by S. Schneider. A front picture shows a gallant helper lifting Molly up, setting the friendly tone of a girls' travel story.

Dorothy sails down the Hudson, joins a race, goes adrift in the great city, and boards the Prince for moonlight and mist on the sea. Safe on shore, she meets a bashful bugler, an oxomobile and a sailboat, and a Digby chicken, before Evangeline land, sightseeing under difficulties, and journeys ending in welcome at camp. Chatterton-Peck held the 1908 copyright.
25661-duffels:
Edward Eggleston, author of The Hoosier Schoolmaster and Roxy, writes Duffels, published in New York by Appleton in 1893. His preface recalls Mrs. Anne Grant of Laggan, who spent part of her childhood in Albany, then a town given to traffic with Native peoples.

Grant described a young American Dutch trader setting out up the Mohawk in a canoe, paddling hard and carrying round rifts and falls toward tribes beyond the Six Nations. The outfit of that young bushloper gives Eggleston his subject: frontier trade, travel, and the rough gear of early American life.
25822-illustrated-science-for-boys-and-g:
Printed in Boston in 1881 by D. Lothrop and Company, this book explains how everyday things are made and done, in short pieces aimed at young readers. A visit to a newspaper office shows news gathered, type set, and pages printed. Other chapters follow umbrellas, combs, gas works, light houses, dishes, shoes, and logs on their way to the mill.

The pieces mix plain facts with small scenes of boys and girls at work and play, such as Paul learning the comb trade and a lad racing a storm. Pictures run through the book, from the Tribune building at night to a proof sheet marked with takes. Montana beavers, winter birds, and archery round out a set meant to feed a child's wonder at the made world.
25893-beatrice-leigh-at-college-a-story-:
Julia A. Schwartz sends Beatrice Leigh to college in this 1907 tale for girls, opening with a song calendar of the four seasons of college days. Autumn sings of bright sunshine and glad beginnings, winter of cozy corners and sleighs, April of bird notes and woodland ways, and June of sad leave takings. The verses set the tone for a year of study, friendship, and fun.

Bea finds a roommate, meets Robbie Belle, and learns the ropes of class life, from daily themes in sophomore English to boat rides where manners are taught by the bank. Miss Anglin, her teacher, groans at gossip dressed as character study and sets a page a day of writing. Through frolic and work, Bea grows steadier, and the book closes the college year with warm praise for its memories.
25948-fifty-two-stories-for-girls:
Alfred H. Miles edits fifty two stories for girls, printed by Appleton in 1912, with a wide table of authors. Evelyn Everett Green, Sarah Doudney, Margaret Watson, Nellie Holderness, Jennie Chappell, Gordon Stables, and many more supply tales of school and home. An index sorts them by subject, from Gloria Dene's schoolfellows to a night on the road and a missing letter.

One tale sails a fairy boat with purple sails that fold like a resting bird's wings, grounding soft on a mossy bank. An old man lifts a little girl ashore to an island of bright flowers and ripe fruit. The king's tragedy, pictured up front, hints at graver tales within. The set gives a girl reader a story a week, mixing school fun, kindness, and mild peril.
26085-robin-redbreast-a-story-for-girls:
Mrs. Molesworth's story for girls centers on a house in a lane, an old lady, and Jacinth. Bessie and Margaret Harper, gentlefolk in every sense, are really very poor, and their parents can no longer afford their school fees, a truth Jacinth thinks useless to mention.

Chapters move through a letter and discussion, an invitation, delicate ground, the Indian mail, and Lady Myrtle's intentions, toward a bitter disappointment and a courageous plea. Frances wonders why the Harper girls may leave school, too unpractical to guess the money trouble. The tale closes with honesty weighed in two degrees and Uncle Marmy's gates.
26365-intestinal-ills:
Alcinous B. Jamison, a New York doctor, argues in this book that many chronic ills begin in the bowel. Constipation, indigestion, diarrhea, piles, anemia, and wasting, he claims, follow when waste matter is left standing in the intestinal canal and its poisons are taken up into the body. The chapters first appeared in Health, a monthly magazine, and were revised for book form.

Jamison opens with a verse tale of a fair figure whose health fails as waste lies neglected within. He then describes, in plain terms, how food moves through the gut's pools and bends, and how he believes delay breeds bacteria and decay. Readers should treat his claims as period medicine, not current advice, since the book dates from 1901.
27114-ancient-states-and-empires-for-col:
John Lord's Ancient States and Empires, for colleges and schools, published by Scribner in 1869, surveys the ancient world in textbook form. Book One covers the ancient Oriental nations, from the antediluvian world and the patriarchs through Egypt, the Jews, and the empires of Chaldea, Assyria, Media, and Persia.

Book Two turns to the Grecian states, from geography and legends through the Persian War, the age of Pericles, and the Peloponnesian War. Later chapters carry Rome from Jugurtha and Marius through Mithridates, Sulla, and the civil wars between Caesar and Pompey.
27272-roy-blakeley-s-camp-on-wheels:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh's Roy Blakeley's Camp on Wheels, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1920 with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America, sends Roy's patrol rolling. Chapters run from Brewster's Center and the housing problem through a wild night to Skiddyunk, labor troubles, and sandwiches.

A wide-awake lot, somewhere in America, and the big B also appear among the chapter titles. A little dog scoots between Pee-wee's legs on the frontispiece, Scout Harris appears, and the patrol meets the cheerful idiot. Grace Bentley invites them by boat for dinner tomorrow, promising pie, in Fitzhugh's breezy scout tale of camp, wheels, and good appetites.
27621-how-i-write-my-novels:
Mrs. Hungerford, Margaret Wolfe Hamilton, wrote this short essay on how she writes her novels, taken from her An Anxious Moment. She contrasts her own way with writers who sit down in cold blood to cudgel a plot from their brains.

Happy people, she calls those deliberate plotters, with their powers of concentration and belief in themselves. As for herself, she lies awake at night longing for inspirations that are slow to come. When one comes, the whole story lies open before her in a flash, a delicate diorama with a beginning and an end. The dressing of the story afterwards is simple enough.
27908-fix-bay-nets-the-regiment-in-the-h:
George Manville Fenn wrote Fix Bay'nets, the regiment in the hills, opening with Her Majesty's 404th Fusiliers marching easy up a Himalayan pass. The so-called road is a stony shelf of rock, full of cracks and holes, polished here and there by ancient avalanches of ice or stones.

The regiment winds upward with mules, ambulance, and baggage-guard, dwarfed beneath deodar cedars a hundred feet tall, while Bill Gedge and his East End Cockney comrades joke through the climb. Fenn's tale of soldiering on India's northwest frontier mixes hardship, humor, and mountain scenery.
27923-betty-leicester-a-story-for-girls:
Sarah Orne Jewett wrote Betty Leicester, a story for girls, published by Houghton Mifflin with copyrights in 1889 and 1917. The novel opens at Young's Hotel in Boston on a pleasant June morning, where two persons sit at breakfast near an open window, looking out at the courthouse walls.

Chapters follow Betty as far as Riverport, on a packet boat, at Tideshead and Becky's house, in a garden tea, and in an out-of-door club, through letters and reflections. Jewett's gentle, observant story of a girl's summer among Maine people shows the local-color writing that made her famous.
27933-forest-neighbors-life-stories-of-w:
William Davenport Hulbert wrote Forest Neighbors, life stories of wild animals, published by Doubleday, Page in 1914 after copyrights in 1900 to 1902, and dedicated to his sister Katharine Grace Hulbert. The introduction recalls his father finding a lovely little lake in the woods of northern Michigan.

Life stories follow a beaver, the king of the trout stream, a Canada lynx, a porcupine, a loon, and a glimmerglass buck, with illustrations of dams, nesting grounds, and hunts. Hulbert writes natural history as biography, and the book belongs with Seton and other early wildlife storytellers.
28037-in-doublet-and-hose-a-story-for-gi:
Lucy Foster Madison's In Doublet and Hose, published in Philadelphia in 1904, is a girls' adventure set in Tudor England. Its heroine, Francis Stafford, dresses as a page and serves in great houses during the reigns of Mary and Elizabeth. Clyde O. Deland supplied the pictures.

Francis carries letters, meets Anthony Babington, faces the queen's anger, and at last lands in the Tower of London. A duel, an escape, and service against the Armada test her nerve and loyalty. The novel mixes court intrigue with a girl's struggle to be judged on skill, not on sex, and ends with pardon and happiness.
28406-why-i-believe-in-scouting-for-girl:
Mary Roberts Rinehart wrote Why I Believe in Scouting for Girls, series number ten from Girl Scouts National Headquarters, New York, as a plea for the movement. Rinehart argues that girls are great idealists, dreaming of happiness, not success, and eager for a cause and a leader. Between babyhood and womanhood, she says, a girl belongs nowhere in social life, and grows moody, dreamy, and idle.

Scouting, Rinehart holds, gives girls clubs, sports, meeting places, and work worthy of their loyalty and unselfish effort. The pamphlet, from Harvard's Women Working collection, speaks to parents and leaders. It offers a clear, early case for Girl Scouting.
28463-not-like-other-girls:
