Rosa N. Carey's Not Like Other Girls opens with five-o'clock tea, a great institution in the town of Oldfield. Ladies gather in pleasant drawing-rooms, sip highly-scented Pekoe from dainty china, and gossip, despite Dr. Weatherby's protests against mild feminine dram-drinking.

Chapters follow Dick, Phillis, Nan, Laddie, and their neighbours through fetes, visits to the Friary and the White House, a van in the Braidwood Road, and a mysterious stranger. Carey writes a long, warm domestic novel of girls growing up, falling in love, and finding their own way in a close-knit town.
28501-construction-work-for-rural-and-el:
Virginia McGaw's Construction Work for Rural and Elementary Schools, copyrighted in 1909, is a teacher's manual for handwork in small schools. McGaw taught in the elementary school of Baltimore, and her book moves step by step from the simplest tasks to harder ones.

Sections cover cord construction, with knots, chains, bags, and miniature hammocks; paper construction, with windmills, trays, boxes, and bound books; and wood construction, with puzzles, plant labels, and kite-string winders. Basketry in reed and raffia follows, with a school garden section to close. The book shows how manual training was taught to children a century ago.
28538-a-bookful-of-girls:
Anna Fuller's A Bookful of Girls, copyrighted in 1905, collects six stories about young women, illustrated by the Knickerbocker Press. The contents run from Blythe Halliday's Voyage through Artful Madge, The Ideas of Polly, Nannie's Theatre Party, Olivia's Sun-Dial, and Bagging a Grandfather.

Blythe's voyage opens aboard the steamer Lorelei past the Azores. There her mother explains that an old Scotch nurse named the baby a blythe lassie when she was not yet three days old. Fuller writes with humour and warmth about girls finding their way in travel, friendship, theatre, and family. The collection is a pleasant example of American girls' fiction of its day.
28703-aunt-fanny-s-story-book-for-little:
Aunt Fanny's Story-Book, published by D. Appleton and Company of New York in 1853, comes from a very little lady with many nephews and nieces. Children loved her as the best little auntie, just the right size for play and storytelling. She told them of George Washington and Monsieur Pop, and made them laugh over the Dutchman Hansansvanansvananderdansvaniedeneidendiesandeusan.

At a niece's urging she wrote the stories down, and here they are, with more promised next year if liked. The Christmas Party leads, with seven Percy grandchildren, a frosty day, icicles, turkeys, dinner, and a dance. The Spider, the Three Bears, the May Queen, the Apple Dumpling, and the Boys' School follow. Young readers get gentle tales with morals.
29067-hurlbut-s-bible-lessons-for-boys-a:
Reverend Jesse Lyman Hurlbut prepared this lesson book in 1907 for use at home, in Sunday school, and in church. It offers a complete course of Bible study in question-and-answer form, designed to carry a student through the Old Testament in a first year and the New Testament in a second year.

Hurlbut shaped the lessons for children from six to sixteen, noting that lessons suited to older children fail younger ones. The Old Testament half runs from Adam to the kingdoms of Israel and Judah; the New Testament half tells the story of Jesus and the early church. Readers get a structured, plain-spoken course that once guided a full two years of young people's Bible study.
29119-they-of-the-high-trails:
Hamlin Garland wrote They of the High Trails, published by Harper and Brothers in New York and London, with copyrights from 1902 to 1916. The volume lists Garland's other books, from Main-Travelled Roads and Rose of Dutcher's Coolly to The Captain of the Gray-Horse Troop and Boy Life on the Prairie. A frontispiece shows Alice saying take me back inside, I feel cold here, on page 220.

Garland writes of mountain folk and high trails with the realism that made his prairie books famous. The stories follow people who live close to rough country, with its beauty and its hardship. Readers get a strong collection of western tales, told plainly and humanely, by a writer who knew the land he described.
29171-the-carroll-girls:
Mabel Quiller-Couch wrote this novel about the Carroll family. It opens in a neglected garden where butterflies drift over rank grass and barren currant bushes. Penelope lies lazy and happy in the coarse grass. She has never known the garden any other way, except when a visitor such as Aunt Julia is expected and a gardener is paid to tidy up.

Around Penelope stand her mother, her sister Lydia, and the household's tight money, which makes even a shilling for gardening a matter of argument. Quiller-Couch builds the story from such domestic details: a family's genteel poverty, its pride, and its daughters' daily lives. Readers get a gentle English family novel, observant about money, manners, and young women making their way.
2932-on-the-relations-of-man-to-the-lowe:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote On the Relations of Man to the Lower Animals to settle humanity's place in nature. He opens with Linnaeus on how hard it is to believe that a noble court lady and a wild forest man share one species. Then he calls the question of questions the problem underlying all others. The essay compares human anatomy with apes, bone by bone.

Huxley notes that the baboon's upper molars differ in pattern from the gorilla's, its canines run longer and more knife-like, and its lower premolar is specially modified. Passing to New World apes brings a change of greater importance. The essay argues from structure that humans belong with the primates, and it remains a classic of comparative anatomy.
29559-they-twinkled-like-jewels:
Philip Jose Farmer's short tale opens with Jack Crane lying all morning in a vacant lot, still as a heap of rags, listening for Bohas agents who never come. Crane never learned the nice man's name until too late to act on it. A housewife's dried rolls quiet the tiger in his belly, which crouches and licks its chops.

Farmer, praised in the headnote as a young man of Peoria whose novel The Lovers won instant acclaim, writes here of hunger, hiding, and strange gifts. The jewels of the title twinkle with menace as well as beauty. Fans of Farmer will enjoy a vivid, offbeat tale of a drifter and a fate he cannot name.
29628-the-golden-woman-a-story-of-the-mo:
Ridgwell Cullum's Golden Woman, a story of the Montana hills, was printed by A. L. Burt Company of New York by arrangement with George W. Jacobs, with copyright in 1913 and publication in February 1916. An elderly woman looks up from a crystal globe as horses' hoofs clatter up to the veranda. Chapters follow Aunt Mercy, a telephone call, the pariah, two men of the wilderness, and the steeps of life.

Cullum, author of The Way of the Strong and The Trail of the Axe, writes a western romance of love, outcasts, and mountain hardship. The golden woman of the title stands at its heart. Readers of classic westerns will find a sturdy, colorful tale of Montana hills and hearts.
29683-the-little-girl-lost-a-tale-for-li:
Eleanor Raper wrote this short tale for little girls, printed in London in 1902 as number fourteen of the Dumpy Books for Children. The series was a set of small cloth books for young readers, each with its own tale and pictures, and this one takes a lost little girl as its theme. The telling is short and plain, sized for a child to hear or read in one sitting.

Raper keeps the focus on the girl herself: where she has strayed, whom she meets, and how she finds her way back to safety. The book's charm lies in its small scale and kind tone, with no long moral tacked on. It stands as a neat sample of Edwardian books made just for small children.
29816-the-industries-of-animals:
Frederic Houssay wrote this study of animal work for the Contemporary Science Series, edited by Havelock Ellis. The London edition of 1893, with 44 pictures, was revised and enlarged with the author's help. Houssay treats animal life as a set of trades: hunting, fishing, war, defense, and the storing of food. He compares hunters of many kinds, from ambush hunters to coursers and users of projectiles.

Later chapters treat flight, feint, sentinels, barns and stores, and the farming ants that keep aphids as stock. Slavery among ants gets its own stark section. The pictures, most drawn from Brehm's great work on animal life, help the plain text. The book is an early, readable account of how beasts work, plan, and guard their own.
29851-dwellers-in-the-hills:
Melville Davisson Post published Dwellers in the Hills in 1901, with G. P. Putnam's Sons. The tale opens in the October land, where a boy sits on the ground with the bridle rein of El Mahdi over his arm. He hammers a copper rivet into a broken stirrup strap while Jud swings a great driving whip down the ridge. The sorrel horse stands calm through the lash play.

Twenty-one chapters follow hill folk and their ways: Hawk Rufe, the waggon-maker, Christian the blacksmith, and the wardens of the river. A petticoat and a pretender, the six hundred, and the art of going to ruin give the tale its color. Post writes the hills with affection and a storyteller's ear. The book is a warm chronicle of a boy's world among strong, plain people.
29862-the-old-countess-or-the-two-propos:
Ann S. Stephens published The Old Countess, or The Two Proposals, in Philadelphia in 1873, entered for copyright that year. It is a sequel to her Lord Hope's Choice. Love lights in two hearts in the first chapter, and Clara appeals to her stepmother in the second. A lovers' quarrel, an Italian teacher, and a mother and daughter in opposition follow.

An operatic supper, a first performance, and two foster-children meeting carry the middle of the tale. The old countess herself, her servant, and the earl's return shape the close, with a stormy night and a sunny morning. Stephens writes in the full, sentimental style of her popular novels. The book is a domestic romance of rank, kin, and two proposals that must both be weighed.
30037-in-the-shadow-of-the-hills:
George C. Shedd sets an adventure novel in rough mountain country east of the Torquilla Range, where the Burntwood River runs out of a gorge into hostile land. Rival claims, a secret conference, a shot in the dark, and an old deposition drive the plot through 33 chapters. Janet Hosmer, Mary, Weir, and Vorse take sides in a feud over land and power. An adobe house, a night watch, and a final challenge all figure before the tale closes.

Copyright in 1919 by the Macaulay Company, the novel moves like a western serial, with each chapter adding a new threat or a new ally. Shedd, already known for mystery and romance titles, keeps the focus on action and on who holds a claim by right of possession. The result is a swift period adventure for readers who like land feuds, masked plots, and a hard-won victory.
30328-a-book-of-cheerful-cats-and-other-:
J. G. Francis offers A Book of Cheerful Cats and Other Animated Animals, published by the Century Company in New York, under copyright by Elsie W. Francis. Some fun with a toy spider, the tea-party, a musical evening, the giraffe ride, a family, and a parent follow, with a case of highway robbery.

They did not have a penny, the reformed lion, quits, the genial grimalkin, euchred, and the bicycle ride carry the fun onward. A study of a hedgehog stealing an apple, the lion in the barber-shop, the bald eagle and the barber, and the spring curtain follow. It is a perfect picnic day, a Tam o' Shanter dog, the donkey and his company, late, and pictures with a moral for boys and dogs follow. The joyful owl, a queer barber-shop, the cat and the cream, and the story of the catnip ball close the contents.
30720-happy-days-for-boys-and-girls:
Happy Days for Boys and Girls, copyrighted in 1877 by Horace B. Fuller and Porter and Coates of Philadelphia, gathers children's prose and verse with one hundred thirty-six illustrations. Contributors include Louisa M. Alcott, Alice and Phoebe Cary, C. A. Stephens, Mary N. Prescott, William M. Thayer, and F. Cheseboro.

Contents in prose open with Alcott's Accident, an adventure in the life of Salvator Rosa, J. G. Wood on the African elephant, an animal in armor, and Aunt Thankful. Barn swallows, birds, bitters, books and reading, Bruin at a maple-sugar party, and camels follow. The volume offers a rich Victorian miscellany for young readers, mixing nature, adventure, and moral tales.
30999-a-new-chipmunk-genus-eutamias-from:
John A. White wrote this short paper on a new chipmunk from the Black Hills. It was published in the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, volume 5, number 19, pages 259 to 262, on April 10, 1952. Material examined from the Great Plains and eastern Rocky Mountains included animals from northeastern Wyoming and South Dakota that Howell, in 1929, had assigned to Eutamias minimus borealis. They belong to a heretofore unnamed subspecies.

White names and describes it as Eutamias minimus silvaticus, new subspecies, with a diagnosis noting large size. The type is a female adult, skull and skin, number 20050, taken three miles northwest of Sundance at 5,900 feet in Crook County, Wyoming, on July 4, 1947, by H. W. Setzer. Its range is the Bear Lodge Mountains of northeastern Wyoming and the Black Hills of South Dakota. It is a precise piece of mammal taxonomy.
31092-hero-stories-from-american-history:
Albert F. Blaisdell and Francis K. Ball's 1903 schoolbook, published by Ginn, retells American history as fourteen hero stories for elementary pupils. The hero of Vincennes opens, followed by a midwinter campaign, palmetto logs in defense, a patriot spy, and the greatest patriot. A midnight surprise, the defeat of the red dragoons, a teamster turned major general, the final victory, and the crisis follow.

Later chapters add a daring exploit, Old Ironsides, Old Hickory's Christmas, and a hero's welcome, with review questions, a pronunciation guide, and reference lists to aid teachers. Written in clear, stirring prose, the book aimed to give young Americans memorable deeds rather than dry dates, and it still reads as a period piece of patriotic schooling.
31136-distribution-of-some-nebraskan-mam:
J. Knox Jones Jr.'s 1954 paper puts on record new distribution notes for several Nebraska mammals, written because military service was about to interrupt his studies. Most records come from specimens he and other University of Kansas Museum collectors had recently taken, with further material borrowed from museums in Washington, Hastings, Lincoln, California, and Michigan.

Among the accounts is a cinereous shrew trapped in April 1952 among rocks by an old railroad fill near Octavia, with measurements in millimeters and colors after Ridgway's standards. Short and factual, the paper helps later workers map where each species actually occurred, county by county, across Nebraska.
31250-old-plymouth-trails:
Winthrop Packard's 1920 book, published by Small, Maynard in Boston, walks the old trails of Plymouth and Cape Cod in twenty-six chapters. From the Mayflower at Plymouth and Forefathers' Day through Plymouth mayflowers, singing pines, Nantucket in April, and footing it across the Cape, Packard mixes Pilgrim history with nature writing. His walk also takes in wild apple trees, salt marshes, and voices of the brookside.

Later chapters add ghosts of the northeaster, Jotham stories, mystical pastures, white pine groves, and a November pasture. They also bring red cedar lore, winter sports, and yule fires, all illustrated with views of the coast and woods. Opening with a nod to Felicia Hemans's poem on the Pilgrim landing, the book is a gentle literary pilgrimage for walkers.
31458-additional-records-and-extensions-:
Stephen D. Durrant, M. Raymond Lee, and Richard M. Hansen wrote this University of Kansas Museum of Natural History paper, volume nine, number two, dated December 10, 1955. It reports additional records and extensions of known ranges of mammals from Utah, in pages 69 to 80. The Museum of Zoology at the University of Utah held about 5,000 specimens beyond those available to Durrant for his 1952 account of the mammals of Utah.

The paper adds new localities and range limits for species already known, and records others in places where they had not been reported before. Such short papers are the working notes of mammalogy: careful, specimen-based, and meant for other specialists. For readers of natural history, it shows how knowledge of a state's fauna grows, one specimen and one county at a time.
31615-chicago-s-black-traffic-in-white-g:
Mrs. Jean Turner-Zimmermann, M.D., president of the Chicago Rescue Mission and Woman's Shelter, wrote Chicago's Black Traffic in White Girls as an illustrated article on the great white slave question, in the period's own term. The book reports on the trafficking of girls and young women in Chicago, drawn from rescue-mission work with its victims. It names the trade plainly and treats it as a city-wide evil.

Turner-Zimmermann writes as a physician and a rescue worker, not as a distant observer, and her account mixes case material with a call for action. The book belongs to the early twentieth-century campaign against commercialized vice, and it shows how reformers framed the traffic for a public they hoped to move.
31687-stories-of-the-foot-hills:
Margaret Collier Graham's 1895 story collection, published in Boston and New York by Houghton, Mifflin and Company, is set in the California foot-hills. Its seven stories include The Withrow Water Right, Alex Randall's Conversion, Idy, The Complicity of Enoch Embody, Em, Colonel Bob Jarvis, and Brice.

The opening tale follows Lysander Sproul driving dun-colored mules toward the mesa, past a winery crowning a low hill, as neighbors scheme over water and advantage. Readers get regional fiction of farms, small towns, and stubborn characters, told with local speech and a sharp eye for country disputes.
3228-poems-of-progress-and-new-thought-p:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox joins two of her verse collections in this 1913 Gay and Hancock volume. Poems of Progress and New Thought Pastels share the book, and Wilcox guards the text fiercely. Any edition of her poems published in England by another firm, she warns, is pirated and not authentic. Her note is dated 12 April 1910.

The poems preach the new thought doctrines of their day: mind over circumstance, courage over complaint, and progress through right thinking. Wilcox writes in plain, musical lines meant to be read aloud and remembered. Earnest, tuneful, and sure of better days, the verse filled parlors that wanted hope set to music.
3248-the-sky-pilot-a-tale-of-the-foothil:
Ralph Connor prefaces this foothill tale with a measure of a man's power to help his brother. That measure, he writes, is the love in his heart and his faith that good will win at last. With such love, seeking not its own, and such faith gripping the heart of things, a man may meet many fortunes, but not defeat. The story follows the people of the Foothill Country.

Those men left homes of comfort, often of luxury, for adventurous spirit and open ground. A sky pilot, a minister to the hills, becomes their center. Connor writes of rough camps made gentler by faith and friendship. Hard country, hard men, and a preacher who earns his hearing: that is Connor's foothill gospel in one line.
3257-new-thought-pastels:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox published these New Thought pastels in 1906 with Elizabeth Towne of Holyoke, Massachusetts. The index reads like a creed in miniature: a dialogue, the weed, strength, affirm, the chosen, and the nameless. The word, assistance, credulity, and consciousness follow, with the structure, our souls, the law, and knowledge.

Give, perfection, fear, and the way continue the sequence, toward understood and his mansion. Wilcox writes short, plain verses for readers of the new thought movement, which taught mind over circumstance. Small poems for daily pondering, confident that thought shapes life: the new thought creed in miniature.
32576-a-novelist-on-novels:
W. L. George's Novelist on Novels, published in London in 1918, gathers chapters written in varying moods on the modern novel and its treatment by the public. George is author of A Bed of Roses, The City of Night, and The Intelligence of Woman. He notes that chapters on Falstaff, the Esperanto of art, and the twilight of genius, though unrelated to the novel, belong artistically with the rest or affect the fiction form. Half the book had not before been published in Great Britain.

Contents include a deceptive dedication, a litany of the novelist, who is the man, and three young novelists: D. H. Lawrence, Amber Reeves, and Sheila Kaye-Smith. Form and the novel follows, with other essays on craft, taste, and fame. George writes with wit and candour about writing, reading, and the business of books, for readers who enjoy literary criticism from a working novelist.
32596-the-revolt-of-the-angels:
Anatole France's The Revolt of the Angels, translated by Mrs. Wilfrid Jackson and printed in London and New York in 1924, begins with the d'Esparvieu family beneath the shadow of St. Sulpice. From 1825 to 1857 Alexandre Bussart d'Esparvieu, a great man of the family, lived in their austere mansion, leaving an incomplete essay on civil and religious institutions.

His heirs carry the family through army service, country life, law, and service to the persecuted Church. Some treat religion as an instrument of government, and others practice it with sincere devotion. The novel moves from that family chronicle toward the revolt its title promises, testing faith, authority, and order.
326-steep-trails:
John Muir gathers twenty-four field pieces in this volume, written across nearly thirty years of western travel. The sketches first ran as letters and short articles, then were set in order by place and date. They range from California and Utah to Nevada, Oregon, Washington, and the Grand Canyon.

Muir walks Mount Shasta, bathes in Salt Lake, notes Mormon lilies, and climbs Mount Rainier in vivid, close detail. He watches forests, farms, dead mining towns, and river country with a naturalist's care. The book keeps the fresh feel of notes made on the trail, and it shows why Muir became a voice for wild land.
32600-history-of-the-reign-of-philip-the:
William H. Prescott writes the history of Philip II of Spain, drawing on archives newly opened to scholars, above all Simancas, where Spain's secrets had long lain sealed. These first two volumes cover a reign that shaped Europe in the latter half of the sixteenth century.

Prescott sets Philip at the head of those defending the old Church as Reformation doctrines shook Christendom, and he follows Spanish policy far beyond Spain itself. The preface weighs earlier writers and defends a history built on documents, not on cheap and handy sources.
32632-the-spy-condensed-for-use-in-schoo:
J. Fenimore Cooper's The Spy, condensed for use in schools with an introduction and explanatory notes, was published in New York and New Orleans in 1898. Its introduction recalls Cooper, born in Burlington, New Jersey, in 1789, raised at Cooperstown, and trained as a navy midshipman and lieutenant before he turned to novels.

The Spy appeared in 1821, only the author's second work, and won readers on both sides of the Atlantic, translated into several European languages. Styled the Walter Scott of America, Cooper drew on the patriot Revolution for his subject, and this school edition keeps the tale within reach of young readers.
32669-the-story-of-john-wesley-told-to-b:
Marianne Kirlew tells the story of John Wesley for boys and girls, with a preface by Dinsdale T. Young dated Manchester, June 1895. Young calls Wesley a great national figure, above mere party, and urges young readers to know his life and work.

Thirty-nine chapters follow Jacky Wesley from boyhood through open-air preaching at Kingswood, where crowds grew from two hundred to twenty thousand. Later scenes count nineteen hundred and fifty London members and record the first Methodist Conference at the Foundry in June 1744, with four clergy and four helpers.
32759-red-nails:
Robert E. Howard tells a Conan tale of a barbarian swordsman, a woman pirate, and a strange roofed city, first published in Weird Tales. Valeria of the Red Brotherhood rides into a somber forest in silk breeches, flaring boots, and a crimson satin band, a straight sword on one hip and a dirk on the other.

She meets Conan, and together they enter a city of devils, where warring factions guard a great bronze door. Techotl guides them past a living skull that housed the brain of a king of magicians. Valeria fights her way through corridors of screams and swords, determined to reach Conan's room and break out of the city alive.
32878-thy-rocks-and-rills:
Robert Ernest Gilbert sets an animal lover and a man-hating bull on a collision course, in a story from If Worlds of Science Fiction of September 1953. M. Stonecypher lifts his square-brimmed reed hat, fielding Dan, a hobbyist who wants a puppy for a dogfight. Stonecypher refuses: the pup is not for sale for that purpose. A bellow from the paddock announces Moe, his bull.

Moe's crest of red and blue-black hair looks purple, and Dan gasps that the bull belongs in the ring. The Manly Age around them prizes duels and blood sport. Catriona stands apart from its standard. On Dependence Day, Moe meets the ring: Neel dies on the horns, Tomas falls with a cape pinned to his chest, and a lancer on a blindfolded horse charges next. Man and bull march to inevitably similar destinies.
32935-what-a-man-wills:
Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's novel opens at the dying of the year in an old country manor. There, New Year guests have danced, sung, and stood hand in hand listening to church bells. Motors hoot and snort as visitors leave. Around the log fire eleven guests still lingered: the hosts, four men, and five young women, the women near twenty-four or five and the men somewhat older.

What a man wills, the title suggests, is tested against what others want and what life allows. Vaizey follows her house party through love, choice, and the quiet pressures of family and fortune. The novel is a domestic tale with a warm, observant eye, fond of its young people while it watches them learn that will alone does not settle a life. It reads as an easy, well-mannered romance of its period.
33282-the-boy-pilot-of-the-lakes-or-nat-:
Frank V. Webster's boys' book follows Nat Morton, a young pilot on the lakes, through a string of perils on water and shore. The story opens with a fall into the water and moves through storms, wrecks, and rivals, as Nat learns to handle a boat and to stand by his friends. Webster, known for many boys' tales, writes in a plain, lively style for young readers.

The book pairs lake lore with moral lessons: courage, care, and fair play matter as much as skill at the wheel. Its short chapters and clear action keep the pace brisk. For readers who enjoy old-fashioned adventure on inland waters, Nat Morton's perils offer a wholesome, fast-moving tale of a boy earning his place as a pilot.
33528-with-edge-tools:
Hobart Chatfield Taylor's With Edge Tools, published in Chicago in 1891, is a novel of society, duel, and ambition. Its contents move from the Staten Club and cross fire to two women, an opera box, a challenge, Spanish castles, and patricians, with gathering clouds and Oakhurst to follow. Taylor writes of a world where sharp tools, literal and social, cut deep.

The novel's appeal lies in its brisk, dramatic scenes of high life, where honor, love, and rivalry drive the plot. Its tone is lively and popular, suited to readers who enjoy society fiction with a edge. For fans of late Victorian American novels, With Edge Tools offers a bright, well-plotted tale of clubs, challenges, and consequences.
33654-the-old-english-herbals:
Eleanour Sinclair Rohde traces the history of English herbals in this 1922 Longmans volume. Rohde, author of A Garden of Herbs, follows herbal knowledge from Anglo-Saxon manuscripts through medieval and early modern books, showing how plants were described, pictured, and used.

Her epigraph from Bartholomaeus Anglicus praises the lily, white-flowered without and golden within. The book combines botanical history with social history, treating herbals as records of medicine, gardening, folklore, and art. Gardeners, historians of medicine, and lovers of old books will find a learned, readable guide to a tradition that shaped how England understood its plants for a thousand years.
33757-the-elements-of-botany-for-beginne:
Asa Gray presents the elements of botany for beginners and for schools in this revised edition of his Lessons in Botany, copyrighted in 1887. The volume replaces his Lessons in Botany and Vegetable Physiology of more than a quarter century before. It follows the same lines but is more extended in some respects and more concise and terse in others. That way competent teachers may develop paragraphs into lectures and illustrate points barely but clearly stated.

Gray means the book to give beginners a grounding in plant structure and the principles of plant life, starting with flowering plants, where botanical teaching should always begin. A companion volume, How Plants Grow and Behave, serves younger pupils and common schools. The book remains a landmark of American botanical teaching, clear, systematic, and shaped by the country's foremost nineteenth-century botanist.
33830-fur-farming-a-book-of-information-:
A. R. Harding published this handbook on fur farming at Columbus, Ohio, in 1909. It opens with supply and demand, then asks what animals to raise and how to build enclosures and box traps. Later chapters take up fox, skunk, mink, opossum, muskrat, raccoon, beaver, and otter in turn.

Harding gives habits, care, and feeding for each animal, with plans for yards, shelters, and fences. A closing section covers killing, skinning, stretching, and deer farming. The book serves readers who want the early fur trade's practical knowledge, gathered in one plain manual.
33870-chess-fundamentals:
José R. Capablanca, chess champion of the world, sets out chess fundamentals in this Harcourt, Brace volume, copyrighted in 1921. Part one covers first principles, endings, middle-game, and openings. It covers simple mates, pawn promotion, pawn endings, winning positions in the middle-game, relative value of the pieces, general strategy of the opening, control of the centre, and traps. Part two gives further principles in end-game play.

Later sections treat a cardinal principle, a classical ending, obtaining a passed pawn, and how to find out which pawn will be the first to queen. Capablanca writes with the clarity of a champion teacher, preferring understanding to memorized lines. The book remains a classic introduction to chess, suited to beginners who want sound principles and to stronger players seeking the champion's own method.
34021-small-souls:
Louis Couperus wrote this Dutch novel, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and published in New York in 1914. Small Souls follows upper-class Dutch men and women and their small, daily souls: parents still called Papa and Mamma, tea after dinner, and talk of Java as India. The translator notes manners that strike English ears as exotic.

Couperus watches family pride, marriage, and reputation with a keen, ironic eye. His people guard form while feeling strains beneath it. The novel offers a subtle portrait of Dutch society at the turn of the century.
34114-soap-making-manual-a-practical-han:
E. G. Thomssen wrote this practical handbook on soap making, published in New York in 1922 by D. Van Nostrand, with pictures. The material first appeared in serial form in the American Perfumer and Essential Oil Review, and requests from readers led to this book form. Thomssen covers raw materials, their handling, analysis, and control in the modern soap plant.

Chapters keep the spelling of their first printing, so a reader meets both cocoanut and coconut in different places. The manual serves soap makers, chemists, and students of factory practice. It gives a clear, working account of an everyday industry.
3428-the-two-vanrevels:
Booth Tarkington sets this novel in an Indiana town where two young lives cross after long separation. One figure is a girl leaving years of strict enclosure within the walls and still gardens of a convent school, for whom the bright world outside flashes like a mystery. Around her gather town families, a firm named Gray and Vanrevel, and the social rules of a growing river town.

The story follows courtship, family pride, and a young man's effort to prove himself in business and love. Tarkington writes the town itself as a character, with its serenades, cupola rooms, and June evenings. Readers who enjoy American town novels will find romance, rivalry, and a careful picture of manners in the mid nineteenth century.
34400-napoleon-s-marshals:
Napoleon's Marshals is a book of lives by Dunn-Pattison, printed at London by Methuen in 1909. The book holds twenty illustrations and a synopsis of the marshals. Twenty six lives follow, one for each of the men Napoleon raised to the marshal's baton.

Bernadotte follows, the marshal who became king of Sweden. Then come Soult, Lannes, Ney, Davout and Macdonald, the great fighting names of the empire. Marmont, Suchet, St Cyr, Moncey and Jourdan fill the middle of the book. The later lives take in Augereau, Brune, Mortier, Bessières and Victor, then Grouchy, Kellermann, Lefèbvre and Oudinot. Pérignon, Serurier and Poniatowski, the Polish prince, close the set. The book gives each marshal his campaigns, his character and his end. It is a group portrait of the men who carried out Napoleon's wars.
34618-twenty-four-unusual-stories-for-bo:
Twenty Four Unusual Stories for Boys and Girls was arranged and retold by Anna Cogswell Tyler, printed in New York in 1921. Maud and Miska Petersham drew the plates. Tyler gives the book to the boys and girls who first heard and loved the tales.

The list draws on many tellers, from Hans Christian Andersen and Joseph Jacobs to Howard Pyle and Selma Lagerlof. Christmas tales hold The Christmas Cuckoo and The Emperor Vision. Greek legends hold The Curse of Echo. Other tales name Katcha and the Devil, the white dogs of Arran, and the well of the world end. One tale asks what the good man does, and holds it is sure to be right. Young readers get world tales retold in clear, warm prose.
34671-camps-and-trails:
Henry Abbott wrote Camps and Trails in nineteen eighteen, a book of hunting and woodcraft in the northern forests. Abbott writes in the first person, from his own days in camp. The book opens at lunch on a log, with his rifle close at hand.

A Canada jay, also called the whiskey jack, watches him eat from a low limb. The bird turns its head to study him with each eye in turn. Abbott tosses it bread and notes how wood birds watch for food and foes at once. Tales of trails, game, and camp life follow in the same close, calm voice.
34894-briarwood-girls:
Briarwood Girls is a college story by Julia Lestarjette Glover, issued by a Columbus book concern. Its motto vows to follow on, sure to meet the sun at last. Eleven chapters follow Alison Fair and her friends at Briarwood College. Alison's Wonderful Lamp is both the first chapter's name and a thread of the tale.

Alison comes home on the first of June after her freshman year ends. Her mother must tell her that hard times bar her return in the fall. Her father cannot pay, though the denial breaks his heart as much as hers. Alison swallows her grief and vows patience, begging her mother not to fret. She thinks of a correspondence course to keep some hold on her studies. Essays, mysteries, and a class prophecy fill the college chapters ahead.
34984-a-guide-for-the-study-of-animals:
Guide for the Study of Animals is a school biology manual by a Chicago teachers committee. Heath of Boston published the guide in 1911 for high school classes. Whitney of Bowen High School chaired the Biology Round Table committee of authors. Lucas, Shinn, and Smallwood of three other Chicago schools share the title page.

Chapter one gives introductory studies of living animals, starting with the fly. Maggot, cockroach, spider, cricket, grasshopper, and butterfly follow in the contents list. Caterpillar, tussock moth, beetle, and damsel fly larva continue the close looking course. Lab method, not lecture, is the soul of this progressive school text.
35118-the-postnatal-development-of-two-b:
The Postnatal Development of Two Broods of Great Horned Owls, by Hoffmeister and Setzer, is a bird study from Kansas. It ran in the University of Kansas Publications of the Museum of Natural History in October 1947. The paper spans pages 157 to 173 of its volume.

A pair of owls nested on the vine-covered north wall of the museum itself. They reared three young in 1945 and one young in 1946, and the men watched both broods. Daily notes in 1945 form the core of the report. The nest sat on a metal-covered ledge two feet wide and forty-eight feet above the ground. A laboratory window let the watchers observe at will without disturbing the birds. Notes ran from egg-laying to the day the young left, early February into April.
35147-a-maid-of-the-kentucky-hills:
Edwin Carlile Litsey's novel A Maid of the Kentucky Hills came from Browne and Howell in Chicago in nineteen thirteen, drawn by John Cassel and dedicated to Sara of the sunny hair. A sick man tells the story in chapters that name his stages. He goes to 'Crombie twice, finds a lodge in the wilderness, and meets a dryad, then a satyr who sits cheek by jowl with him.

Mid-March convinced him he was wrong, he confesses. A hacking cough with chest pains had grown all winter, and with masculine mulishness he had refused to own the symptoms. The hills, an oratorio, and a hilltop of reflection to no advantage carry his cure and his romance.
35704-wonder-stories-the-best-myths-for-:
Wonder Stories, the best myths for boys and girls, by Carolyn Sherwin Bailey, was copyrighted in 1920 at Springfield, Massachusetts, with six color pictures by Clara Burd. Bailey wrote many books for the children's hour and for storytellers. An opening chapter asks how the myths began, then the tales start with Prometheus and his bit of clay.

Stories retell how Perseus conquered the sea, how Pegasus flew, how Midas lost his ears, and how Phaeton's chariot ran away. Two tales come from Nathaniel Hawthorne. Iris crossing the rainbow bridge fronts the book. Bailey keeps the old Greek and Roman tales clear, short, and warm for young readers hearing them first.
35985-amy-in-acadia-a-story-for-girls:
A girls' travel novel by Helen Leah Reed. Little, Brown and Company published it at Boston in 1905. Katharine Pyle drew the illustrations. Reed also wrote the Brenda books. Her heroine Amy tours Acadia, the old French country of Nova Scotia. The dedication names the author's niece Constance. She had journeyed through Acadia with Reed herself.

The chapters move from place to place. Meteghan, Digby, old Port Royal, and Halifax all host episodes. Fog, a tea party, a fire, and found cousins vary the road. One chapter enters Evangeline's country, Longfellow's Acadia. Amy's opening quarrel with Fritz sets the personal stakes. She refuses to ask her mother to invite him along. The tour unfolds from there.
36184-great-englishwomen-an-historical-r:
Great Englishwomen is a school reading book of short lives, made as a mate to Great Englishmen. It stands in Bell's list of Continuous Narrative Readers, bound strong and priced at one shilling. The series aimed at school standards, with tales and lives cut down by taking out parts while keeping the words of the first text.

The makers hoped the lives would prove as much use in schools as the men's volume had. Short lives let young readers meet women of note from English history in brief, clear form. The book shows how Victorian schools taught the past: through brief lives meant to stir pride, duty, and a wish to read more.
36281-the-slayer-of-souls:
The Slayer of Souls is a novel by Robert W Chambers, published in New York in nineteen twenty. Chambers's earlier tales, including In Secret and The Common Law, are listed on the title page. A playful verse dedication to a friend opens the book, begging him not to denounce this poor romance. Chambers hopes it will amuse on a rainy night, he writes.

Behind the light verse stands an occult thriller in Chambers's line of weird tales. A soul slaying cult and secret powers in New York were his new ground after the King in Yellow made his name. Dedication jokes aside, menace drives the plot. The book shows a best seller turning wartime spy fears into supernatural dread.
36429-randy-s-summer-a-story-for-girls:
Amy Brooks wrote a story for girls about Randy Weston's summer. Lee and Shepard issued Randy's Summer at Boston in 1902, rights from 1900. Brooks drew the pictures herself, as with her other Randy books. Twelve chapters run from fairy tales to a wedding feast at the close.

Randy sits lost in a book while calls ring from the kitchen at the start. Little sister Prue, a brook, a picnic, and an apple-bee fill her warm days. Randy outwits Jason Meade in one bright chapter of the tale. Young readers gain a sweet, old-fashioned tale of sister love and country fun.
36740-peggy-owen-patriot-a-story-for-gir:
Lucy Foster Madison wrote this tale of the Revolution for girls, third in her Peggy Owen line. The Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia printed Peggy Owen Patriot in 1917, with plates by Peck. Peggy Owen at Yorktown and Peggy Owen and Liberty stand beside it.

On the Road to Philadelphia opens the tale, then a home-coming. An old-time advertisement, a girl's sacrifice, and a trip up the attic fill the early list. Tea at headquarters brings Peggy face to face with the great. Her resolve, a hero's tale, and a plea for Drayton mark her growth. The camp at Middlebrook, two warnings, and stolen thunder crowd the list shown here.
36815-advanced-toy-making-for-schools:
David M. Mitchell wrote this book on the make of toys for schools, printed in 1922. He taught the arts of the hand at a high school in Cleveland, Ohio. The list of parts shows the plan of the book. Its first part treats of the acts of work in the make of toys, and starts with work that makes things of worth. It gives a plan for the set-up of the shop, the group of the class, and the clerk who keeps the time.

The book is a guide for the teach, part by part, in how to run a class that learns by the hand. The toys are the means; the ends are skill, care, and the habit of good work. Cuts by the count go with the text of the print book.
3697-a-century-of-roundels:
Algernon Charles Swinburne writes a hundred roundels in this volume, second edition 1883, dedicated to Christina Rossetti. The roundel, a short French form Swinburne loved, runs eleven lines with a refrain repeated from its opening. Contents include Death and Birth, Birth and Death, A Ninth Birthday, and dozens of brief lyrics on love, time, and nature.

Swinburne's dedication says songs light as these may sound, though deep and strong the heart spoke through them, and he hopes they please ears tuned to finer music. The poems favor music over argument, with rhyme and refrain carrying feeling. The book suits readers who enjoy formal lyric poetry and Swinburne's mastery of sound.
37299-talks-to-freshman-girls:
Talks to Freshman Girls is a book of advice by Helen Dawes Brown, printed at Boston and New York in 1914. Houghton Mifflin issued it. Brown also wrote Two College Girls and The Petrie Estate. Her first talk takes its text from Francis Bacon: studies serve for delight, for ornament, and for ability.

No man, she says, wrote that sentence with more authority than Bacon, who took all knowledge for his province. At thirty-five he could say what studies had been worth to him. Brown hears girls say they go to college to have a good time. Studies, she answers, will secure a good time for the rest of a life. The talks guide new students through their first year.
37304-those-dale-girls:
Frances Weston Carruth wrote Those Dale Girls, published by A C McClurg and Company at Chicago in 1899. A motto from Longfellow heads the book: be a hero in the strife. Carruth dedicated it to Edith, her sister and comrade, the bravest of soldier girls. The frontispiece shows a girl shaking a wire cage of popcorn over the coals. Six illustrations carry the tale. The first chapter opens on the two sisters at home.

Hester Dale kneels before the open fire, popping corn. Julie, her sister, lies curled in the window-seat, reveling in a fascinating Kipling. Hester calls her the laziest thing in creation and bids her come down and help. Julie answers that she is as comfy as comfy can be. Peter Snooks, the fox-terrier, takes Hester's side in the quarrel.
37335-brenda-s-bargain-a-story-for-girls:
Brenda's Bargain is a story for girls by Helen Leah Reed, published at Boston by Little, Brown in 1903. Ellen Bernard Thompson drew its illustrations. Brenda Barlow is the heroine of a small shelf of Reed's books. Her school, her club, and her summer at Rockley have their own volumes. This tale opens with The Broken Vase. On a fine October afternoon Brenda walks across Boston Common toward the shops. She half begrudges the time indoors on so fair a day.

She must pick a present herself, and knows just what she wants. A frontispiece shows what startles her: a girl sunk in a heap beside broken glass. A family council and a visit to a mansion follow. The bargain of the title is Brenda's own doing and undoing. Reed writes of Boston girls and their schools with a kind, clear hand.
37405-a-maid-at-king-alfred-s-court-a-st:
Lucy Foster Madison wrote A Maid at King Alfred Court, a tale for girls put out at Philadelphia in 1900. Ida Waugh drew the plates. A verse at the front calls Alfred the just and the great, a pure and mild king. Madison had told a tale of a maid of the first age of faith in a past book.

The tale starts with a meet in the woods, then moves to Winchester and the hall of Alfred. A thief in the night, the death of a hero, and a pack of wolves raise the stakes. Egwina goes as a herald, hears Danish tales, and falls in a magic sleep. Saxon wins, dark days, and a trial of Egwina fill the last half. Adiva takes charge at one sharp turn. The close brings peace and a glad shock for the court.
37839-my-experiences-in-manipur-and-the-:
My Experiences in Manipur and the Naga Hills is a record of service in north-east India by Major-General Sir James Johnstone. The book came out in London in 1896 from Sampson Low, Marston and Company. It has pictures and a memoir of the author at its front. The author gives the book to the memory of his wife. She shared, he says, in many of his tasks and cares in Manipur and the Naga Hills.

In his preface Johnstone tells how he first brought his wife out to that post. The work is a first-hand account by a British officer of his years in that border region. His wife's spirit, he writes, drove him in his last venture there. Had she lived, he says, she would have written a better record of their shared years than he has been able to do.
38315-artistic-anatomy-of-animals:
Artistic Anatomy of Animals is a guide to the build of beasts for art. Cuyer, a teacher of the craft, wrote it for those who draw. The book asks first if its own use is plain to the reader. It then sets out to prove that use in full for the class.

An artist must know what lies beneath the skin of a beast. Bone, cord, and flesh shape the flank and the stride he draws. The forms are named and shown so the hand can learn them by eye. A horse's neck, a dog's chest, and a bull's hump each teach a law. The book is in English dress for schools of art in the West. Its notes tell how the fine print of the first form was kept.
38783-women-of-achievement-written-for-t:
Women of Achievement was written by Benjamin Brawley for the Fireside Schools, under the Woman American Baptist Home Mission Society, with a 1919 copyright. Brawley was Dean of Morehouse College and had written a short past of the American Negro. The book honors Black women of mark.

An opening part treats the Negro woman in American life as a whole. Named lives follow, on Harriet Tubman, Nora Gordon, and Meta Warrick Fuller. Mary McLeod Bethune and Mary Church Terrell close the set. A front note tells of Joanna P Moore, who began the Fireside Schools in 1884 to join Bible study with home duties. Students get short, warm lives meant to teach and lift.
38960-the-traditional-text-of-the-holy-g:
John William Burgon defended the traditional text of the Holy Gospels at length. Edward Miller arranged and finished the work after Burgon's death. George Bell and Sons issued it in London in 1896. Burgon had served as Dean of Chichester, as the title page states. Miller had been rector of Bucknell and had edited the fourth edition of Scrivener's Plain Introduction.

Twelve chapters run from first grounds to the seven notes of truth. The Vatican and Sinaitic manuscripts get close, hostile study. Early fathers, Syriac forms, and Latin texts witness for the old readings. Church scholars gain a fierce, learned brief against the new critical text.
39214-when-love-calls:
A novel by Stanley J Weyman, published at Boston in 1899. Weyman also wrote A Gentleman of France and The Castle Inn. The contents promise two accounts of one affair. One is called Her Story. The other is called His Story. Shorter pieces follow, among them A Strange Invitation and Along the Garonne. Romance and short tales share the volume.

Her Story opens in Norway. Two girls lie on a mossy bank above the Sogn Fiord. They eat cloudberries and tease each other. Their talk runs to dress, sweethearts, and a young man up the river. The fresh voice and northern scenery give the book a lighter start than Weyman's sword-and-cloak tales.
39232-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Britannica eleventh edition volume here runs from Hinduism to Home, Earls of. Long articles treat Hindu worship, Siva, and the Lingayat sect. Hobbes life and thought take a major article in the volume. Hinterland and Hippodrome stand among the shorter entries in range.

Hirsau abbey and its building school get an article with sources. The volume is one slice of the great 1910 to 1911 reference set. Entries carry dense fact, maps, and cross references for the reader. Scholars of the day wrote the signed articles in the set. Home, Earls of, the Scottish title line, closes the letter range of this volume.
39483-farm-boys-and-girls:
William A McKeever wrote Farm Boys and Girls, in the Rural Science Series edited by L H Bailey, issued in nineteen twelve. The series list in front runs from The Soil and Milk and Its Products to Plant Breeding and Dry Farming. A first plate shows a farm father combining work with children play. The book treats the raising of country children as a science and an art.

McKeever, a professor of philosophy working in child welfare, argues that farm life can hold its young folk. Chapters treat play, work, schooling, and the social life of farm youth. The drift to the city is his great worry throughout. Plates and tales show boys and girls at chores, fairs, and clubs. Rural teachers and parents get an early classic on country child life.
39518-the-little-washingtons-travels:
Lillian Elizabeth Roy wrote a travel tale for young readers, printed in New York in 1918. Roy also wrote the Polly Brewster books and the Girl Scouts books. Her young heroes are George and Martha Parke and their cousin Jack Davis of Philadelphia. The tale opens on a train as the children ride in a Pullman car.

The children tour New York first, with its sights and crowds. Then they visit spots tied to George Washington and the war for freedom. Chapters tell of his headquarters, of battle grounds near Philadelphia, and of a fight with Hessian troops. The trip mixes fun, facts, and pride in the nation's past for young readers.
39663-home-occupations-for-boys-and-girl:
Home Occupations for Boys and Girls is a book by Bertha Johnston, printed at Philadelphia with copyright in 1908. Jacobs issued it. Johnston edited the Kindergarten Magazine, and Fanny Chapin helped her. A line from Aristophanes heads the contents, praising a clever child who built mud houses and carved boats from the earliest years.

Twelve chapters run from the secrets of the market basket to kindergarten gifts and occupations. The market basket, Johnston says, holds many ways to employ a child's creative instinct with mind and body both busy. Other chapters treat the scrap basket, the sewing basket, the paint box, and dolls. Plays, games, and festival occasions take their turns.
39936-meg-s-friend-a-story-for-girls:
Alice Corkran wrote a story for girls that Burt of New York published with five full page pictures by Robert Fowler. Chapter one shows a queer old house in Bloomsbury, fine two hundred years before and sunk since into neglect. The hall door was dim for want of paint.

On the top stair, toward sunset, a child sits and watches through the banisters. She waits for the scrape of a latchkey and the sound of steps in the hall. Then she runs down and stops with grave poise before a tall, robust man. That child is Meg. The chapters ahead take her to school at an establishment for young ladies. A diamond, a party, and an editor of a country paper all play their parts. Poor Meg has her sorrows, and peace comes near the end.
39993-gardening-for-little-girls:
Gardening for Little Girls is a book of the farm craft for girls by Olive Hyde Foster. Her past books of the same set are named on the title leaf. The set holds books on cook work, sew work, and house keep for girls as well. Each book of the set is sold at one price, with plates. The front plate of this book is a trick plate: find the small girl.

The book is sworn to two of the most dear young folk who ever showed love for the soil. Its parts start with first steps past a gar den. Plan and plant of the flower beds come next. Then the blooms that must be made new each year have a part of their own.
40458-the-real-jesus-of-the-four-gospels:
The Real Jesus of the Four Gospels is a study of the gospels by Atwater, printed at Minneapolis in 1922 and copyrighted the year before. The book is dedicated to all who suffered or shed their blood, in ages past, on account of creeds, dogmas, theologies, and inquisitions. Against those perversions it sets the simple religion Jesus taught: love of God and of neighbour.

Part one begins with the genealogy of Jesus. Mark and John, Atwater notes, give no genealogy, beyond naming Joseph and Mary and calling Jesus the son of David. Matthew gives a line from Abraham down to Joseph. Luke gives one from Joseph up to Adam. The two lines agree from Abraham onward. Atwater works through the four accounts verse by verse, seeking the man behind the creeds in the plain record of the texts.
4056-two-festivals:
A children's book of festivals opens on the evening before May Day, as boys look forward to a May festival with neighborhood children. Mrs. Chilton reads aloud Milton's lines on the bright morning star, dancing from the east with the flowery May.

Other pieces follow a birthday and a true story, in the same fireside manner as the author's travel tales. The book mixes verse, story, and holiday custom for young readers. Families who like old-fashioned seasonal reading will enjoy short pieces meant to be shared aloud at festival time.
40576-smiles-a-book-of-recitations-for-g:
Smiles, a book of recitations for girls by Alice Lewis Richards, was published at Akron, Ohio, in 1900, from an 1899 copyright. Richards also wrote Winks, for boys, and Thoughts, readings for the girls and boys in teens. A front piece shows Laila's smiles. The contents list near ninety short pieces in verse and prose, meant to be spoken aloud.

Titles run from Robin's Return and Papa's Best Girl through Does Jesus Know, Only a Sparrow, and The Little Crib Bed. Pieces for Easter, Thanksgiving, and Santa sit beside pet poems on kittens and robins. Months of the year close the set, January through June in the visible list. Books of this kind fed the school and parlor culture of recitation, where a girl's piece, memorized and delivered, was a small public art.
40772-human-animals:
Human Animals, by Frank Hamel, is a study of the belief that men change into beasts. Stokes printed the book in New York, in a London issue of 1915. Hamel had written on the dauphines of France and the women of Fontainebleau.

The first chapter states the root idea: the belief is as old as life itself. All things, it argues, spring from one stuff, mind or spirit, taking shape by chance or design. Hamel quotes Leland: in the beginning, men were as animals and animals as men. The chapters then sort the lore by kind. Transformation, the bush-soul, and souls in animal bodies come first. Wer-wolf trials and wer-wolf legend take two chapters, with lion-men, tiger-men, and wer-foxes after. Witches and their familiars, ghosts of animals, and spirits in magic fill the later run.
40873-paths-of-the-mound-building-indian:
Paths of the Mound-Building Indians and Great Game Animals is volume one of Historic Highways of America, by Archer Butler Hulbert. The Arthur Clark Company published the line at Cleveland, Ohio in 1902. Hulbert dedicated the series to his father. Maps and pictures support the text, including old maps of remains in Wisconsin, Ohio, Illinois, and Indiana.

Part one studies the mound-building Indians: where their works lie, early travel in the interior, and moves along the watersheds. Hulbert holds that writers on the mounds began from set guesses and so shut the door on free study. Part two turns to the buffalo: its range and habits, the early use of buffalo roads, and the great thoroughfares those roads became.
40880-our-british-snails:
Our British Snails, by Canon Horsley, was published at London in 1915. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge issued the little nature book that year. Horsley also wrote folk lore and legends of birds, the title page notes. A frontispiece shows the canon in his study with a rare whelk.

That whelk came from a stall in the Walworth Road, the caption tells its readers. It rests now in the South Kensington Museum, the caption adds in pride. Plates show the great edible snail at half natural size in the list. Love darts much magnified and a snail at rest on hawthorn follow in the pictures. Names of parts of shell and body get a teaching plate in the book. A clergyman naturalist teaches shell lore to general readers here.
40999-stolen-souls:
Stolen Souls is a tale by William Le Queux, opening in winter in Saint Petersburg. Chapter one is called The Soul of Princess Tchikhatzoff in the contents of the tale. The narrator walks the Nevski Prospekt wrapped in furs until only his nose and eyes show. Almost without willing it, he turns into the Dominique, a fashionable restaurant of the avenue.

Inside, the place blazes with electricity and is heated by high, grotesquely ornamented stoves for its guests. It is filled with officers, ladies, and cigarette smoke at the dining hour. The savoury smell of national dishes mingles with those of foreign lands in his account. Le Queux fed the British taste for tales of Russian courts, spies, and stolen secrets for decades. The princess of the first chapter gives the soul stealing plot its first victim and its title its meaning for the reader.
41010-a-colony-of-girls:
A Colony of Girls is a novel by Kate Livingston Willard, copyrighted in 1892 by Dodd, Mead and Company of New York. The colony is a summer houseful of young people under the Lawrence roof. Helen, Nathalie, and Jean Lawrence open the book on the veranda, Nathalie swinging in a hammock and resenting the children who swarm about them.

The chapters promise a season's worth of incident. Nan's ship arrives, a leaf from Helen's past is turned, and the party sails on the Cyclone. There is a dinner at the Manor, a walk in the shrubbery, and Nan in open rebellion. A flying machine and what came of it, Miss Stuart's arrival, and a dance at Crescent Beach follow. A cablegram, eddying currents, and a Christmas close bring the colony to its settling.
41075-the-curiosities-and-law-of-wills:
The Curiosities and Law of Wills, by John Proffatt, was printed in San Francisco in 1876. Proffatt was a lawyer and the author of Woman before the Law. The book formed volume two of a series called Legal Recreations. Its catalog title is garbled, but the title page is clear. A quote from Coke on the puzzle of wills opens the work.

Chapters trace the origin and history of wills, then their form and rules. Later parts deal with who can make a will, gifts left by will, and limits on giving. Revocation, domicile, and the reading of will terms close the book. Proffatt uses apt cases to make the rules plain for students, lawyers, and general readers.
41077-may-carols:
May Carols, by Aubrey de Vere, is a book of poems in honour of the Virgin Mary. Longman printed the volume in London in 1857. De Vere gives the poems to Henry Edward Manning with warm affection.

His introduction explains the thought behind the set: the Church consecrates the seasons of time to eternity. May, the birthday feast of creation as he calls it, belongs to Mary above all. Each poem sets out one great idea within the mystery of the Incarnation, he says. Some stress the highest excellence a creature can reach, and others the vast gap between creature and Creator. De Vere warns that the two views may look contrary yet in fact complete each other. The carols thus form a linked meditation for the Marian month.
41524-marion-berkley-a-story-for-girls:
Elizabeth B Comins wrote a story for girls about Marion Berkley and her school life. Henry T Coates and Company issued it at Philadelphia, with rights held in 1870. Comins gave the book to her twin sisters with warm love. A plate called The Two Bouquets fronts the tale.

Marion rushes from home to catch a train for boarding school in New England. Her brother Fred frets over a lost ball match while she flies about. On the train she finds her friend Flo, to her great relief. School joys, scrapes, and bonds of youth fill the chapters that young readers of the time loved.
41573-south-sea-idyls:
South-Sea Idyls, by Charles Warren Stoddard, gathers sketches of life in the Pacific islands from the author's years of travel and residence there. The book was published in Boston in 1873.

The sketches move between Hawaii and Tahiti. Early pieces tell of life in the cradle of the deep and of friendship with a Hawaiian host at Kana-ana. Others describe a feast day in Tahiti, pearl hunting in the Pomotou group, and a canoe cruise in the Coral Sea. Later sketches give the night dancers of Waipio, the house of the sun, and a chapel of palms. A poem called The Cocoa-Tree opens the volume, and a tale of a prodigal in Tahiti closes it.
41797-the-story-book-girls:
Christina Gowans Whyte wrote this girls' tale for Frowde and Hodder and Stoughton of London in 1906. The Story Book Girls sold at a shilling net in the Girls' New Library, with a coloured front plate. Bessie Marchant and Meade stand on the same list.

Elma Leighton opens the tale, and Miss Annie follows. A flower show ticket and Cuthbert come next. The Story Books Call names the heart of it: girls who live half in novels must meet the real world. The mayonnaise, visitors again, and the party fill the fun. A burglar and a split infinitive share the list. A reconciliation and the first peal lead home.
41837-the-secret-mark-an-adventure-story:
Roy Snell wrote this adventure story for girls, The Secret Mark. Reilly and Lee printed it at Chicago in 1923. Lucile Tucker stands by a steel bookcase, fingers trembling, at start. A mysterious visitor has shaken her nerves in chapter one.

Elusive Shakespeare, a gargoyle, and a papier mache lunch box follow. A vanishing Portland chart and sea mysteries fill the mid chapters. Lucile shares her secret, faces a trial by fire at night. Night visitors, a battle, theft, and revealed secrets close the tale. Inside the lines and better days end the contents of the girls adventure tale.
42016-the-purple-flame-a-mystery-story-f:
Roy J Snell wrote The Purple Flame, a mystery story for girls, issued at Chicago by the Reilly and Lee Company with copyright in nineteen twenty four. Twenty seven chapters fill the book. Chapter one is The Mystery of the Old Dredge. Marian Norton is the heroine, up in the Alaska reindeer country. She started, took one step backward, then stood staring, the tale opens.

Startled by her action, the spotted reindeer behind her lunged backward into the brown one that followed, the tale says. All three reindeer got into a general mix up for a full minute, it adds. Patsy from Kentucky and The Range Robber follow. Planning a Perilous Journey and The Enchanted Mountain fill the early chapters. The Girl of the Purple Flame and Ancient Treasure stand at the centre. Girls get northern adventure with reindeer, gold, and a strange flame.
42114-franz-hals:
Edgcumbe Staley wrote Franz Hals, a volume in the Masterpieces in Colour series edited by Hare. The line gives each great painter a small book in the same form. Velazquez, Reynolds, Turner, Raphael, and Rembrandt stand in the list with Hals. Plate one is The Laughing Cavalier, the frontispiece of this book. The canvas hangs in the Wallace Collection at London and was painted in 1624.

Hals called that work Portrait of an Officer, and no one knows how it gained its present title. Words on the back of the canvas give the sitter's age as twenty-six in that year. The young face is handsome, and the dress is rich in detail. Yet the colours are few and beautifully blended, the note holds. Staley gives Hals, his sitters, and his bold brush in a short, pictured life.
42221-the-world-of-h-g-wells:
Wells and his ideas are the subject of The World of Wells, a critical study by Van Wyck Brooks issued at New York in 1915. Brooks sorts the career of Wells into phases. Chapters treat the first phase, the turn towards socialism, and true and false socialism. Later chapters take up human nature and the spirit of Wells.

Brooks opens with a bold claim about his man. Wells once wrote that he was, by a sort of fate, a socialist. All that can be said of him, Brooks argues, explains or refines that statement. The habits of mind behind it show in the first phase of the work. Those are the famed tales of time and space that won Wells his first fame. The study reads a living author as a force in modern thought.
42230-esther-s-charge-a-story-for-girls:
Esthers Charge is a story for girls by E Everett Green. Its full title in plain words calls the tale a story for girls. A print shows cheers and a kind hand laid on the girls head. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

Esther runs a house as a small chief from the first part of the tale. Boys, a hard charge, and days of sun at a crag fill the early course. A town of refuge, a cave of tricks, and plain talks mark the mid turns. A new charge at the end tests all she has learned in trust. Faith and pluck guide the young girl through her load of care.
42381-watched-by-wild-animals:
Enos A Mills wrote Watched by Wild Animals, issued at Garden City, New York, by Doubleday, Page and Company in nineteen twenty two. Photographs and drawings by Will James illustrate the book. Mills had earlier written Adventures of a Nature Guide. He dedicated this one to Esther and Enda. Many chapters first ran in magazines. A Rocky Mountain goat photograph opens it.

The Rocky Mountain Goat is chapter one. The Haymaker of the Heights and Introducing Mr and Mrs Skunk follow. The Persistent Beaver and The Otter Plays On come next. The Bighorn in the Snow and The Clown of the Prairies stand in the middle. The Black Bear, Comedian, gives the bear his due. On Wild Life Trails and Rebuilding a Beaver Colony follow. The Wary Wolf closes the survey. Nature lovers get close watched Rocky Mountain animal lives.
42549-indoor-and-outdoor-recreations-for:
Indoor and Outdoor Recreations for Girls, by Lina Beard and Adelia B Beard, was published by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York, under copyrights of 1904 and 1906. The sisters Beard were pioneers of the scouting movement for girls. Their note to the new edition explains the shorter title: the book first appeared as Handicraft and Recreation for Girls, but recreation alone, they found, named its contents better. The handicrafts in it are play.

Part one teaches old crafts with home made tools. Spinning comes first, with wheel, spindle, distaff, and the handling of flax. Weaving on a home made loom follows, down to a tiny Navajo blanket. A ball of twine becomes a hammock, a school bag, and curtains. Wood shavings are woven into baskets and a handkerchief case. Reed curtains and things made of common grasses round out the indoor work.
42813-mrs-vanderstein-s-jewels:
Vanderstein's Jewels, a novel by Bryce, was published in London and New York in 1914 by John Lane. Chapter one opens in a cool room in afternoon light. Bowls of white roses lend the place an air of more than usual specklessness. Into it steps Madame Querterot, a woman of no taste, to whom the airy lightness recalls the convent school of her youth.

Vanderstein, ever the essence of punctuality, lies ready on a silk-covered sofa in a diaphanous white dressing gown. She lazily watches the hairdresser unpack the little bag of her trade. You must make me very beautiful tonight, she says: we are going to hear La Boheme, and the Queen will be there. Her box stands nearly opposite the royal box. Bryce sets a society tale where jewels, beauty, and money circle one another.
42964-bible-animals:
Bible Animals is a natural history of every living creature mentioned in the Scriptures, by Wood. Longmans printed this new edition at London in 1883. Its range runs from the ape to the coral. One hundred new designs by three artists fill its pages, engraved by Pearson. A front picture shows the ostrich, with Job's words about her scorning the horse and his rider.

Wood's preface argues that the Bible cannot be rightly read without natural history. Its metaphors come from common life, from rocks and valleys, trees and fishes, birds and beasts. Unless we know those creatures as the first readers knew them, we shall misread the text. The book pairs each animal with its verses.
43125-blanche-a-story-for-girls:
Blanche is a story for girls by Mrs Molesworth, with pictures by Barnes. Chambers of London and Edinburgh issued the novel for young readers. Chapter one, The Sunny South, opens about twenty five years in the past. A young English girl, Anastasia Fenning, visits family friends in France.

Anastasia health was frail, and a mild winter climate was sought for her. A month or two made her well and fair again in that home. Her few weeks visit turned into a stay of fully twenty years. Henry Derwent, the orphan grandson of her hosts, fell in love with her. No bar stood in the way, as the families were old friends.
43177-the-protection-of-fresh-water-muss:
R E Coker wrote The Protection of Fresh-Water Mussels in 1914. The Bureau of Fisheries issued it as Document 793. Coker directed the United States Biological Station at Fairport, Iowa. Hugh M Smith led the bureau then. Present conditions open the contents. The mussel industry follows at page three.

Depletion of the resource fills page four. The community's interests come at page five. Government breeding of mussels gets its own part. Results hang on protection, a head warns plainly. Two measures stand fit for quick use, he finds. A two-inch size limit gets a long defense. Reasons for that limit fill page sixteen. Waste in the fishery stands pictured and named. A fisheries brief for the pearl-button trade's living stock shows science asking law to save a river crop.
4320-an-enquiry-concerning-the-principle:
David Hume published this enquiry as his mature statement of moral philosophy, and the present text follows a 1912 reprint of the 1777 edition. Hume asks what makes actions good or bad, and he answers by looking at human feeling and usefulness rather than at abstract reason alone. Justice, benevolence, and the social virtues take center stage.

The enquiry is short, clear, and arranged in sections with appendices, including a discussion of justice and its place among the virtues. Hume kept the original spellings, such as connexion and labour, in this reprint. It remains a standard entry point for readers new to Hume, and to the question of where morals come from.
43256-witches-cove-a-mystery-story-for-g:
Roy J. Snell wrote this tale, printed in 1928 as one of a set of mystery tales for girls. The list of parts sets the tone of the book at a glance. Its heads speak of the riddles of the night, of a boat rowed in the dark, of a den, of a face in the fire, and of three gray witches. Later heads name a red light that shakes, a small man of the cove, a chase, and a fire on the beach.

The first part opens on Casco Bay off the coast of Maine. It is night, with no moon, and the stars are hid by a thin haze. The far lights of Portland, eight of them, shine in pairs like the eyes of a cat. They serve but to make the dark of the water more black.
43272-american-weasels:
Hall wrote a full science study of American weasels, issued by the University of Kansas in December 1951. The work runs to 466 pages, with forty one plates and thirty one figures. A color plate at the front shows the head marks of ten races of the long tailed weasel, all males at half life size.

That plate teaches the book's big theme: coat color tracks rainfall. In wet lands the black spreads back over the neck and the white face marks shrink. In dry lands the black fades and the white grows. Tests show the trait is bred in, not changed by a move in a few generations. Range maps and skull and tooth facts fill the dense text.
43299-square-pegs-a-rhymed-fantasy-for-t:
Clifford Bax wrote a short play in rhyme for two girls to act. The book came out in London in 1920. It was first played at Farthingstone on June 19, 1919. Phyllis Reid and Margot Sieveking took the two parts that day. Bax gave the play to Rubinstein in its front pages.

Hilda Gray is one girl's name in the play's cast list. Square pegs in round holes is the old saw in its name. Two young hearts test their fit with the world in rhyme. Bax wrote verse plays and songs in those same years. His front list names poems and a verse comedy from then. Small stage groups get a light, neat piece.
43375-measuring-tools:
The Industrial Press of New York issued a shop handbook on measuring tools in 1910, as number twenty one of a machinery reference set. Chapter one gives the history of standard measures. Few mechanics, it says, know the tale of the standards they use each day.

The first units were parts of the body. The foot was said to come from the foot of Hercules, and Charlemagne set his own foot as the standard of his land. In England before the conquest the yard ran long. Henry the First cut it in 1101 to the length of his own arm. A law of 1324 set the inch at three barley corns, round and dry, laid end to end. Later chapters treat calipers, surface gages, and the micrometer.
43439-short-studies-in-ethics-an-element:
Short Studies in Ethics is an elementary text book for schools by Miller, principal of Bishop Ridley College. The Bryant Press published it at Toronto in 1895. The contents list twenty four short studies. Duty opens the course, and Conscience closes it. Obedience, truthfulness, courage, and purity come early in the list. Unselfishness, honesty, faithfulness, and justice follow in order. Profanity, benevolence, ambition, and patriotism get studies of their own.

Later studies treat habit, industry, self control, and self reliance. Friendship, gentlemanliness, courtesy, and repentance round out the virtues. The first study defines duty as something which is due. It is owed by everybody to God, to self, or to others, the text says. No word is more disliked by the slothful than duty, it adds. Liking the word comes only by performing it a little at a time. The book teaches character in short, direct lessons.
43616-the-quaint-companions-with-an-intr:
Leonard Merrick wrote The Quaint Companions, for Hodder and Stoughton in 1919. Wells wrote an introduction for the London and Toronto book. A verse from Galatians heads the tale. Neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female, it runs. Chapter one opens with a singer not returning alone from his concert.

Lee is gregarious at all times, and excited by his own applause. Two fellow soloists drive to his hotel and share his champagne. Fat cigars pass round his sitting-room as they sprawl and talk. He has changed into a plum velvet smoking-jacket for the hour. His slippered feet cross on the window-sill in ease. His silk socks show for his bitter guests to notice, he knows. Behind the silent parade, Brighton's sea shimmers under a full moon. Merrick opens on art, envy, and an unlikely bond.
44062-the-crystal-ball-a-mystery-story-f:
Roy J Snell wrote The Crystal Ball, a mystery story for girls, issued by The Reilly and Lee Company in Chicago in nineteen thirty six. Twenty six chapters fill the book. Florence Huyler and Jeanne are the chief girls. Chapter one is called Midnight Blue Velvet. Later heads name a Tiger Woman, a bright shawl, and a voodoo priestess.

Florence reads a door number and finds no light within, the glass like a slab of ebony. In a city office block ten stories up, she turns the knob slow and silent, as a robber might turn a safe dial. Later chapters bring Florence gazing into the crystal, gypsies that are not gypsies, and a vision for an other. Fire, a secret of Lost Lake, and a battle royal add peril. Girls got sleuth work, fortune telling, and treasure in one tale.
44133-the-girl-warriors-a-book-for-girls:
The Girl Warriors, a book for girls by Adene Williams, was printed in 1901 by the David C. Cook Publishing Company of Chicago. Its heroine is Winnifred Burton, a small girl curled up in a big chair by the fire on a snowy January day. She is deep in a book called The Giant Killer, reading of Fides in the Pit of Despair.

The opening chapter sets the Burton home and Winnifred's love of reading. The book she reads tells how the tempted Fides fell back bruised and bleeding again and again as he tried to cut and climb his way out of the pit. At last he found a cord of love strong enough to draw him out with scarcely an effort of his own. The tale frames a story of girls' courage and Christian faith for young readers.
446-a-book-of-remarkable-criminals:
H. B. Irving profiles notorious killers and swindlers in this study of crime and motive. Charles Peace, Robert Butler, Derues, Dr. Castaing, Professor Webster, and the mysterious Mr. Holmes each get a full career, trial, and fall. Partners in crime, from the widow Gras to Eyraud and Bompard, close the set.

Irving writes as a lawyer and historian, weighing evidence, motive, and the law's slow net. He stresses how passion, greed, and pride tangle men in their own deeds. The book reads as both true crime and moral study, careful with facts and keen on why ordinary folk turn to murder.
44873-third-warning-a-mystery-story-for-:
