Roy Snell wrote this mystery tale for girls, printed in Chicago in 1938. Florence Huyler sails Lake Superior with young Captain Davie at the wheel. Strange yellow clouds roll low on the horizon at the start. Florence loves the water but feels a chill of doubt.

Chapters promise a flaming isle, night signals, and a rescue at sea. A dog parachute, a moose ride, and a phantom add thrills. Threats, a crimson spot, and a weird rest place raise the stakes. The tale keeps a brisk pace through storm and dark.
45038-perlycross-a-tale-of-the-western-h:
Perlycross, a tale of the western hills, is a novel by Blackmore. Sampson Low of London issued the book in eighteen ninety four. Blackmore wrote Lorna Doone, Clara Vaughan, and Springhaven before this tale. The thirteenth thousand of Perlycross is the printing held in this text.

Chapters open in the lap of peace, then turn to fairy faith and a lych gate. Nicie, a fair bargain, and three doctors follow in the early pages. Devon village life among western hills forms the ground of the story. Church, parish folk, and old customs fill the quiet rural scene. Blackmore West Country tales were famed for rich local colour and speech.
45078-how-the-world-travels:
How the World Travels is a picture book of conveyances by Methley. Holloway drew the many pictures that fill the book's bright pages. Stokes of New York put the work out for young and old alike. Twelve chapters run from travel in the olden days to travel tomorrow. A front picture shows a rider mounted on a bullock in Africa.

Coaching days and strange vehicles of Europe fill the early list here. Journeys through India, China, and Japan come in the middle chapters. Africa and the New World give each a chapter of their own. Travelling in the wilds and through ice and snow follow in turn. Pictures show Egyptian chariots, Roman litters, sedan chairs, and dog carts. A seaside carriage drawn by a goat stands among the odd sights. The book pairs each way of riding with its land and age.
4546-memoirs-of-the-union-s-three-great-:
Three famous Civil War memoirs stand together in this volume: the personal memoirs of Ulysses S. Grant, William T. Sherman, and Philip H. Sheridan. Grant opens his own account by saying friends often urged him to write, and he had long refused. Near sixty-two, a fall confined him to the house, a business partner failed, and falling securities threatened his income, turning study into a welcome pastime.

Each general tells his war in his own voice, from early life and West Point through Mexican War service to the great campaigns of the 1860s. Together they give a Union commander's view of strategy, hardship, and politics, with the plain detail only a participant could supply. Readers get three classic American war memoirs in one file, best read as history told by the men who made it.
45636-stolen-idols:
Stolen Idols is an adventure novel by Phillips Oppenheim, published by Little, Brown and Company at Boston in 1925. Book one opens on two ships, pursuer and pursued, lying becalmed in a basin where two turgid rivers meet in China. The water is thick, oily, and yellow. Rice fields and a Chinese village stand far off under a beating sun.

From the smaller boat, oars slip suddenly from opened hatches and the dhow creeps forward. At the helm stands a huge Chinaman. He is Wu Abst, who loves to hear himself called the Mighty Terror of the Great River. He grins back at his pursuer, sure that no such craft can follow into the shallow water he seeks. His men sweat at the oars like galley slaves of old Rome.
45641-vesper-talks-to-girls:
Vesper Talks to Girls is a book of counsel by Laura Knott, principal of Bradford Academy, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1916. She dedicated it to the students of Bradford Academy, past, present, and future. The first talk, New Starts in Life, holds that life is full of chances to begin again. Courage and hope leave a person only when he stops believing one more chance remains.

Fourteen talks follow the same pattern. They treat school friendships, the art of living with others, enduring hardness, and the uses of trouble. Later talks weigh school spirit, clashing loyalties, the worth of discipline, and the progress of woman. Sources of happiness and life after graduation close the book.
46008-the-room-with-the-tassels:
The Room with the Tassels is a tale of a haunted house by Carolyn Wells. It came out in New York in the year 1918 as a thrill tale. Its first part is named for a want ad for just such a house. Eve Carnforth, a red haired girl, tells the claim that starts it.

She holds that a friend of hers saw the ghost, and heard it too. The old house of a great clan is the scene the crew takes up. Black trees, the tale of the house, and Eve's own night fill the start. A death at four of the clock makes the tale a hunt for a hand. Wild claims fly: was the thing of earth or past it, all ask. A keen man of facts steps in late to sort the claims of the house.
46048-the-turned-about-girls:
Beulah Marie Dix wrote The Turned-About Girls, a tale of two girls who trade places. The Macmillan Company issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred twenty two. Blanche Greer drew its plates of night flights and meetings. Dix gave the book to her daughter Evelyn Greenleaf Flebbe.

Strangers on a fast train open the tale of swapped lives. Mildred, mistress of ceremonies, sets the big idea in train. The girls are claimed and called for like lost bags at a depot. Life in the new house feels like a dream to each of them. Penelope unbends, and a half aunt is captured for the plot. Teacups and a darning basket carry their small wars at home. A letter from Alaska breaks in late to stir the pot. Turn about again, the next to last chapter cries in triumph.
46273-church-bells:
Church Bells is a short book on the bells of the church and their use. Walters, a scholar and a fellow of the old-lore guild, wrote it. It stands in a set on the arts of the church as a whole. A church man of note shaped that set for the press.

The set is small in size and rich in plates, by its own note. Its books take the crafts of the church one by one for the reader. This book takes the bell: its make, its hang, and its voice. Bells mark the hours of prayer and the rites of the folk. The set aimed to teach parish folk the worth of their own goods. Plain words and clear plates serve that aim throughout the book.
4682-nonsense-novels:
Stephen Leacock gathers ten parodies in Nonsense Novels, offering the book to the public without apology. His contents run from Maddened by Mystery, or The Defective Detective, and Q, a psychic pstory of the psupernatural. They go on to Guido the Gimlet of Ghent, a romance of chivalry, and Gertrude the Governess, or Simple Seventeen. A hero in homespun follows, with the life struggle of Hezekiah Hayloft.

Later parodies include Sorrows of a Super Soul, or The Memoirs of Marie Mushenough, Hannah of the Highlands, and Soaked in Seaweed, or Upset in the Ocean, an old-fashioned sea story. Caroline's Christmas, or The Inexplicable Infant, and The Man in Asbestos, an allegory of the future, close the set. Leacock mocks detective tales, romances, and sea yarns with glee. Readers get a short, funny book, best read when the originals it teases are fresh in mind.
47141-painted-veils:
Painted Veils is a novel by James Huneker, published in New York by Boni and Liveright in 1920. Huneker was a noted critic of music and letters. His motto page carries a French line: the naked truth, and a note that he vomits his masters. The novel opens under an older sign than either.

Before the story begins, Huneker prints the descent of Istar, daughter of Sin, to the land of the dead. At each of seven gates the warder strips her: tiara, pendants, necklaces, jewels, girdle, and rings. At the seventh gate the last veil goes. She enters the abode from which there is no return and receives the waters of life. The myth sets the book's theme in advance. Veils, paint, and stripping away run through a tale of art and appetite in the modern city.
4735-the-shepherd-of-the-hills:
Harold Bell Wright published The Shepherd of the Hills in 1907, dedicating it to Frances, his wife, in memory of a summer in the Ozark hills. They followed an old trail around the rise of Mutton Hollow, nobody knows how old, and from Sammy's lookout watched the day go over western ridges. A Troilus and Cressida passage stands at the head.

Contents open with a stranger, Sammy Lane, and a voice from out the mists. A chat with Aunt Mollie and a chapter called Jest Nobody follow. The story, what is love, and why ain't we got no folks follow. Sammy Lane's folks, a feat of strength, Ollie Stewart's good-by, and the shepherd and his flock come next. Sammy Lane's ambition, the common yeller kind, and a party at Ford's lead onward. Readers get a popular Ozark romance of a mysterious shepherd, a mountain girl, and old secrets.
47429-windfalls:
Windfalls, by Alfred George Gardiner, who wrote as Alpha of the Plough, was published in 1920 with drawings by Clive Gardiner. Gardiner dedicates the book to Gwen and Phyllis and jokes that, despite its title, the book is about bees, or about those who love them most. Light essays on country life make up the volume.

The first piece follows Jemima, a drake in a flock of Indian runner ducks who got a hen's name by chance at hatching. Gardiner watches the birds trail him to the artichoke bed and turns small farm acts into warm, funny scenes. The tone is gentle and observant, with wit used on pets, gardens, and daily habits rather than on grand events.
4768-let-s-collect-rocks-and-shells:
Let's Collect Rocks and Shells is a short booklet for beginners, published with Shell Oil Company's interest in its subjects. Its contents cover collecting seashells, what seashells are, the shell as an architect, meeting some shells, where to look, and starting a collection, with how to begin. Collecting rocks follows, with rocks made of minerals, main kinds of rocks, and collecting gems for the lucky few.

The introduction says millions of people have found pleasure, adventure, and education in collecting rocks or shells. This booklet will not tell everything, since that would need many large volumes. It aims to arouse curiosity about two delightful pastimes, broad enough to lead to a career or a satisfying hobby. Shell's name, it notes, comes from seashells brought from the Orient for mother-of-pearl buttons and knife handles, long before oil drilling. Readers get a friendly starter guide, clear and encouraging.
47739-the-wyndham-girls:
Marion Ames Taggart wrote The Wyndham Girls. The Century Company issued it at New York in 1902. C M Relyea drew its pictures. Taggart gave the book to Carolyn Wells. Eighteen chapters carry the tale. Poor Humpty Dumpty heads the first.

Friends, Counselors, and Plans fills chapter two. Ways and Means and Making the Best of It follow. Phyllis and Barbara enter the lists at five. Mark Tapley's Kind of Days heads chapter six. A sea of troubles gets arms taken against it. Discoveries and Loyal Phyllis build the middle. The Square Becomes a Triangle turns the plot. Holly wreathing and a harvest moon close the tale. A front plate shows Tom cooking steak at camp. Plucky sisters facing lean times anchor this bright family tale of work, love, and holding a home together.
47854-greenacre-girls:
Greenacre Girls is a novel for young readers by Izola Forrester, published in 1915. The story gathers a household of girls under their motherbird, with chapters titled The Finger of Providence, Breakers Ahead, Kit Rebels, White Hyacinths, and Spying the Promised Land. The girls plan lawn fêtes, Valentines with a boy Cupid in a white suit hung with red hearts, and rescues by Cousin Roxy.

Forrester writes the warm, bustling domestic fiction that series publishers sold to American girls before the First World War. Kit, Helen, Jean, and Doris scheme, quarrel, and make up across twenty chapters, ending with Roxana's romance. The book preserves the texture of that world: church socials, hired girls, and hope harvested in season.
47956-christmastide-its-history-festivit:
Christmastide is a book on the past and the rites of the feast. William Sandys, a fellow of the old-lore guild, wrote it. It came out in London with plates of feasts of past reigns. One plate shows a play staged for a great queen of old.

Sandys traces the gifts, games, and great meals of the twelve days. The boar's head borne in with song gets a plate of its own. The lord who ruled the fun of the feast is set out in the text. The tree that now marks the feast has its own place late in the book. A long run of old songs fills the back of the work. Songs of the birth, of ships, and of the saints are all there.
48063-a-little-garden-calendar-for-boys-:
A Little Garden Calendar for Boys and Girls is a children's nature book by Albert Bigelow Paine. Altemus of Philadelphia published it in 1905 with forty six illustrations. Paine had written The Arkansaw Bear and The Little Lady. A word to teachers and parents opens the book. It borrows a motto from the Smithsonian's Children's Room: knowledge begins in wonder. Curious eggs, nests, and insects there excite the young mind.

Paine offers the calendar in that same spirit. Simple language tells a few wonders of plant life. Easy methods of observation run month by month through the year. Planting, tending, and gathering the harvests give the frame. Human like instincts and family relations among plants draw the eye. The struggle for existence of all living things underlies the lessons.
48959-moorland-idylls:
Moorland Idylls is a book of nature essays by Grant Allen, the author of The Evolutionist at Large. It was published in London by Chatto and Windus in 1896. The essays watch one stretch of moor and copse through the year.

The first piece listens to the night-jar on a late verandah. Others treat the adder at rest, a flight of quails, and a butterfly in passing. Winter brings the frozen pond and the leafless woods. Spring brings coltsfoot flowers and the chrysalis year. A moorland fire, a gnarled pine, and the crouch oak each get a study. The set ends with the harebell and the untamable shrew. Allen writes as a neighbour to the wild things he names, in a plain and fond style.
4914-the-motor-girls:
Margaret Penrose's Motor Girls opens with Cora Kimball and her brother Jack sparring over a mysterious object, setting the tone for a lively girls' adventure story. Cora, quick with sarcasm and ready for a joke about kindling wood, leads a circle of friends whose motoring trips bring scrapes, rivalries, and small mysteries.

The book belongs to the early automobile age, when a car meant freedom for young women as well as trouble on rough roads. Penrose keeps the dialogue brisk and the friendships warm. Readers get a light, cheerful serial adventure, written for girls who wanted heroines behind the wheel rather than waiting at home.
49274-a-guide-to-the-exhibition-of-engli:
A Guide to the Exhibition of English Medals is the British Museum's guide to its medal cases. Herbert Grueber of the Department of Coins and Medals wrote it. This second edition was printed by order of the trustees in 1891. The medals shown were picked for their historical interest from the larger series in the Medal Room.

They stand in cases marked E, F, G, and H. The gold pieces are shown as electrotypes, and lead pieces as coloured plaster casts. Each medal is labelled and numbered to match its description in the guide. The introduction gives as much background as its limits allow. The book is both a visitor's guide and a short history of England in metal.
4930-paste-jewels:
John Kendrick Bangs's Paste Jewels gathers stories about domestic servants, all based, the author insists, on incidents he observed over ten years. With one stated exception, every servant in the tales was hired only after presenting references from responsible persons, references that could properly have gone only to domestics of sterling character.

The moral points itself: fine references proved no guard against trouble, and paste jewels glitter beside real ones in these tales of theft, deception, and household chaos. Bangs tells the stories with dry humor. Readers get a witty, slightly worldly set of servant tales, where respectability itself becomes the joke.
50543-short-stories-for-high-schools:
Rosa M R Mikels edited Short Stories for High Schools in nineteen fifteen, with an opening essay and notes. Mikels taught at Shortridge High School in Indianapolis. The book was meant for classroom use, with guidance on how to use it.

Her essay states that a short story must make one single strong effect. Tales by Henry van Dyke, Joel Chandler Harris, and Ruth McEnery Stuart open the set. Poe's Gold Bug, O Henry's Ransom of Red Chief, and a tale by Mark Twain follow. Work by Stevenson, Wharton, and Galsworthy rounds out a strong school reader.
51031-more-about-the-squirrels:
More About the Squirrels continues a nature diary by Eleanor Tyrrell. Nelson published it in London, Edinburgh, and New York. Tyrrell had earlier told how she tamed wild squirrels. That book appeared in the autumn of 1914. Coloured plates show the animals at play.

A foreword explains the sequel's birth. Readers wrote from across the kingdom and empire. Their letters thanked her for relief from war sadness. Many asked for more news of Fritz. Fritz, her first squirrel, has enjoyed the garden four years. His first wife deserted him. A fierce red successor bore him a charming son. The book divides into three parts. The last is called Freedom and Happiness.
51122-the-men-in-the-walls:
William Tenn wrote The Men in the Walls, a short tale with drawings by Finlay, first printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in October nineteen sixty three. The head note says the tale came from that magazine. The world is split between the Men and the Monsters, but which are which is the riddle. Mankind counts just one hundred twenty eight people in more than a dozen burrows.

Bands of the Male Society hold the outer four burrows with twenty three young men in their prime. They stand to take the first shock of any danger. Eric the Only is a young trainee, a fetcher and carrier for proved men. On his birthday he must go forth to Steal for Mankind. If he comes back, he wins the straps of a warrior and a voice in council. A strange, tense tale follows.
51315-how-or-spare-hours-made-profitable:
How, or Spare Hours Made Profitable for Boys and Girls, by Kennedy Holbrook, was printed in New York by Worthington in 1887, under an 1886 copyright. Holbrook said the book grew from work for the children of his own family. He meant it for rainy Saturdays and the long vacation.

In his preface he says all in it comes from his own trials or those of trusted friends. He aimed to meet the wants of children of all ages and conditions, and to shun any subject that could worry a careful parent. The index runs to pets, plants, and aquariums, with notes on keeping a gold fish globe, plants for fresh water tanks, and salt water tanks. Young readers get pastimes that fill spare hours with useful fun.
5145-the-heart-of-the-hills:
John Fox Jr.'s mountain novel opens in June 1912 with twin spirals of blue smoke rising over the Kentucky hills, and it stays close to that country throughout. Mountain families, feuds, and the slow arrival of the outside world shape the lives of its people, as the hills themselves, in their moods and seasons, press upon every choice.

Fox dedicated the book to his father's memory, and its affection for mountain life runs through the story. Readers will find feuds, love, and loyalty set against a landscape Fox knew well, in a novel that helped fix the popular image of Appalachia for a generation of readers.
51669-the-lamps-of-the-angels:
The Lamps of the Angels is a tale by Richard Sabia from Galaxy Magazine. Dick Francis drew the pictures for the June 1962 printing of it. Golden guardians bar mankind from the stars in the tale's first lines. Those guardians wield might no man can resist, and something more. The tale then drops to a small kitchen patio on Earth.

Mrs Sanchez asks her son Roberto why he crept in like a thief. He swears he moved quiet as moonlight through the late night house. She hears her children always, even the little one in his grave. His father teases that she keeps the old ways of the soil. Their children freed the house from bondage to field work, he says. Yet she bakes her own bread and works a garden by hand. Sky men and farm folk meet in Sabia's quiet, strange tale.
51899-loafing-along-death-valley-trails:
William Caruthers tells his own loafing along Death Valley trails here. Death Valley Publishing printed it at Ontario, California, in 1951. He gives the book to his wife, who shared desert hardships. She urged it into print, the dedication says with warmth.

Contents open with what caused Death Valley and the Winters tale. John Searles lake of ooze, valley geology, and Indians follow. Desert gold, Greenwater boom town, and the Amargosa country appear. Death Valley Scotty, lost mines, and Panamint City fill later chapters. Shorty Frank Harris and a million dollar poker game fill two more of the chapters.
51949-horse-stories-and-stories-of-other:
Thomas Knox wrote tales of horses and more beasts for boys who love them. His book came out in New York in 1890. Knox wrote Dog Stories and The Boy Travellers in past works. Two boys' own work with horses frames the book's bright core. Charley and George and what they sought lead the first part.

The rule of kind acts is taught ere tales crowd the page. Old Jane's tale and a horse that ran for aid stand there. A glad sick horse and fire horses of New York fill it. Fire house drill for beasts shows in Knox's keen watch notes. Likes, spites, and sharp minds in horses fill the mid tales. Old army horse lore closes it.
52084-the-wire-devils:
The Wire Devils is a crime novel by Frank L Packard, printed in New York by A L Burt Company in 1918. Packard had written Greater Love Hath No Man and The Adventure of Jimmie Dale. Twenty chapters trace a gang that works the telegraph wires.

Heads open with the secret code, the ten dollar counterfeit note, and the paymaster safe. At Bald Creek Station, a cash box vanishing, and some of the little spiders follow. Wanted, the Hawk, dead or alive, threads in the web, and the looting of the fast mail pace the mid tale. The ladybird, an even break, and a hole in the wall raise the stakes. The tale opens at a siding between two switch lights, all else black, with the Rockies rearing westward. Crime fans get wire age robbery and a hunt.
52085-half-hours-with-the-lower-animals:
Charles Frederick Holder wrote a nature book for young readers, printed in New York in 1905. Holder had written a life of Louis Agassiz and tales of animal life. His half hours start with the inhabitants of a drop of water. Sponges, jellyfish, sea anemones, and corals follow in short, clear chapters.

Stone lilies, starfish, sea urchins, and sea cucumbers come next. Shells with two valves, univalves, and cuttlefish lead on to crustaceans. Crabs that glow in the dark earn a chapter of their own. Insects close the book, from spiders and grasshoppers to butterflies, ants, bees, and wasps. Plain facts and wonder fill each brief lesson for the school and home.
52214-bessie-on-her-travels:
Bessie on Her Travels is a girls' story by Joanna H Mathews. It is one of the Bessie Books, a set of six tales for young readers. Bessie Bradford and her sister Maggie stand at the heart of the series.

The tale opens with packing up in the girls' own room. Four little girls are to start on their travels the next day. A sea voyage of three or four days lies ahead of them. None but Belle has ever been to sea before. Chapters on small acts of kindness and water lilies mix fun with gentle lessons. The Bradford girls were loved figures in Mathews' long series.
52289-a-vendetta-of-the-hills:
A Vendetta of the Hills, a novel by Willis George Emerson, author of Buell Hampton and The Builders, was published at Boston in 1917. Emerson dedicates the book to his wife Bonnie, with a verse on their fleeting years of pleasure. Thirty-nine chapters run from Guadalupe and Charmed Lives through old bandit days, a letter from San Quentin, and a jail delivery, to love and revenge.

Chapter heads name La Siesta, Tia Teresa, a rejected suitor, and a sped bullet. A quarrel opens the feud; Pierre Luzon returns to stir it. Caverns, underground wonders, and a debt of honor thicken the plot. Emerson sets his tale in the old Spanish-California world of dons and bandits, where family honor drives men to prison, ambush, and late comprehension.
5253-the-maid-of-the-whispering-hills:
Vingie E. Roe's Maid of the Whispering Hills, published in January 1912, is a romance of the Canadian North-West. Its chapters follow venturers, new homes, a stranger from civilisation, Nor'westers, spring trade, forest news. Gold fire follows, as a young woman's life intertwines with traders, trappers, and the peoples of the hills.

Roe dedicated the book to her mother, her father, and her little brother, long asleep on the hill at Carney. The novel offers readers a vivid frontier romance, with long trails, fellow captives. A compelling power draws its heroine onward through the whispering hills.
52627-library-ideals:
Library Ideals gathers the addresses and papers of Henry Legler, compiled and edited by his son and issued at Chicago in 1918. A portrait of Legler faces the title. The contents open with the problem of the cities. Phases of library extension, next steps, and the world of print and the world's work follow in the first half.

Library work with children, travelling libraries, and the handling of library funds close the list. The opening paper takes the census as its text. Its maze of figures holds a foretelling as well as a record, Legler argues. For those who care about making wise citizens, the striking fact is not the growth of trade but the amazing growth of the cities. Public libraries, in his creed, are the city's answer to its own crowds.
5268-courts-and-criminals:
Arthur Train's Courts and Criminals gathers essays written between 1905 and 1910 on the American criminal courts. Opening with the fiction that every accused man is presumed innocent, Train follows the case of a young man named Duffy, dragged to headquarters. He was photographed without leave. Train then examines how cases are prepared, how juries are swayed, and why men kill.

Train, a New York prosecutor turned writer, uses statistics on murder and conviction alongside courtroom stories. The book offers a lively, critical portrait of early twentieth-century justice. It remains readable for anyone curious about how courts really worked behind their formal rules.
5274-the-chaplet-of-pearls:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Chaplet of Pearls is a historical novel of France in the Wars of Religion. It opens with the bridal of the white and black, follows a separation and a family council. It moves through a convent bird, a wedding with crimson favours, and a king's tragedy. A palace of slaughter follows, toward the hearths and thickets of the Bocage.

Yonge sets Catholic and Huguenot loyalties against family honour and love, in the manner of her historical romances. The novel offers readers a dramatic, richly detailed picture of sixteenth-century France, where a chaplet of pearls passes through danger, disguise, and devotion.
52818-that-awful-letter-a-comedy-for-gir:
That Awful Letter is a comedy for girls by Edna Randolph Worrell, issued in Paine's Popular Plays by the Paine Publishing Company of Dayton, Ohio, at twenty-five cents. Worrell was a supplier of school entertainments, and the pamphlet's covers advertise her entertainment songs for school programmes at the same price.

The play belongs to the world those advertisements describe: school and parlour performance by children, with songs to open and close the programme. The song list promises welcome songs, a patriotic marching song, a lullaby for a solo girl with a chorus of girls with dolls, and duets for little folks. The play itself, a girls' comedy built around a letter, was sold as part of that repertoire. Such pamphlets were the working stock of the American school entertainment, cheap, portable and endlessly reusable.
5311-parnassus-on-wheels:
Christopher Morley's Parnassus on Wheels presents itself as the story of a woman who told it to Morley with inimitable vivacity. Morley sends the book to David Grayson of Hempfield with an acknowledgment, noting that Mrs Mifflin, unskilled in authorship, hardly realised how much her story owed to Grayson's own writings.

The tale follows a travelling book wagon, Parnassus, and the woman who buys it and takes to the road selling books. Readers get a charming, bookish road novel, celebrating reading, independence, and the open road. The story launched Morley's beloved bookseller Roger Mifflin.
53675-the-story-of-the-gravelys-a-tale-f:
Marshall Saunders wrote The Story of the Gravelys for girls. L C Page and Company issued it at Boston in 1904. Saunders wrote Beautiful Joe before this. A child's needless tear is a blood-blot, the motto says. Cardinal Manning spoke those words first. The book goes to her sister Grace.

Grace was her faithful helper in literary work. The Quarrel opens the tale in chapter one. Grandma's Watchword follows with family counsel. Saunders's other books line the front pages. Beautiful Joe's Paradise costs a dollar twenty there. Tilda Jane and Rose a Charlitte stand at a dollar fifty. Kindness to the weak runs through all her work. A girls' tale from the Beautiful Joe author carries her humane creed into family quarrels and making up.
5438-glenloch-girls:
Grace M. Remick wrote Glenloch Girls as the story of a pleasant winter in the lives of some everyday girls and boys. The introduction admits the tale may not sound exciting, then argues that most young people live simple lives, and that ordinary friendship can still make a good story. Ruth Shirley, one of the girls, expects changes that will test her circle.

Chapters follow three chums, a newcomer, a new club, the Social Six, caps and aprons, Christmas presents, and a lost-and-found adventure. Illustrated by Ada C. Williamson, the book favors warmth over danger. Young readers get a gentle school story about friends, clubs, and small troubles handled with kindness.
54649-dorothy-dale-s-school-rivals:
Margaret Penrose sends her schoolgirl heroine back to Glenwood in a series tale issued by Cupples and Leon at New York in 1912. Six Dorothy Dale books and five Motor Girls books fill the author's list.

The frontispiece shows Tavia calling to someone in the water: don't be afraid, it can't sink. Dorothy rides the train with her blue eyes on the window and sees nothing. Her mind bends on an unpleasant thought. Tavia fusses in the next seat, scattering books, candy boxes, and gloves. The contents promise rival runs, chocolates and sandwiches, and a lunch counter run by the girls. An upset canoe and a rescue wet the middle chapters. Dorothy's worries drive the plot. Penrose was a house name for several swift writers of girls' series.
54801-the-garden-without-walls:
The Garden Without Walls is a novel by Coningsby Dawson, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1913. Its first book is called The Walled-In Garden, under a motto from Genesis about the garden and the flaming sword. The narrator tells his own story from its very start. His earliest recollection is of six in the morning in a large red room, a bar of sunlight streaming in with dancing dust-motes.

He stands in his cot plucking at his mother with podgy fingers. She stirs, smiles, and draws him under the bed-clothes beside her, while his father sleeps on. If the soul is born with the first glimmering of memory, he says, that was the morning his soul entered the world. He doubts he has ever grown wiser than that first scene holds.
54847-the-red-house-mystery-the-piccadil:
Mrs Hungerford wrote this novel of the Red House on a high hill. The Piccadilly Novels set carried the tale for Boots shops sale. Chapter one sets the house bleak, lone, and cut off from sun. Cypress trees in a dense row shade the hall door darkly.

A barren rock rises sheer at the back of the house plot. From it, clear days give a grand view of the warm vale. Folk on the road wonder at its dark red, blood like hue. Doctor Darkham took the place ten years before the tale opens.
55067-yorkshire-dales-and-fells:
Gordon Home painted and described the dales and fells of Yorkshire in a travel book printed in London in 1906. Home had also made a book on the Yorkshire coast and moors. The book holds thirty two full page pictures in color. It opens with a broad look at the dale country as a whole.

Chapters then lead the reader town by town and dale by dale. Richmond, Swaledale, and Wensleydale come first, then Ripon and Fountains Abbey. Later parts cover Knaresborough, Harrogate, Wharfedale, Skipton, Malham, and Settle. Falls, castles, old houses, and high moor views fill the pages, and the text tells what a visitor will see at each stop.
55609-the-squirrel-s-pilgrim-s-progress-:
Williams wrote this animal story for boys and girls, published at Chicago by Laird and Lee under a 1915 copyright, with fifty illustrations by Wood, five of them colored plates. Its full title promises the adventures of Tiny Red Squirrel and Chatty Chipmunk. It names the pupils of Miss Hare's school: Reynard Fox, Pussy Cat, and others, with Wise Owl as a director and Billy Beaver as janitor.

Williams grounds the tale in his own boyhood, when his parents took him from city noise to a log house in a great forest clearing. The story, he says, should teach young readers to see material things as they really are, and to observe nature closely, from nest building and bird music to the growth of plants. A Longfellow motto heads the book, of nature the old nurse taking the child on her knee with a story-book his father wrote.
55891-the-family-on-wheels:
The Family on Wheels is a story adapted from the French by Oxley, author of The Boy Tramps. Thomas Crowell published it in New York in 1905. The tale introduces the Tamby family, travelling performers with a caravan. Their elephant Nalla stands at the centre of the adventures.

Chapters show the family in public, at the Beaulieu fair, and before a magistrate. Nalla stampedes, is lost, is recovered, and plays pranks and rescues in turn. A remarkable fencer and a record collection of coins add to the turns. Nadine's illness brings the family to a desperate strait before the return to Morainville. The story ends with the family reunited at last.
55907-the-golden-circle-a-mystery-story-:
Roy Snell wrote The Golden Circle, a mystery story for girls published by Reilly and Lee in Chicago in 1931. The story opens on Friday the thirteenth. Petite Jeanne, a little French girl, sits up in bed and sings that this is her lucky day. Her friend Florence Huyler threatens her with a heavy sofa pillow if she does not lie down and sleep. Florence has muscle, the narrator notes, and has been developing herself of late.

Thirty-six chapters of incident follow. A magic umbrella, six ferocious bears, and a marble falcon appear early. Gypsy gods of fire, a hole in the floor, and bags of forbidden treasure fill the middle. A kidnapping, tilting floors, and a pursuit lead to Florence getting her man and the golden triumph. Snell wrote fast-moving mysteries for girls between the wars, with plucky heroines and Chicago streets for a playground.
56128-the-cottage-on-the-fells:
H de Vere Stacpoole, author of The Blue Lagoon, opens a mystery tale on the pier at Boulogne. Henry Frowde issued the Toronto printing. Two friends watch the Folkestone boat leave in an east wind.

Comyns cannot see why Hellier lingers in such a benighted hole. Comyns is handsome and wealthy. His father made bicycle lamps and motor horns in Wolverhampton. His grandfather laid railway plate. Hellier's family runs the other way, downward. Hellier is a briefless barrister with two hundred and fifty pounds a year. His chambers sit in Clifford's Inn. Gaboriau's novels, read as a boy, pushed him toward the law. He calls housebreaking the most romantic of professions. The fells cottage of the title waits to test that taste.
56503-tyburn-tree-its-history-and-annals:
Alfred Marks wrote Tyburn Tree, its history and annals, published in London by Brown, Langham and Company. Marks had written on the murder of Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey. His subject here is the famous gallows at Tyburn, near modern Marble Arch, where London executed its felons for centuries. A picture shows a gibbet on Kennington Common about 1748.

The title pages gather grim testimony. Thomas More, writing about 1516, praised the strait and rigorous justice executed there, with twenty hanged together on one gallows. Chief Justice Fortescue had noted that more men were hanged in England in a year than in France in seven. Verses from The Ship of Fools describe the condemned man's clothes sold at Newgate and his body ascending the gibbet. Marks assembles the records of the place: its processions, its crowds, and its long roll of the executed, famous and forgotten alike.
5682-fundamental-principles-of-the-metap:
Immanuel Kant's 1785 work on the foundations of morals, translated by Thomas Kingsmill Abbott, asks what makes an act right before asking what results it brings. Kant begins from the old Greek division of knowledge into physics, ethics, and logic, then separates what we learn from experience from what reason alone can supply. Morals, he argues, need principles that hold for every rational being, not rules fitted to one person's wishes.

The book builds its case step by step. It moves from ordinary ideas of duty and good will toward a strict test for maxims. Act only on a rule you could will as a law for all. Readers need not agree with every step to gain from it, since Kant's clarity forces a reader to state plainly why an act is justified. It remains a central text for ethics, law, and any debate about duty versus outcome.
57095-a-chronicle-of-jails:
Darrell Figgis wrote A Chronicle of Jails as a journal of his time held as a political prisoner. The third edition was published in Dublin by the Talbot Press in 1918. A note dated May 28, 1917, says the pages were first kept as a private record of days when his own fate crossed a wider national cause.

The narrative opens on Tuesday, April 25, 1916, with spring weather, farm work, and a book long overdue to its publisher. Figgis admits the record is not complete and explains why gaps must wait for a later edition. Readers get a calm, close account of arrest and jail life in Ireland at a tense moment.
5725-english-literature-for-boys-and-gir:
H E Marshall introduces English literature to young readers in a long, story-driven survey, from the listening time of oral tale to modern writers. Early chapters cover the cattle raid of Cooley, Fingal, old Welsh storytellers, Arthur in English, Beowulf, Caedmon, Alfred the Great, Havelok the Dane, and Piers the Ploughman. Later chapters reach Chaucer at the Tabard Inn, Barbour's Bruce, and the poet kings of Scotland.

Marshall tells literary history as a chain of stories, so a child meets each writer through a tale rather than a date. Readers gain a map of English letters that is easy to follow and pleasant to read aloud. The book remains a useful family introduction, especially for homeschooling or bedtime reading, since it treats old books as adventures waiting to be heard.
57339-the-fox-that-wanted-nine-golden-ta:
The Fox That Wanted Nine Golden Tails is a children's tale by Kathleen Gray Nelson, published by the Devin-Adair Company of New York in 1915. Its hero is a Japanese fox who knows secrets his American brothers have never heard.

The first chapter lays out the rules of fox magic. If a fox lives a hundred years without ever being chased by a dog, he can become a beautiful woman. Five hundred years of peace would make him a mighty wizard who knows more than any man on earth. Best of all, after a thousand unchased years he would turn into a celestial fox with nine golden tails. A beautiful woman does very well in her place, and a wise man is a great honour. But a fox with nine golden tails is the most wonderful thing in all the world. An exciting adventure settles his course.
57467-lauds-and-libels:
C L Graves gathered his light verse in Lauds and Libels, issued at London in 1918. Most of the pieces had first run in Punch, whose owners and editor let him reprint them. The book falls in three parts: Men, Women, and Books; War Workers and Others; and Lays of the Larder, with a close of mixed pieces. The first part holds verses to Stephen Leacock, lines on re-reading Barchester Towers and Bleak House, and a house-master, an old matron, and Constable Jinks.

The war part treats Mr Balfour on his return, the flapper, and a new knight. The larder lays sing of sugar, tea shortage, margarine, eels, and the war pig, all under the pinch of food rules in wartime. Graves writes praise and blame in the same neat, laughing vein: a light verse view of London in wartime.
57551-confidential-chats-with-girls:
Confidential Chats with Girls, by William Lee Howard, a physician who wrote plain-spoken health books, was published in New York in 1911. Howard addresses mothers' daughters directly, in chapters on growing into womanhood, menstruation and general health, skin and complexion, nerves, will power, and keeping attractive. A companion volume did the same for boys.

Howard explains the body in simple terms, using plants and animals to show how mating and growth run through all living things. His tone is frank for its day, aiming to replace rumor and fear with fact. The book belongs to the early sex-hygiene movement, when doctors first wrote openly for young readers, and it shows both the candor and the limits of that moment.
57774-a-sheaf-of-bluebells:
Orczy's A Sheaf of Bluebells, printed in Toronto in 1917, is a novel of France under Napoleon by the author of The Scarlet Pimpernel. It opens with petitions from exiled nobles begging leave to return home under the new Emperor's conditional amnesty.

Two petitions matter most: one from the Marquise de Mortain and her son Laurent, aged twenty-one, and one from the Comte de Courson for himself and his daughter Fernande. Fouché, the feared minister of police, calls the returning nobles a brood of plotters and wants them kept out. Napoleon, about to march into Prussia, leans toward mercy. The clash between police suspicion and old loyalties drives the tale that follows.
5804-the-story-of-a-lamb-on-wheels:
The Story of a Lamb on Wheels follows a toy lamb through small adventures told in short chapters. The lamb wishes, meets a jolly sailor, finds a home on shore, and slides downhill into great danger. Later chapters send the lamb down a coal hole, carried away, sailing down a brook, and riding on a load of wood, until Mirabell is happy at last.

Young readers join a world where toys wake, wander, and worry, much like children themselves. The story favors gentle mishaps over real fright, with each chapter ending safely enough for bedtime. It suits early readers and read-aloud families who enjoy old-fashioned toy tales, where a lamb on wheels learns the world one bump at a time.
5830-a-garland-for-girls:
Louisa May Alcott gathers flower-named stories for girls in A Garland for Girls, affectionately inscribed to a friend. Contents include May Flowers, An Ivy Spray and Ladies' Slippers, Pansies, Water-Lilies, Poppies and Wheat, Little Button-Rose, and Mountain-Laurel and Maiden-Hair. Each story takes a flower as its emblem, weaving blossom, season, and girlhood into a gentle tale.

Readers get Alcott's warm moral storytelling at its most charming, with heroines learning kindness, patience, and courage through everyday trials. The stories favor home, friendship, and nature over grand adventure, and they suit read-aloud families and young readers. Fans of Alcott will recognize her voice here, softer than in her novels but just as sure about what matters.
58407-bill-bolton-and-the-winged-cartwhe:
Bill Bolton and the Winged Cartwheels is a boys air tale by Noel Sainsbury. Bill stands in a line of tales as a young flyer of the sea arm. A gift page names a real friend as more brave than the tale shows. Rights date the work to the year nineteen thirty three.

A first find and a mark of number fifty seven open the chain of clues. Theft, a home raid, and a hunch of Bills drive the mid parts in turn. A shift to the great seat of rule and a man with a wheeze raise stakes. A shot flame, a wise man talk, and a vast gun close the tale. Air craft and spy craft share the pull of the swift boys book.
58785-the-gray-angels:
Nalbro Bartley wrote The Gray Angels, a novel dated nineteen twenty at Boston. Bartley had written A Woman's Woman and Paradise Auction. The scene is Birge's Corners, a quiet small town.

The young folk insist nothing stirring has happened since a love affair in eighteen sixty-seven. Their elders answer that Thurley Precore is bound to create excitement. The Hotel Button, a two-story house with ramshackle sheds, anchors the town. Travellers praise Prince Hawkins's welcome and his wife's cooking. In cold snaps at twenty below, sleigh riders gladly end at her oyster suppers. Lena Button, once an only child, now works like a slave there. Generations clash gently.
58928-princess-kiku-a-japanese-romance-a:
Princess Kiku, A Japanese Romance, is a play for girls with female characters only, sold at twenty five cents. It was issued in New York by a publisher of amateur plays whose catalogue fills the front matter. Comedies and dramas at fifteen cents each are advertised around it, with cast counts and running times. School and parlour theatricals were the market for such scripts.

A Japanese princess romance in girls' hands offered costume, manners, and a far off court in safe form. Amateur play catalogues of this kind list each piece by acts, hours, and numbers of male and female parts. Princess Kiku's all girl cast suited schools and clubs that staged plays without boys. Exotic setting sold the script.
59236-the-ingoldsby-legends-or-mirth-and:
Ingoldsby Legends, or Mirth and Marvels, is a set of comic verse tales. Thomas Ingoldsby was the pen name of the Reverend Richard Barham. Warne published this edition in London and New York in 1889. Eighteen illustrations by Cruikshank, Leech, and others enrich the book. A memoir and a preface front the three series of legends.

The Spectre of Tappington opens the first series of tales in rhyme. The Hand of Glory, Grey Dolphin, and The Ghost follow in that list. The Jackdaw of Rheims is the most famed piece in the set. Lays of saints Dunstan, Gengulphus, Odille, and Nicholas mix mock awe. Barham's rhymes turn ghost lore and church legend into broad fun.
59385-the-street-of-precious-pearls:
The Street of Precious Pearls is a tale of life in China by Nora Waln. It was put out at New York in nineteen twenty one. Its rights were held that year by a board of young women's bands. The book is sworn to the women of America. Its tale is that of a friend and teach of the hand in China. A word of thanks at the front names the maid who first urged the trip east.

From the women of China, the hand says, she learned a great truth. World kin ship is not a thought of the mind a lone. It is a law of birth, by which the hearts of all women beat to one beat of the whole. The tale is as true as the two could make it.
59618-the-history-of-court-fools:
The History of Court Fools, by Doctor Doran, was issued at London by Richard Bentley in 1858. Bentley was publisher in ordinary to Her Majesty in that year. Doran had written Table Traits, Habits and Men, and Queens of the House of Hanover. A life of Young the poet also stands in his list at the front.

His subject is the licensed jester of kings and great lords. Fools by office wore the cap and bells in courts across Europe. They alone might mock a monarch and live to laugh again. Doran gathers their sayings, pranks, and strange ends from the records. Some were wits, some were half mad, and some were wise men in motley. The book is a merry and melancholy history of a dead profession.
60100-anthony-trollope-his-work-associat:
Anthony Trollope, His Work, Associates and Literary Originals, by T H S Escott, was printed in London and New York by John Lane in 1913. A drawing of Trollope by Samuel Lawrence stands at the front. Escott gives the book to Trollope kin and to the few friends whose memory of him is fresh and dear.

The first chapter, Apprenticeship to Life, tells of Trollope ancestry, true and fabled, and of the Hampshire novelists. Frances Milton girlhood, her marriage to Thomas Anthony Trollope, and the settlement in Keppel Street follow. The American experiment, the sale of their goods, and Mrs Trollope rise as a famed authoress pace the tale. Anthony school days at Harrow and a family flight to Bruges close the chapter. Life fans get a full portrait of the novelist and his circle.
60517-the-courtship-of-animals:
The Courtship of Animals is a work of natural history by Pycraft, of the zoological department of the British Museum, published in London by Hutchinson in its third edition. Forty plates on art paper carry more than eighty illustrations. A frontispiece plate is titled Love-Making.

Pycraft dedicates the book to Eliot Howard, whose observations of bird courtship he calls a beacon for students of animal behaviour. The early chapters treat mankind in the making, with the use of the word courtship itself examined. Man's cousins the apes follow, including musical chimpanzees and an orang-utan improving his voice. The book argues that display, song, and ornament run through the animal world. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
60816-the-elements-of-perspective-arrang:
Elements of Perspective is a teaching treatise on drawing in perspective. The text forms part of the library edition of John Ruskin complete works. Ruskin arranged the elements for the use of schools and art students. Diagram letters in the old printing use italic and small capital forms.

A transcriber note lists the angle, ratio, and proportion signs used here. Prime and double prime marks label the figures in the lessons. Ruskin builds the rules of perspective from plain geometry step by step. Students learn how lines meet, vanish, and measure on the picture plane. The treatise served school art teaching in the Victorian age and after.
6085-the-code-of-honor-or-rules-for-the-:
John Lyde Wilson, former governor of South Carolina, published his Code of Honor in 1838 as a 22-page booklet, sized to fit in the case with one's duelling pistols. An appendix of the 1777 Irish code, added before his death, reached print only in 1858, making a 46-page small book.

The code is far less bloodthirsty than many suppose, Wilson's transcribers note, but built on a closed caste and standards alien to today. A rencontre, a fight in heat of offense, counted as manslaughter, while a duel in cold blood counted as murder. Posting an offender meant publishing notice of his behavior in a club.
6111-over-prairie-trails:
Frederick Philip Grove writes Over Prairie Trails from years teaching in a small prairie town. His wife and little daughter lived near the northern timber, not far from a great lake's western shore. His wife, to round off a far-from-imperial income, took charge of a rural school with a residence.

Grove procured a buggy and horse and drove home Fridays after school, returning Sunday evenings. The trip ran sixty-eight miles each way in clement seasons, and ninety from the second week of January when straight roads failed. Chapters on farms, fog, dawn and diamonds, snow, wind and waves, and skies and scares follow the trail.
6128-his-sombre-rivals:
E. P. Roe writes His Sombre Rivals with regret akin to sadness, taking leave of people who became very real to him, whose joys and sorrows he made his own. Though a Northern man, he believes Southern readers will feel he sought justice for their motives.

At distance from the Civil War, Roe argues, passion and prejudice should sink below the horizon, as among surviving soldiers arrayed against each other they have practically disappeared. Stern conflict taught mutual respect, convincing Northern men they fought Americans whose patriotism was as pure as their own. The novel pleads for large-minded reunion.
61568-when-they-were-girls:
Rebecca Deming Moore wrote When They Were Girls, with drawings by Mabel Betsy Hill and editing by Helen Mildred Owen. F A Owen Publishing Company at Dansville, New York, issued the book in nineteen twenty three. Short lives of famed American women fill the book. Each life stresses the girls traits and links them to the womans later work. The editor intro states that aim in plain terms.

Lives include Jane Addams, Louisa M Alcott, Susan B Anthony, and Clara Barton. Later lives treat Helen Keller, Maria Mitchell, and Harriet Beecher Stowe. Singers, artists, teachers, and reformers share the pages, from Louise Homer to Frances E Willard. One life calls Willard the girl who fought the dragon, drink. Young readers get clear models of grit, study, and service. The book was made to spur girls to aim high and work hard.
61574-selenium-cells:
Selenium Cells is a practical manual on the construction, care, and use of selenium cells, by Thomas Benson, issued in 1919. Special reference is made to the Fritts cell throughout the book. Spon and Chamberlain of New York and Spon of London published it. The work is dedicated with thanks to a man named Steltzer.

Chapter one treats selenium the element, its discovery and naming. Selenium cells change their resistance under light, the fact the book exploits. Makers, telephone men, and experimenters used such cells in that age. Benson tells how to build the cell, mount it, and keep it true. Wiring, testing, and uses fill the working chapters. The manual is a handbook of photo-electric craft before vacuum tubes ruled.
61589-the-training-of-wild-animals:
Frank C Bostock wrote an account of training wild animals, copyrighted in 1903 and edited by Ellen Velvin. Velvin says she lived for some weeks in one of Bostock's animal exhibitions before editing. She wanted to see things as they were, not as she had heard of them. Bostock dedicated the book to his son Francis Edward.

The first chapter tells how he became the boy trainer and hunted a lion in a sewer. Later chapters cover the history of training, housekeeping, and feeding snakes and elephants. Animal character, capture, and the teaching of tricks follow. Famous trainers and guarding against accidents close the book. Many photographs show lions and trainers.
61765-the-pleistocene-of-north-america-a:
Oliver Hay wrote a big science book on the ice-age beasts of North America. The book came out in Washington in February 1923. Hay was a mate of the Carnegie Institution of that town. Its scope is the states east of the great river. The north lands east of a set line share the scope.

First parts fix the bounds and parts of that cold age. Land links to South America and Asia get their due. Rich life, slow change, and loss of kinds fill the sums. The Nebraskan and the warm gaps twixt ice sheets come next. Bone beds and old teeth ground each claim he makes. Beast past fans get a vast, sourced store.
61785-the-plus-food-for-minus-meals:
Plus Food for Minus Meals is a recipe folder for Kellogg All Bran, issued by the Kellogg kitchen. It is arranged in three parts: best for cooking, best for mixing, and best as a cereal. A seal at its head records acceptance by the American Medical Association committee on foods. The folder promises more complete meals with the bran for the housewife.

Perhaps the meals you serve are bulk minus meals, the folder begins in its address. All Bran is the bulk plus food necessary in the well balanced diet, it answers for the reader. All the recipes have been triple tested in the company Cottage Kitchen, it assures the cook.  The piece is Depression era food advertising in pamphlet form, selling a boxed cereal as kitchen science and household economy at once.
62607-in-lakeland-dells-and-fells:
In Lakeland Dells and Fells is a book on England's Lake Country by Palmer. The front pages carry reviews of his earlier Lake-Country Rambles. The Academy calls that volume observant and pleasant, with sound advice. Vanity Fair can hardly imagine a reader unmoved to keen pleasure by it.

The London Quarterly Review found no dull page in the earlier book. The Pall Mall Gazette praises Palmer's range across branches of country sport. The Monthly Register says the spirit of the place is upon him. His pages reflect scenes with a truth that recalls Richard Jefferies. This volume continues the same author's walks through the lakes he knows and loves.
62810-how-to-visit-the-english-cathedral:
How to Visit the English Cathedrals is a guide book by Esther Singleton. Her name fronts a long list of books described by great writers. Turrets, Towers, and Temples heads that list of her earlier volumes. Great Pictures, Wonders of Nature, and Romantic Castles follow in print. Famous Cathedrals, described by great writers, stands among her own works.

Historic Buildings, Famous Women, and Great Portraits fill the list onward. Paris, London, Russia, Japan, Venice, and Holland close the travel shelf. Singleton now turns guide herself to England's great churches for visitors. What to see, and in what order, fills her practical pages. Art, tombs, and architecture get plain directions for the traveller.
62942-modern-short-stories-a-book-for-hi:
Frederick Houk Law edited this school book of modern short stories, first issued in 1918 and printed by the Century Company in New York in 1921. Law taught English at New York University and led the English work at Stuyvesant High School. A long preface asks what a short story is, traces its family tree, and tells pupils how to use the book and where to find more tales.

The tales come from Joel Chandler Harris, Mary Mapes Dodge, Lafcadio Hearn, Ernest Thompson Seton, Leo Tolstoy, and others. Notes and a short guide to books about the short story close the volume. It was made to teach young readers both taste and craft through good models.
63016-masterpieces-of-adventure-adventur:
Nella Braddy put in order Adventures Within Walls, one of four books in a set of great tales of risk. The book came out at Garden City in 1922, with rights from the year past. Braddy gave it with thanks to Blanche Colton Williams. Eight tales make up this book of the set.

Robert Louis Stevenson leads with The Sire de Maletroit Door, a tale of old France. O Henry gives a tale of a twice dyed cheat, and Irving a tale of a bold horse man. Chekhov stakes a bet, and Balzac tells of a great house with a dark past. Poe brings his famed tale of the red death at a masked ball. Dickens gives the hand writ tale of Doctor Manette from his great novel. A tale named Silence, by a man of Russia, closes the set in a grave key.
63104-amid-the-high-hills:
Amid the High Hills, by Sir Hugh Fraser, was printed in London by A and C Black in 1923. Sixteen plates stand in the full book, some in color. A plate shows September snow at Loch Carron in Ross shire, by Finlay Mackinnon. Fraser gives the book to all who love the high hills, and in special to his kinsmen and friends.

A line from Richard Monckton Milnes heads the title, on nature heart beating strong amid the hills. Fraser thanks helpers for photos, among them one named Among the Western Islands. He thanks his son in law, Mr Noel Wills, for a pencil sketch of Donald McIver. McIver was his gamekeeper and constant companion on the hill for many years. Hill fans get Scottish deer forest days, weather, and sport in a laird own words.
63455-the-vanishing-comrade-a-mystery-st:
Ethel Cook Eliot wrote The Vanishing Comrade, a mystery story for girls, from the Sun Dial Press in New York. Copyright rests in nineteen twenty four, and the edition here is nineteen thirty seven. Eliot gave the book to her sister Helen. Twenty one chapters fill the tale. Chapter one is Great Aunt Katherine Commands. A blurb calls it an unusual mystery about a strange orchard house.

Two boys and a girl climbed down from the Middletown bus at the summer hotel, the tale opens. A plate asks, Was it Kate Marshall, she scarcely knew. The Boy in the Flowery, Dragony Picture Frame follows. Little Orchard House, Beware and Kate Makes Up a Face bring the haunting closer. Kate Meets a Detective and Something of Fairy in It fill the middle. Girls get a brave heroine straightening out a haunted house.
6360-half-a-dozen-girls:
Anna Chapin Ray offers memories of a happy, naughty childhood, dedicated to her parents, with Kingsley's verse on being good and doing noble things. Polly Adams chants a rhyme at a guest, little girl with a curl, very good when good and horrid when bad. Then she climbs down from the front gate, shakes her curly head, and runs indoors. Upstairs her mother and aunt sew behind closed blinds on a sultry July day, to locust whir and a rocking chair's creak.

The Adams family opens a book of six girls, their mothers, maids, and mischief. Molly asks why a cross maid is kept, and Polly answers that nothing else can be got. Ray writes childhood as it feels, warm, funny, and unforced, where a rhyme, a gate, and a hot afternoon hold a world. The book is a girl's story of home, not of adventure far away.
63619-land-and-sea-tales-for-boys-and-gi:
Land and Sea Tales for Boys and Girls is a story collection by Rudyard Kipling, gathered for young readers. The front matter of this copy lists Kipling's books at length, from The Jungle Book and Kim to Captains Courageous and Puck of Pook's Hill. The dedication, preserved in the copy, is a verse blessing to all to whom the little book may come. It wishes them health for themselves and those they hold dear.

Content abroad and happiness at home come next in the blessing. Then comes one grand secret in the reader's private ear. Nations have passed away and left no traces, and history gives the naked cause of it. One single, simple reason holds in all cases, the verse begins, before the copy breaks off.
63692-familiar-animals:
Familiar Animals is a picture book for young children in the Friendly Animal Series. It was printed at New York by McLoughlin Brothers, with copyright in 1904. The animals tell their own stories in the first person. The first to speak is Molly the cow. The Project Gutenberg copy notes a companion file with the pictures in full colour.

Now she is grown and gives milk to all the children at the farm. Nancy the milkmaid comes with her pail, and Molly is glad she has plenty to give. She tells how cream, butter and cheese are all made from milk. Then she marches down to the river to cool herself and whisk away the flies. The tales teach farm life in the animal's own voice.
63705-buffalo-bill-s-bold-play-or-the-ti:
Buffalo Bill's Bold Play, or the Tiger of the Hills, is a dime novel by Prentiss Ingraham. Ingraham wrote the famed Buffalo Bill tales in the Border Stories line. Street and Smith held the rights from 1909 in New York. A note in front praises William Cody, the scout the tales follow. Twenty chapters run from Juniper Joe's jubilee to a trap sprung late.

Jackson Dane, a detective, and a wandering baron join the scout's ride. Suspicions, strange vanishings, and a startling find crowd the early list. A worried sheriff, an assassin at work, and shifted prisoners follow on. White-Eyed Moses rides on a mission in the mid chapters of the tale. The fool of Folly Mountain lends the plot its odd wild card. Chase and trap close out the bold play of the hills.
64033-betty-wales-junior-a-story-for-gir:
Margaret Warde wrote Betty Wales, Junior, a story for girls issued at Philadelphia in 1906 with pictures by Eva Nagel. Warde had already told Betty's freshman and sophomore years. Betty opens the book on the floor of her own long coveted single room at college, ringed by her unpacked things. All of it came out at once by her own system, and now it is hard to place.

The fun of junior year gives the first chapter its name. A club of Merry Hearts forms, and Georgia Ames enters the tale, widens her sphere, and joins the club. A trip abroad lands the Merry Hearts in Nassau at Easter. Doctor Eaton, Helen, and Eleanor carry subplots, and a dress reform and the return of Georgia close the year. It is college life for girls of its day.
64068-the-platinum-metals:
The Platinum Metals is a monograph by Lumb, printed at London in 1920. It stands in the Imperial Institute's series on mineral resources of the British Empire. Lumb had served in the Institute's scientific and technical department. A map accompanies the text, and John Murray published it.

The Institute's own pages explain its work. It exhibits and studies minerals with a view to their trade growth. Its laboratories assay minerals for governments and firms. A staff gathers facts on supplies, chiefly within the Empire, and on new uses. This volume applies that machinery to platinum and its sister metals, naming where they occur and what they are worth.
6432-betty-wales-sophomore-a-story-for-g:
Margaret Warde, author of Betty Wales, Freshman, Junior, Senior, and B.A., follows Betty into sophomore year in 1905. Betty sits on the one bare spot of her Belden House room floor, sighing with relief and weariness. She tells a green lizard on pillows that things are out of trunks, if not yet in their places. At quarter to eight, Eleanor Watson raps, and Betty leaps over cups and saucers, knocks a Japanese screen onto a bed, and hugs her friend.

Isn't it great to be back, Betty asks, setting the screen up and moving trays so they can sit on the bed. Later, Betty advises Roberta, who gets on with children and older people but not her age, to practise as she would chemistry problems. Figure out what freshmen like, give it to them, and have a party with the Jabberwock. Warde writes college girls' life with humour and warmth.
64452-the-bad-little-owls:
John Breck wrote The Bad Little Owls, book seven of his Told at Twilight Stories, issued in 1923 with art by William Andrews. Breck's tales of woods folk star Nibble the bunny, Tad Coon, and Silvertip the fox. Here a pair of young owls earn the bad name of the title by their deeds.

Ten parts open with the woods folk learning the rules about fire, a grave theme for dry woods. Chaik the jay carries bad news, and Mrs Owl calls in Killer the weasel as an ally, a rash move. Fur and feathers plan a campaign, and Killer plans his own. A big rain ends the evil deeds for a time. The tale teaches care with fire and care with friends.
64978-the-blue-birds-at-happy-hills:
The Blue Birds at Happy Hills is a tale for the young by Lillian Elizabeth Roy, out in nineteen nineteen. Roy was known past a set of tales of five small stars. Parts tell of a date kept with an uncle, of a drill corps of boys, of a street sweep squad, and of a fair of the small folk. A part on the plan of a city home stands in the list.

The tale opens as the Starr twins are lost at the start of a trip. Their kin and a next door chum wait past three beats past them. A shrill pipe from the woods tells that the twins are half way to the meet spot. The girl band and the boy band that prints a sheet meet at a barn house. Two cars must bear the whole crew to the train for the great city.
65558-by-honour-bound-a-school-story-for:
By Honour Bound, a school story for girls by Bessie Marchant, was issued by Nelson in many lands. Marchant also wrote Diana Carries On, as the title page notes for her fans. Chapter one is called What Dorothy Saw in the contents. A shock, pride of place, and a disappointing brother follow in the early heads.

Rhoda jumper, the enrolling of candidates, and a torn book build the school plot. Under a cloud, fair fighting, and Dorothy scores mark the middle turns of the tale. Dorothy is approached, Tom proves hard up, and top of the school comes in reach. A startling revelation and setting the pace close the list of chapters shown. Honour among schoolgirls is the test that the title promises for its heroine.
65576-the-goslings-a-study-of-the-americ:
The Goslings, a study of the American schools by Upton Sinclair, was published at Pasadena in 1924. Sinclair had written The Goose-Step on the colleges the year before. First edition copies ran to five thousand in cloth and five thousand in paper. Chapter one is called Land of Orange Groves and Jails. Later heads name the spy system, lies for children, and the schools of Mammon. A letter to Woodrow Wilson appears as a chapter.

Sinclair attacks graft, timid boards, and business sway over schools. Heads speak of teachers' soviets, honest graft, and the Tammany tiger. Chicago, Colorado, and the lumber country each get chapters. The book is a muckraking tour of public schooling, written to rouse parents and teachers alike.
65907-wounded-souls:
Wounded Souls is a novel by Philip Gibbs, published in New York by George Doran in 1920. Gibbs had written accounts of the war in Flanders and the battles of the Somme. The novel is built in three books, titled The End of the Adventure, Through Hostile Gates, and Builders of Peace.

The opening scene fixes the moment. The narrator finds it hard to recapture the spirit of the day his party entered Lille. After four years of slaughter, the city, which had seemed a world away, stood open at last. Other things since that day, he says, have blurred its fine images. The three book titles trace the arc of the tale: the war's end, a passage through hostile lands, and the slow work of making peace. It is a story of the peace as much as of the war.
66018-miss-lochinvar-a-story-for-girls:
Marion Ames Taggart wrote this tale for girls, printed at New York in 1902. W. L. Jacobs and Bayard F. Jones drew its cuts. It is sent forth to Polly and Jo in the West. A cut at its front shows its maid, Janet: she looked up and down the house that was to be her home. The list of parts is made in a feat of craft. Each head is a line from the old song of young Lochinvar, Scott's tale of the knight who came out of the west.

He lit down at the gate of Netherby, in the first of the heads. Bold in the hall he stood, with no arms but his good broad sword. He rode all on his own, and would not stop for brake or stone.
66393-the-battle-of-the-bells:
The Battle of the Bells, a story by Jerome Bixby, ran in Imagination in September 1954. Charley’s practical joke opens the frame of the tale. It was usually good for a laugh when a city fellow made a rest stop. It also aroused heavenly concern, the first line warns.

The trick worked once or twice a week, never much more. Things had to be just right for it, and daytime was needed. At night, nobody would notice the chain with the handle on its end. The victims had to be city folk, used to reaching up and pulling. Bixby wrote sly science fiction with a backwoods grin. Here a country joke pulls heaven itself into the quarrel.
67431-the-buckaroo-of-blue-wells:
Buckaroo of Blue Wells is a western novel by Tuttle of Hashknife fame. Hashknife and Sleepy meet again in this complete novel, the cover promises. Chapter one, Bookkeepers, opens far from the range in a city. James Eaton Legg hooks his heels over his high stool there. He stretches wearily and looks out at fog over the traffic.

Heavy trucks lumber past, grinding harshly over the cobbles outside his office. A street car motorman does a trap drum effect on his gong. Legg, under thirty, thin faced, with mild blue eyes behind glasses, yawns. For years he has kept books for Mellon, wholesale grocers of San Francisco. The trail from ledger to Blue Wells drives Tuttle's tale west.
67522-rainbow-gold-poems-old-and-new-sel:
Sara Teasdale, a lyric poet, picked a small set of poems old and new for boys and girls called Rainbow Gold, issued in New York in 1922. Dugald Walker drew the art, and Teasdale gave the book to the memory of her father. Her plan, she says, was plain: choose poems that would have pleased the child she used to be.

Above all she kept the book small, since the big verse books of her youth sat untouched on the shelf while the little ones grew worn with love. A year of work went to the choice, and she grants that much she loved had to be left out for space. Songs of the Elizabethans, ballads, and verse by living hands share the pages.
67811-roosevelt-in-the-kansas-city-star-:
Roosevelt in the Kansas City Star collects Theodore Roosevelt's war-time editorials, published at Boston in nineteen twenty-one by Houghton Mifflin. Ralph Stout, managing editor of the Star, supplied the introduction. The volume is the second publication of the Roosevelt Memorial Association. Copyrights run nineteen seventeen through nineteen nineteen, the editorial years.

The contents list Roosevelt's pieces by date, beginning in September nineteen seventeen. Blood, Iron, and Gold and The Ghost Dance of the Shadow Huns set the tone early. He demands universal military training at once and mocks broomstick preparedness. The Liberty Loan, the pro-Germans, and a square deal for the training camps recur. Roosevelt wrote as an ex-president hammering a sitting one toward total war. The editorials keep his wartime voice at full volume.
6804-general-history-for-colleges-and-hi:
P. V. N. Myers bases his General History for colleges and high schools on his earlier Ancient History and his Medieval and Modern History. In places he shifts perspective and proportion, yet the book follows the same lines as those earlier works. A frontispiece shows the Attic plains with a glimpse of the Acropolis at Athens.

Myers admits that, in so wide a field, some error is bound to slip in, though he took great care to check facts and to give the latest finds and criticism. The result is a broad, schoolroom survey from ancient times to modern days. General History is a solid, old-style textbook, clear and well ordered for students.
68074-old-indian-trails:
Old Indian Trails is a book of Blackfoot life by Walter McClintock, printed at Boston and New York in 1923. McClintock took the photographs himself. He dedicates the book to his mother, Clara Childs McClintock. Forty-four chapters and an appendix fill the volume.

The tale opens with his Indian guide and a crossing of the Rocky Mountains. Mad Wolf adopts him, and he receives an Indian name and tribal membership. Chapters give marriage customs, the legend of the Beaver Bundle, and a night with a grizzly bear. Brings-Down-the-Sun tells of men's societies, birds, and stars. The Sun Dance closes the book, with an appendix on Blackfoot plants.
68232-the-story-of-the-thirty-third-n-y-:
David W Judd wrote The Story of the Thirty Third New York State Volunteers, issued at Rochester by Benton and Andrews in eighteen sixty four. Judd was a correspondent of the New York Times. Illustrations come from drawings by Lieutenant L C Mix. Colonel R F Taylor commanded the regiment. A preface states the aim plainly.

The volume does not propose to review the causes of the unhappy civil strife, Judd says. Neither is it designed to describe all the operations of the war in Virginia and Maryland, he adds. It aims merely at a narrative of one regiment the Empire State sent into the field, he writes. The members and friends of the command wanted their scenes and incidents collected in readable shape, he says. The plan gives separate sketches of each company first. Civil War readers get a regimental history written during the war itself.
6850-esther-a-book-for-girls:
Rosa Nouchette Carey tells Esther's story from her last day at Redmayne House to her arrival at Combe Manor, with Dot, Uncle Geoffrey, and an old house at Milnthorpe ahead. A flitting, neighbors over the way, Flurry and Flossy, and the Cedars follow, with a wish for a Dot of her own and a nurse named Miss Ruth. Esther feels she is not like other girls.

A smugglers' cave, a long night, a brave girl's praise, and a letter from home lead toward Christmas and a walk to Eltham Green. Carey writes with gentle, domestic warmth. Esther is a kind, old-style girls' book of home, friendship, and growing up.
68530-crystals:
A E H Tutton wrote Crystals, issued at London in nineteen eleven with one hundred and twenty pictures. Tutton held high posts in the learned bodies for minerals and chemistry. The book formed volume ninety-eight of a science series for general readers.

Early chapters show how sameness of form can hide behind unlike looks. The work of the Abbé Haüy and the seven styles of crystal build follow. Tutton then explains how crystals are described and how their faces are mapped. Mitscherlich and his find of like forms in unlike stuffs get a chapter. Colour plates show quartz and benzoic acid in polarised light.
68551-betty-wales-co-a-story-for-girls:
Margaret Warde wrote this story for girls of Betty Wales and company. Penn printed it at Philadelphia in 1909, Nagel drew plates. Betty Wales Freshman through Senior and her degree book precede it. Contents open with unpleasant discoveries, then Betty Wales with a degree.

That tea room again, plans and parties, and the real thing follow. Eugenia Ford luncheon and Mary the perfect patron fill the middle. A tragic disappearance, more side lines, and a mystery solved come late. Betty calls coming home from abroad the loveliest part of travel. Margaret Warde wrote the college girls story.
69151-the-siege-of-vicksburg-from-the-di:
The Siege of Vicksburg is a Civil War diary edited from the notes of Seth Wells. The book was published at Detroit in 1915. May Wells Bliss and Sarah Ewell Krolik hold its copyright. The diary also covers weeks of march before the siege. It runs on past the surrender into the occupation. A dedication keeps the memory of two Wells men.

The entries begin at Dunlap Springs in November 1862. Wells tells of a snug log house built, then left. New regiments from Jackson strut with fresh pride. Old troops mock them as bounty men and home guards. A review by General McPherson fields ten thousand men. Then the columns march toward Grand Junction. Such diaries fix the war as one soldier lived it. Day-by-day notes carry a weight that memoirs lose.
69382-quaker-idyls:
Sarah M H Gardner wrote Quaker Idyls, tales of quiet Friends at home. Henry Holt and Company issued the book at New York in eighteen ninety four. Twelfth Street Meeting opens the set in a June Sabbath calm. Lucretia Mott takes her place beside a coloured man in one plate.

A Quaker Wedding and Two Gentlewomen fill the next two tales. Our Little Neighbors and Pamelia Tewksbury’s Courtship add home spice. Some Ante Bellum Letters from a Quaker Girl fills the longest span. Uncle Joseph and My Grandame’s Secret close the gentle set. John and Martha Wilson walk to meeting at half past ten. Elders and ministers sit in the gallery in folded hand calm. Cassy Wilson drops her eyes as George Evans marks her coming in. Plain dress grows plainer with age among the older Friends there.
69526-arizona-ghost-trails:
Arizona Ghost Trails is a 1969 reprint by the Frontier Book Company of Fort Davis, Texas. Its substance comes from a handbook to Arizona first issued in the late 1870s and credited to Richard Hinton. The reprint was limited to one thousand copies.

The contents promise a summary of mining laws, federal, territorial, and local. Desert and timber lands, homestead and pre-emption rights, and Spanish and railroad grants are covered.
