Routes, distances, fares, altitudes, weather tables, and mineral springs fill out the guide. The text opens with the history of mineral land policy before the Act of 1866, when ownership stayed with the nation. A prospector or settler could learn the whole land system from one volume. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
70026-a-world-of-green-hills:
A World of Green Hills is a book of nature observations by Bradford Torrey, published by Houghton, Mifflin in 1898. Its subtitle promises observations of nature and human nature in the Blue Ridge. Torrey was the author of Birds in the Bush, A Rambler's Lease, and A Florida Sketch-Book.

The North Carolina half holds four essays: A Day's Drive in Three States, In Quest of Ravens, A Mountain Pond, and Birds, Flowers, and People. The opening drive carries him from a train at Seneca in a buggy toward Walhalla with a young driver who has been a Pullman porter and waited in Florida. The boy likes to go round and see the world, and holds that a man who lives nowhere has no business with a wife. The Virginia half adds A Nook in the Alleghanies and At Natural Bridge.
70339-furniture-upholstery-for-schools:
Emil A Johnson, assistant professor of manual arts at Bradley Polytechnic Institute in Peoria, wrote a school textbook on furniture upholstery, copyrighted in 1919. Part one opens with a historical chapter. Tools and materials follow. Part two treats upholstery without springs. Board structures come first: a low footstool, a cart, and a leg rest.

Chair seats, plain and set in, get a chapter of their own. A framed structure follows, with another footstool. The Manual Arts Press issued the book for shop classes. Johnson wrote for teachers training boys in practical trades. Project based manuals like this one structured the manual training movement in American schools.
7144-while-the-billy-boils:
Henry Lawson's While the Billy Boils gathers bush stories in two series, opening with an old mate of your father's, settling on the land, and Enter Mitchell. Stiffner and Jim, thirdly Bill, when the sun went down, and the man who forgot Hungerford follow, with a camp fire yarn, his country after all, and a day on a selection. That there dog of mine going blind, Arvie Aspinall's alarm clock, and stragglers lead to the union burying its dead.

On the Edge of a Plain, In a Dry Season, He's Come Back, Another of Mitchell's Plans, Steelman, Drifted Back, and Mitchell Doesn't Believe in the Sack follow. Shooting the moon, his father's mate, and an echo from the old bark school close the first series, while the second brings the drover's wife, Steelman's pupil, and an unfinished love story. Lawson writes the bush in yarns of mateship and hard times.
71753-college-girls:
College Girls is a book of short stories by Abbe Carter Goodloe, illustrated by Charles Dana Gibson. Scribner's Sons published it in New York in 1895. The stories turn on the lives and loves of young women at college and just beyond it.

The contents list a dozen pieces. A Photograph and An Aquarelle open the volume, followed by La Belle Hélène and As Told by Her. A Short Career, Her Decision and Revenge keep the themes of choice and consequence. The College Beauty, A Telephoned Telegram and Miss Rose follow, and a short study in evolution and Time and Tide close the book. Gibson's drawings, famous from the Gibson Girl craze, show the heroines at parties and under the porte cochère, stealing glances and making farewells. Goodloe writes the new woman of the nineties with a light, ironic hand.
72183-the-mongols:
Jeremiah Curtin wrote The Mongols, a history of the great horse folk of Asia. Little, Brown, and Company issued the book in Boston in nineteen hundred eight. Theodore Roosevelt wrote a foreword for the wide tale. Curtin had won leave to give the book to Roosevelt in nineteen hundred one.

Two hurt tribes of California first brought the men to meet. Wintu and Yana folk begged Curtin to plead their cause in Washington. President Harrison heard them and sent their plea to his staff. Roosevelt, then a civil service chief, backed the just claim. Curtin sets that tale of trust at the front of his book. The Mongols’ own vast tale then rolls east to west. Steppe wars, world raids, and great khans fill its long span. Curtin knew the folk of the wilds at first hand from his years.
72188-how-old-are-fossils:
How Old Are Fossils is a science leaflet by Sharat Roy of the Field Museum in Chicago. Issued in 1927 as Geology Leaflet number nine, it was written for museum visitors who ask the question of its title. Roy states plainly that a precise answer is impossible, and that a short answer only feeds doubt.

The leaflet gives a condensed account of the methods used to date ancient life, drawn from various authors and especially from Barrell's work on rhythms and measurement in geologic time. It starts from the birth of life and the evidence that land life emerged from the sea. Dating fossils means dating the rocks that hold them. The aim is a clear statement for interested readers without the library for a full study.
72311-the-deep-space-scrolls:
The Deep Space Scrolls is a science fiction story by Robert F Young, with plates by Schelling, taken from Amazing Stories for May 1963. A house note says Young mines myth for his tales, and here asks a question on one of man oldest memories and on the nature of God.

The tale is cast as a transcript of a closed Senate hearing held on June 18, 1969. Senator Larch chairs the panel on space progress. The witness is Lieutenant Colonel Willard S Greaves, companion pilot of the Camaraderie 17. Larch praises the flight of last week as a glowing landmark. The flight ran far out, to test men in deep space past the rim of past orbits. Readers get a hearing that turns into a tale of myth found in space.
72904-within-these-walls:
Within These Walls is a novel by Rupert Hughes, a known teller of tales. The book came out in New York and London in nineteen twenty three. Prints in the book show tears, oaths, and a glow of sun on a face. Past hits by the same hand crowd the front page of the work.

A vast tulip tree, tall as a tower, opens the tale in a lush key. A man and a girl can just span its bole with arms spread wide. Bright plates hint at guilt, sworn hush, and rapt joy to come in the plot. The walls of the title hem in lives that strain at their bounds. Hughes blends lush scene work with sharp talk in his trade style.
7430-familiar-spanish-travels:
W. D. Howells first met Spain as a boy of seventeen, reading Spanish tales of the vanished Moorish kingdom in a little room under the stairs. Familiar Spanish Travels, published in 1913, returns to that boyhood dream as an old traveler. The route runs through San Sebastian and Biscay, Burgos in its bitter cold, Valladolid, and Madrid, then on to Toledo, Cordova, Seville, Granada, and Ronda.

Howells writes familiarly, as the title says: not as a guidebook author ticking sights, but as a friend telling what he saw and felt. He lingers over markets, cathedrals, and the contrast between Moorish past and Spanish present. For readers who know his Italian travels, this is the Spanish companion, warm, observant, and unhurried.
74601-the-black-forge-mills:
The Black Forge Mills, subtitled Up the King's Highway, is a religious novel by William Pendleton Chipman, published at Philadelphia in 1889 by the American Baptist Publication Society. Chipman calls it a true story, and dedicates it to his wife. The hero, Ralph Carleton, is pastor of the First Baptist Church in Afton, a mill town under abrupt green hills.

Chapters follow Carleton's ministry among mill families: a new scholar at Miss Squire's school, trials across a last year at Easton, a summer vacation, and lives surrendered and fulfilled. The novel works in the tradition of the Sunday-school story, where faith is tested in work, love, and duty. It shows how Baptist publishers used fiction to carry doctrine into mill-town homes.
74813-the-commonwealth-of-cells:
Commonwealth of Cells is a set of popular essays on human physiology. Spurrell, an Oxford bachelor of arts, wrote them for Bailliere Tindall of London. The firm issued the essays in nineteen o one from Henrietta Street. Spurrell gives the book to his esteemed friend and tutor, Gustav Mann.

Five essays treat living matter, the chemistry of the body, and its mechanics. The nervous system fills essay four, and the body as a whole essay five. Diagrams show the amoeba, the paramecium, and stages of an embryo growing. One side of the hollow cell ball pushes in to form a gut. Special digestive cells lose their sturdy traits as layers specialise there.
74872-shells:
Shells is a book of verse by Ella Wheeler, out in eighteen seventy-three. Wheeler was known past this book for a set of verse on drops of drink. The book is writ with thanks to the folk of her home state, from whom she had had much praise and cheer. Their grace made her glad work more glad and her glad life more glad, she says.

The list of verse runs past one hundred heads, from our lives to love past wealth. Themes of faith, grief, love, and the small hours of home fill the rows. The first verse holds that our lives are songs whose words God writes. We set those words to tunes at our will, and the song grows glad, sweet, or sad as we shape its beat. That rule of choice sets the tone of the book.
74919-schoolgirl-rivals:
Brenda Page's Schoolgirl Rivals was first published by Cassell in nineteen thirty-seven, with a colour frontispiece and three black and white plates. The story opens on a train bound for Easthampton. A kind friend waves off a girl who promises she will never forget the trouble taken over her, then settles into the straightforward run toward Carslake's school.

The chapters promise a full school term of schemes and tests. There are the seniors of Carslake's, the rival set called the P Squareds, the Richoter science prize, a trial by jury, sports day, a cycling expedition, and a night on the Downs. One plate shows the Principal's sharp question about someone interfering with Constance's balances.
75156-where-sunlight-falls:
Where Sunlight Falls is a book of cheerful verse by Wilhelmina Stitch, issued by Methuen in 1929. A second edition followed the March 1929 first printing in the same year. Stitch had written Silken Threads, Silver Linings, and The Golden Web before this volume. Contents open with a song to cheer, at a dog home, and the wayside pulpit.

Spoons, above defeat, courtesy, and building palaces show her homely range of subjects. Preserves, conkers, an umbrella poem, and an Easter song fill the middle list. Thoughts when ill and seeking happiness close the little book of comfort. Stitch verses were broadcast favourites, plain rhymes for hard pressed listeners.
75334-the-girls:
The Girls is a tale by Edna Ferber. It was put out in nineteen twenty one at a gar den town and at a town of the north land. Its rights were held that year in two names. The book is sworn to a dame who shies at the fly blooms but not at life. The tale starts with a word on its own way of work. It is a point of way, that start says.

Shall I rush you up to the girls at full speed, that word asks. Or shall I slip you so sly in to their house life that they will not glance up when you come in the room. Or shall I set the three of them in grave line by age, age span, and tale.
75363-the-eater-of-souls:
The Eater of Souls is a short tale by Henry Kuttner. It was put out in Weird Tales in January 1937. The head note calls it a five-minute tale of a strange being on a distant world. The tale opens in Bel Yarnak, in a tongue not of Earth.

They tell it there that a foul and dire being once dwelt in the vast gulf called the Gray Gulf of Yarnak. Bel Yarnak is not on Earth, nor on any planet that spins about a star in our skies. It lies beyond Betelgeuse and the Giant Stars, on a green and young world. Its towers and silver spires rise there, and its folk are in no way man-like. Yet fires burn in strange hearths through the long warm nights, the tale says, as the account of the being begins.
7546-quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of:
William Dean Howells, the dean of American realism, wrote novels, criticism, and essays for half a century, and this volume gathers quotations from his writings with images. The entries show his mind at work: absolutely, so positively, so almost aggressively truthful. An account of one's reading is an account of one's life. Affections will not be bidden.

Other sayings touch his age's nerves: industrial slavery, lewd literature giving sanction to lewdness in life, and critics who are in no sense the legislators of literature. Clemens, he wrote, was sole and incomparable, the Lincoln of American literature, and Dickens rescued Christmas from gloom. The collection is a portrait of Howells himself: honest, humane, and quietly radical about truth in fiction.
75567-highland-annals:
Highland Annals is a set of sketches by Olive Tilford Dargan. Scribner's Sons published it in New York in the year 1925. The first six sketches ran in the Atlantic Monthly in earlier years. A seventh sketch appeared in the Reviewer before book form came. Dargan thanks both magazines for leave to reprint her pieces here.

Contents open About Granpap and Trees, then Coretta and Autumn in turn. Serena and Wild Strawberries and a sketch called Sam follow in order. Evvie: Somewhat Married and a wild hog claim vary the mountain fare. Serena Takes a Boarder closes the set of seven sketches in all. Carolina highland folk speak in their own voice through Dargan's pages.
76171-derelicts-of-the-hills:
Derelicts of the Hills is a western tale by W C Tuttle, author of Magpie's Nightbear. A first person narrator rides up to a mining cut in the hills. He finds a prospector cursing over three split fuses in a gopher hole, ready to blast.

The grumbler takes the stranger for Magpie, his partner, who should be cooking dinner at the cabin. Apologies follow once the mistake clears. The narrator reports a curious silent man sitting on a log down the trail. Six feet long and ten inches wide, roan, with sparsely settled whiskers, the description fits Magpie exactly. Tuttle's Hashknife and Magpie stories made him a pulp western favourite. This tale runs on his usual fuel: dry dialogue, desert hills, and two derelict prospectors whose partnership is half quarrel, half devotion.
76443-tennis-for-girls:
Tennis for Girls is a sports guide in the Spalding Athletic Library, the official handbook series of its day. The library list at its front prices the Spalding guides at ten and twenty five cents. Baseball, foot ball, ice hockey, and basket ball guides stand at the head of that list. 

The lawn tennis annual and a soccer guide stand in the twenty five cent part of the list. Golf, indoor baseball, and the athletic almanac complete the shown catalogue of the library. Into that shelf of official rules the girls tennis guide takes its place for its readers. Spalding handbooks fixed the rules and the form of American sport in print. A girls guide to the lawn game marks the arrival of women on the courts as players to be coached, not merely as spectators in white dresses.
76628-beyond-the-hills:
Maysel Jenkinson wrote Beyond the Hills, published by Frederick Warne in London and New York. She dedicated the book to Marie, founder of the Sunshine Guild, who had led her little travellers toward the enchanted unknown hills. The story opens across a broad golden river. From the garden wall three children can see the whole long range of hills, tantalisingly near and altogether unattainable.

The river and the forest belong to everyday life, the narrator explains, and romance cannot live there. The children want the unknown beyond the hills. Chapters bring a great-aunt, a prior, a rose-vicar, and a fight on the hills themselves. Exploring with Dick, a race, half-confessions, and a derelict car lead to an awakening at the close. Jenkinson wrote a children's adventure in which the hills stand for everything beyond the home fields.
76644-clicking-red-heels:
Clicking Red Heels is a horror story by Paul Ernst, from Weird Tales of June 1937. Its headnote gives the plot away in one breath. Nobody knew that Gruin had killed his sweetheart. But her little red heels tapped a march of death wherever he went. The sound drove him toward a desperate resolve. The story opens by dividing fear into two kinds.

Fear of the known — death, disease, disgrace — is bad enough, Ernst writes. Fear of the unknown freezes the brain and stops the breath. Eldon Gruin begins inside the first fear only. His dread takes the shape of a girl, Maria José. Her father cuts and stitches leather in a basement shoe shop on Eighth Avenue. Maria herself is fire: black eyes, red lips, and tiny red heeled shoes that danced. Guilt finds its sound in those heels.
771-biographical-notes-on-the-pseudonymo:
Charlotte Brontë wrote these short pieces to clear up a common error: that the works signed Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell came from one hand. She states plainly that three sisters wrote them, Currer being herself, Ellis being Emily, and Acton being Anne. The notice was prefixed to a reprint of Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey.

Brontë tells how the sisters chose male pen names, how their books were received, and how Emily and Anne lived and died. Her tone is proud and mournful, defending her sisters' fame while mourning their loss. The pieces are essential reading for anyone who wants the true story behind the Bell name, told by the sister who survived.
77207-quite-wild-animals:
Quite Wild Animals is a nonsense picture book by Beatrice Curtis Brown. Dodd, Mead published it in New York in 1923. Each creature gets a portrait and a sketch. Some sketches are prose and some are verse. The animals are invented from start to finish.

Growp opens the menagerie. He has a beak and two wings and calls himself a birst. He lives alone in a muddy field. His house is built of old tins and broken saucers. He is apt to eat his visitors. Doolyboo follows in verse. She is sweet, neat, and beloved by all. Bawgum looks fierce but owns the softest heart. His playful tail betrays him to everyone.
77220-tabby-s-travels:
Tabbys Travels, or the Holiday Adventures of a Kitten, is a tale for the young by Lucy Guernsey. The book came out in Edinburgh in the year eighteen sixty four. Tabby tells her own tale in the first person from a snug kitchen. Her flight from home starts the whole chain of events.

Eight short parts track her path through a kind house, a party, and hard roads. A river, a police office, and a prize for a good girl mark the turns. The tale aims its soft morals at girls who serve in great houses. Warm hearth scenes frame the lessons on thanks and care for beasts. Small prints dress the text at the part heads.
77366-among-the-isles-of-shoals:
Celia Thaxter wrote these sketches of the Isles of Shoals, the rocky islands off the New England coast where she lived. Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York reissued them with illustrations, from a first copyright of 1873. Her frontispiece shows White Island looking southwest from Appledore. Thaxter says she lets the book appear only reluctantly.

The sketches are fragmentary, she admits, but summer visitors incessantly call for some account of the place, and an imperfect chronicle is better than nothing. She contrasts her bleached, low rocks with Melville's Enchanted Islands under the equator, calling the Shoals enchanted in a better sense. Their strange charm, she says, makes people forget the hurry and worry of life, as the eternal sound of the sea softens every sharp outline of thought like a sketch in charcoal.
77803-matabele-land-and-the-victoria-fal:
Frank Oates, a naturalist, wandered in the interior of South Africa and wrote letters and journals home. His brother edited them in London in 1881, after Frank died of fever days after leaving the Zambesi on his way home. The editor owns the book's faults. The notes were kept for the writer's own use, and the letters were never meant for print.

Yet friends judged the record worth giving to the public. Oates travelled through Matabele Land to the Victoria Falls, watching beasts, birds, plants, and peoples. Fever cut his work short on the homeward road. The book preserves a keen field eye and a pioneer's hardships in a land then little known to English readers.
77974-modern-educators-and-their-ideals:
Modern Educators and Their Ideals is a work on the teach craft by Tadasu Misawa. It was put out at New York in nineteen nine. Its rights were held that year by its print house. The list of parts gives its plan in full. A lead in heads the run. Then come the lives and thoughts of the great teach men of the past ages, one to a part.

A church school man of the age of kings heads that run. A deep thought man of this land and a wild child man of France come next. Two men of the north land share a part past them. The great school man of the Swiss hills and a state thought man of the north fill the mid run.
78310-modes-and-morals:
Modes and Morals is a book of short prose by Katharine Fullerton Gerould. It was put out at New York in nineteen twenty. It was print in the last month of that year and print once more the next month. Parts of it had run in great sheets of the past ten years, as the rights list at the front owns. Her past books are named past the title leaf.

The list of parts gives the span of her themes. The new plain way heads the run. Dress and the woman, a rich dish held as a rule of life, and the root out of high thought come next. Modes in men, the most new woman, and ban and cast of mind fill the first run.
78427-the-bracknels:
The Bracknels is a novel by Forrest Reid, subtitled A Family Chronicle. Edward Arnold published it in London in 1911. Reid had earlier written The Kingdom of Twilight and The Garden God. The story opens at a family breakfast table in morning sunlight.

Amy Bracknel sits watching her father over the meal as the tale begins. Her dark-red hair catches the sun in threads of gold. The talk turns to a stranger expected in the household, a young teacher. Amy asks her father plainly what the man is like, and whether he is handsome. May declares that no one who teaches could possibly be good-looking. Bracknel answers dryly from behind his newspaper at last. The young man has coached his own brother through an examination, he reports.
7867-crooked-trails:
Frederic Remington's Crooked Trails, first published in 1898 and pictured by the author, opens in a San Antonio club. The Deacon promises a talk with Colonel Rip Ford of the old Texas Rangers. White-haired and bent yet unwithered, Ford sinks into an armchair to tell tales.

Contents run from how law got into the chaparral and the blue quail of the cactus through a sergeant of the orphan troop. Massai's crooked trail, cracker cowboys of Florida, and the Soledad girls follow. Through Rangers, cowboys, and frontier fights, Remington records a West already fading.
78695-blind-trails:
Blind Trails is a Western novel by Tuttle, author of Reputation and The Misdeal. The tale opens at the Cross L ranch, where a cowhand turns from unsaddling a sweat marked gray horse. Peace River Parker is tall and gaunt, with bat wing chaps polished by long use. His face is plain, but his gray eyes are clear and wide set.

Parker studies a black horse tied at the ranch house porch. Its silver mounted saddle flashes in the sun as the animal stirs. He looks long, then turns to his own saddle as if puzzling out a thought. A slight shake of the head answers some unspoken question. He walks slowly toward the bunk house as another man steps from the kitchen. Tuttle builds his tale from such quiet signs before the guns come out.
78756-sun-dog-trails:
Sun Dog Trails is a western novel by Tuttle, author of other tales named on the title page. The story opens at speed, with a team of pinto horses running away with a lumber wagon. Two men cling to the seat of the swaying wagon, with nothing to say about the pace. An observer might call the driving cruel, the narrator jokes, but the men might answer back.

The wagon sweeps around a curving grade, skidding and bouncing, its wheels near the outer edge. Just ahead, blocking the road, stands a stage coach with four horses, headed the same way. A sharp curve and a strong wind down the canyon have masked the runaway's approach. There is no time for either party to act, and the opening holds on that brink.
78938-over-the-falls:
Over the Falls is the own tale of Annie Edson Taylor, the woman who rode the great falls in a barrel and lived. Its rights were set in law in the summer of the first years of the last age, and she put it out in her own name. A print shows the path she and her barrel took on the plunge.

Its first part tells of the feats at the falls through the past age. A famed leap from a tower came first, in the late eighteen twenties. From then on, men and women came to the falls to win fame and gold by some brave deed. To ride the whirlpool rapids in a boat or barrel was the most loved feat for years. Her ride tops them all.
79145-tangled-trails:
W C Tuttle wrote Tangled Trails, a Western tale of a stage hold up that was not. Romeo Kendall drives the first scene with his wild claim of loss. The Marlin City bank men check his strong box and laugh him down. Ten thousand dollars in cash lies safe and whole in the box.

Romeo drove stage for Pelham and Malvene on the Silverton lines. Sun Dog County holds him a fool and a liar in one breath. He swears two men robbed him at gun point on the road. His odd name has a tale: once he was Bad-Eg Kendall in town. Love for Soapy Caswell’s girl set him to sing at her pane by night. Wrong room: Soapy crowned him with a water pitcher from above. He woke with a new name and a sore head, town sport ever since.
79459-midst-granite-hills:
Midst Granite Hills, the story of a Dartmoor holiday, is a tale by Eglanton Thorne. It was issued in the Girl Own Annual, volume twelve, of 1891 at London. The Leisure Hour office at Paternoster Row published the annual for its girl readers. Thorne is named as author of My Brother Friend and Aldyth Inheritance.

Contents list five chapters for the holiday story in the annual. They are A Business Transaction, Trematon in the Moor, New Friends, An Unwarrantable Liberty, and Forgiven. The tale opens on the second day of August, a close and oppressive day in its first lines. At that date the Cambridge colleges are supposed to be deserted for the vacation. From that Cambridge opening the story moves to a holiday among the granite hills of Dartmoor, where new friends, a liberty taken, and a forgiveness shape the short plot of the piece.
79516-edible-fats-and-oils:
W H Simmons and C Ainsworth Mitchell wrote this handbook on edible fats and oils, printed in London in 1911. Simmons lectured on soap making at the Battersea Polytechnic, and both men had written trade books before. Scott, Greenwood and Son issued it from the offices of The Oil and Colour Trades Journal.

Chapters open with fat as food and the make-up of fats and oils. Raw materials, refining, bleaching, and deodorising follow, by both physical and chemical means. Butter substitutes and margarine get a full chapter, as do salad oils and chocolate fats. The last part turns to analysis, with general methods and special tests for single oils, butter, lard, and cheese.
8502-common-diseases-of-farm-animals:
R. A. Craig, a doctor of veterinary medicine, wrote Common Diseases of Farm Animals for farmers and stockmen. The frontispiece warns, with a picture of an insanitary dairy stable and yards, that disease and financial loss are to be expected when animals are kept in filth. Contents open with a general discussion of disease, and diagnosis and symptoms, before treating diseases in turn.

Craig's manual belongs to the age when veterinary science reached the farm, and clean stables became an economic argument. Readers get practical advice on recognizing and treating illness in cattle, horses, sheep, and pigs. The book interests historians of agriculture, and anyone curious about animal care before modern drugs.
8590-auld-licht-idyls:
J. M. Barrie, later famous for Peter Pan, sketches the strict Auld Licht folk of Thrums, his fictional version of his native Kirriemuir in Scotland. A schoolmaster narrator opens the book in his glen school-house, wakened by a starving sparrow at a frosted window. The chapters move through the kirk, the school, courtships, funerals, and a small literary club. Lads and lasses, old dominies, and village worthies fill the pages.

Barrie's humour is gentle but not soft: the Auld Lichts' stern religion, thrift, and pride are shown with affection and with a clear eye for their narrowness. The idylls made his name, proving a Scots village could carry a whole book of stories. Readers who know Barrie only from Neverland will find here the roots of his art, in dialect, memory, and the comedy of small-town dignity.
8939-with-edged-tools:
Henry Seton Merriman wrote this adventure novel of trade and peril in Africa, first in the late 1800s. Its hero, an Englishman of two generations of traders, sails to the West African coast to seek ivory and a lost secret, facing rivals, fever, and war among the trading stations. The title points to tools that cut both ways.

Chapters move from London farewells to Loango, to deals struck in bad faith, panics, and a race to the rescue. Merriman keeps the pace brisk and the moral lines clear, though modern readers will note its age in its view of Africa. It still works as a swift, old-style tale of risk and nerve.
9048-ballads-founded-on-anecdotes-relati:
William Hayley wrote these ballads in 1805, with prints designed and cut by William Blake, for young readers. Each poem grows from a true tale about an animal: a loyal dog, a kind horse, or some other beast that showed courage or love. Hayley states his aim at once, that the book is meant for boys and girls.

The verse is simple and moral, praising faith, kindness, and care for creatures that cannot speak for themselves. Blake's art gives the small book extra worth, since his prints are now prized far past Hayley's verse. Together they make a charming relic of a time when children's books taught through story and song.
9923-the-box-with-broken-seals:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's 1919 thriller opens in a Chicago hotel, where the Englishman James Crawshay and his American fellow traveler Hobson wait, uneasy, for the chief of police. Both men have just finished a long journey, and something crooked about their business waits to be explained.

The broken seals of the title point to a secret opened before its time, and the story follows Crawshay through suspicion, pursuit, and revelation in Oppenheim's brisk popular manner. Readers who like Edwardian crime tales with an American setting will enjoy its quick pace and confident hero.
a-book-of-remarkable-criminals:
H. B. Irving wrote these true-crime lives of notorious offenders. The contents promise studies of Charles Peace, the burglar and murderer; Robert Butler of the Dunedin murders; the poisoners Derues and Dr. Castaing; Professor Webster; the mysterious Mr. Holmes; and a closing part on partnerships in crime, from the Widow Gras to the Fenayrou case and Eyraud and Bompard.

Irving's introduction argues that crime deserves serious study: the connection between motive and act, he writes, is as necessary to the jurist as to the student of human nature. Each life is then told as a narrative, from early years through trial and execution or decline. Irving, a lawyer's son steeped in famous trials, writes as an essayist rather than a sensation-monger, which gives the book its lasting place in crime writing.
a-book-of-scoundrels:
Charles Whibley profiles famous rogues of past centuries with open delight in their skill. His contents list Captain Hind, Moll Cutpurse, Jonathan Wild, Ralph Briscoe, and Gilderoy, then Jack Sheppard, Cartouche, George Barrington, Deacon Brodie, and Charles Peace. Each life is told from the records and old pamphlets.

Whibley pairs many of his rogues and draws parallels between them, thief against thief. He treats a masterly theft as a kind of dark art and writes with wit rather than moral horror. The chapters mix true history, anecdote, and shrewd character study. Readers who enjoy old London crime and highway romance will find a rich store here.
a-century-of-roundels:
Algernon Charles Swinburne fills a whole book with one small form: the roundel, a short poem with a refrain that returns like a bell note. This second edition of 1883, from Chatto and Windus, dedicates the volume to Christina G. Rossetti. The contents number the poems to a hundred, as the title promises.

In Harbour, The Way of the Wind, Had I Wist, Time and Life, and A Baby's Death stand among the early titles. A roundel on the death of Richard Wagner joins them. Two preludes are named for Lohengrin and Tristan. Swinburne makes the tight form sing of children, seasons, friendship, and grief. The book is a jewel box of Victorian lyric craft.
a-garland-for-girls:
A Garland for Girls, by Louisa May Alcott, gathers seven stories named for flowers, written, she says, for her own amusement during enforced seclusion. Alcott signed the preface in September 1887 and inscribed the book to R A Lawrence, her grateful friend. The flowers that were her solace in illness suggested the titles: May Flowers, Pansies, Water-Lilies, Poppies and Wheat, Little Button-Rose, and two more sprays of blossom.

The first tale opens in Boston, where six girls, descendants of Pilgrim Fathers as Alcott notes, form a club for mental improvement and call it the Mayflower Club. Each story in the garland ties a girl's work, pride, or kindness to its flower. Alcott writes for the readers who grew up with her: young women earning, helping, and deciding, with sentiment kept on a short stem and moralizing woven into incident rather than preached.
a-pagan-of-the-hills: Charles Neville Buck sets this mountain novel among hill people whose speech, trading, and pride shape every encounter, opening with a tall mountaineer puzzled by a timber buyer. The buyer has haggled with old man McGivins over logs, yet has never met Alexander, a name that carries weight in the valley. From that small mystery the story builds a world of ridges, bargains, and loyalties tested by outsiders.
a-practical-physiology-a-text-book-for-h: Albert Franklin Blaisdell prepares this textbook of human physiology and hygiene for higher schools, normal schools, and academies. His plan gives the anatomy of each organ before describing its function, since structure must be grasped before the body's workings make sense. Chapters move through bones, muscles, exercise, food, digestion, blood and circulation, respiration, skin and kidneys, and the nervous system, in a practical manual for students.
all-aboard-a-story-for-girls: Fannie Ellsworth Newberry writes a story for girls called All Aboard, dedicated to the memory of a happy visit. The tale follows young heroines through travel, friendship, and the small adventures of a holiday, in the cheerful manner of girls' books of its time. Light dialogue and wholesome incident make it an easy, pleasant read for its intended audience.
an-enquiry-concerning-the-principles-of-:
David Hume's Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals recasts his earlier moral philosophy in clearer form. Hume explains in his advertisement that the work restates ideas first printed in his Treatise of Human Nature. This edition follows the posthumous printing of 1777. The subject is why people praise some traits and blame others.

Sections treat benevolence, justice, and political society in turn. Hume argues that utility, meaning usefulness to people, explains much of our approval. Other chapters sort qualities that serve ourselves and qualities that please others at once. Four appendices handle moral sentiment, self-love, justice, and disputes over words. The book remains a founding text of modern ethics, valued for its calm tone and its test of moral rules against human feeling.
auld-licht-idyls:
J. M. Barrie gathered these sketches of his home town, thinly renamed Thrums, under the title Auld Licht Idyls. Barrie writes as the new dominie in the red-stone school-house in the glen of Quharity, succeeding a cantankerous old schoolmaster. The Auld Lichts were a strict Scottish church congregation, and their kirk, manners, and courtships supply his material.

Chapters introduce the Auld Licht kirk, its folk in arms, and the old dominie himself. Cree Queery and Mysy Drolly, the courting of T'Nowhead's Bell, and Davit Lunan's political reminiscences follow, down to little Rathie's funeral and a literary club. Barrie treats Thrums slowly, as its people took everything: things struck them gradually, and even the new cemetery was only so called because it had been new once.
b09-brant-ship-of-fools:
Sebastian Brant, a Strasbourg lawyer, launched his Narrenschiff, The Ship of Fools, in German in 1494. The poem loads every kind of fool onto one ship bound for folly's land. Alexander Barclay turned it into English verse in 1509, and that rendering, in T H Jamieson's 1874 edition, fills this text.

Across 157 chapters Brant mocks greed, vanity, bad manners, false learning, and folly in church and state. Each fool gets a portrait in verse sharp enough to sting and broad enough to fit any age. The image of the ship sailed on through European art and letters, from Bosch to Bruegel. The satire still lands.
ballads-founded-on-anecdotes-relating-to:
William Hayley published these verses in 1805, with prints designed and engraved by William Blake. Hayley, Blake's patron at Felpham, aimed the book at young readers, taking Horace's virginibus puerisque canto — I sing for girls and boys — as its motto. Each ballad builds on a true anecdote about an animal, told in smooth, moralising stanzas.

The Dog leads off: of all the speechless friends of man, the faithful dog deserves the tenderest esteem, a guardian given by powers above. Later verses tell of a girl whose gentle mind wild birds learned to trust, taming even halcyons, the shy kingfishers whose feathers flame. Blake's plates give the slight poems their lasting interest: a minor poet's animal tales, preserved by a major artist's hand at the engraver's bench.
betty-wales-sophomore-a-story-for-girls:
Betty Wales, Sophomore, a story for girls, is credited on its title page to Margaret Warde. Warde's contents open with Moving In and Eleanor's Freshman. Parades and Parties, Points of View, and On Ambition carry the college year. The First Four, In the Argus Sanctum, and A Problem in Ethics raise the stakes toward midyears. Eva Nagel illustrated the 1905 volume.

Betty's sophomore year is the middle of a five book progress through college and beyond it. Freshman, junior, senior, and B A volumes stand around this one. The author's name on the title page is a pen name, and the series became a standard of girls' college fiction. Classes, the college paper, and friendship's ethics fill its world. No one fails out of Warde's college. The examinations that matter are social and moral, and Betty Wales passes them in a way meant to be copied.
biographical-notes-on-the-pseudonymous-b:
Charlotte Bronte wrote this biographical notice to end a mistake: readers believed Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell were one person. She states plainly that the Bells were three sisters, and that Ellis and Acton, Emily and Anne, were now dead. The notice prefaced a reprint of Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey.

Charlotte describes Emily's fierce, home-loving nature and Anne's quieter patience, borne through illness by firm Christian faith. She watched them, she writes, follow the same path at different steps toward early graves. A companion piece, her editor's preface, defends Emily's rough genius. Together these short pieces are essential documents for understanding the Bronte sisters and their chosen masks.
book-about-animals:
Rufus Merrill printed Book about Animals at Concord, New Hampshire, in 1850, as a small picture book for young children. Merrill writes each entry in short, plain lines meant to be read aloud. Cuts show the animals as the text names them, from a Laplander travelling at the front.

Short entries treat the elephant, the ourang outang, the opossum, the antelope, and the rabbit in turn. A musk deer hunted for its scent bag and a polar bear on the ice follow. Each entry tells where the beast lives, what it eats, and one odd fact, like the opossum's pouch. The flying squirrel closes the set. Early American children met the wider world of beasts through just such cheap, plain readers as Merrill's.
boy-scouts-in-northern-wilds-or-the-sign:
Major Archibald Lee Fletcher wrote Boy Scouts in Northern Wilds, printed at Chicago in 1913, though the record credits G Harvey Ralphson. Fletcher sends four Beaver Patrol scouts from Chicago to camp on Moose River, three hundred miles of wilderness in the British north-west. A little brass god starts the trouble.

A cabin in a swamp, a cave of two bears, and a trapper's treachery test the boys. Drugged tea puts George under, and a scout call through a wall saves him. Antoine runs, a pillar of fire rises, and the signal from the hills answers at last. Twin brass gods close the hunt. Fletcher packs scout craft into every scrape: wigwag signs, tracking, and cool heads in a tight place.
britannica-1911-agriculture-the-diseases:
The Diseases of Animals, part of the Agriculture article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, records how outbreaks were tracked in Great Britain. Under the Diseases of Animals Acts of 1894 and 1896, the Board of Agriculture issued weekly returns. They covered anthrax, foot-and-mouth disease, glanders, pleuro-pneumonia, rabies, and swine fever, with monthly returns for sheep-scab.

Tables trace foot-and-mouth disease from 1877 to 1905, naming counties, outbreaks, and animals attacked by kind. Cattle plague, or rinderpest, had not appeared since 1877, when 47 outbreaks struck five counties. Foot-and-mouth disease reached its worst in 1883, while several later stretches passed with no outbreak at all. Anthrax figures for 1895 to 1905 follow in a further table.
britannica-1911-alcohols:
Alcohols, in organic chemistry, are defined and classified in a technical article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. An alcohol is a compound formed from a hydrocarbon when one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by hydroxyl groups, the oxygen-and-hydrogen group that gives alcohols their character. The entry limits the term to compounds where that group joins an aliphatic residue, excluding the hydroxy-benzenes.

Two ways of sorting alcohols run through the article. By the number of hydroxyl groups they are monohydric with one, glycols with two, and glycerols with three. By the carbon atom carrying the group they are primary, secondary, or tertiary. Long reaction schemes follow, showing each type passing through iodides and nitro compounds to distinct products. Tertiary alcohols are tested by heating to naphthalene's boiling point. The article is a working chemist's reference rather than a general reader's survey.
britannica-1911-bathurst-earls:
Bathurst is an earldom whose holders are traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Allen Bathurst, first earl (1684–1775), sat for Cirencester from 1705 and was made a baron in 1711. A keen Tory and a foe of Walpole in the Lords, he was given the earldom only in 1772, late in life. Poets and wits of his age, Pope, Swift, Prior, and Congreve among them, were his friends, and his letters with Pope were later printed.

Later earls held high office in turn. Henry, the second earl, became lord chancellor in 1771 and is judged a weak holder of that post, though fair with patronage. Henry, the third earl, was secretary for war and the colonies from 1812 to 1827. He ran the Peninsular War from London and defended the government's care of captive Napoleon. He backed Catholic relief but fought the reform bill of 1832. The line then runs to the fourth, fifth, and sixth earls.
britannica-1911-bhils:
Bhils, also spelled Bheels, are described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as a people of central India. Their name is linked to a word for a bow, and the entry calls them bowmen. It treats them as an old stock of the land, first noted as folk of Marwar. They live spread over a great part of India.

The text maps their range from the Aravalli Hills to Sind, Rajputana, Khandesh, and Ahmedabad. They are named in old Sanskrit works, and Greek writers may name them too. Driven by the Aryans from rich low land, they now live most thickly in the hills of central India. A rite at Rajput courts, where a Bhil marks the new prince with blood, hints at their old power. The entry blends place, past, and custom well.
britannica-1911-brownhills:
Brownhills is an urban district in Staffordshire, England, 6 miles west of Lichfield, on branch lines of the London and North-Western and Midland railways and near the Essington Canal. Its people grew from 11,820 in 1891 to 15,252 in 1901. Coal rules the district: extensive mines form part of the Cannock Chase deposit.

Older traces line the Roman Watling Street, on which the town lies, with earthworks at Knave's Castle on the street itself and at Castle Old Fort 2 miles south-east. Ogley Hay, a large adjoining village, sits beside it, with Great Wyrley and Norton Canes to the north-west and north, both with collieries, and brick, tile and edge-tool works at Church Bridge. Wyrley Grove, a picturesque mansion of the 17th century, closes the short gazetteer account.
britannica-1911-brussels:
Brussels is the capital of Belgium and of the province of Brabant. It stands in the valley of the Senne. The site lies about 70 miles from the sea at Ostend. The 1911 Britannica article covers the lower and upper towns. It also covers the ring of self-governing suburbs. Laeken, to the north, is practically part of the city.

The history runs from the marsh village Broeksele to the charter of 1312. In 1695 a French bombardment burned sixteen churches and 4000 houses. A fire destroyed the palace of the Netherlands in 1731. The entry describes the church of Ste Gudule and the Grand Place. It notes the Porte de Hal gate of 1381, still standing. It also gives the university, the lace and furniture trades, and a total population of 630,649 in 1904.
britannica-1911-cheviot-hills:
Cheviot Hills form a range that makes about 35 miles of the border between England and Scotland. The line of greatest height mostly marks the boundary, but more of the range lies in Northumberland than in Roxburghshire. Its axis runs north-east to south-west, and the ridge culminates in the Cheviot at 2,676 feet. Grass covers most of the conical, high arched hills, and deep narrow glens score their flanks in every direction.

Headwaters of the Till, Coquet and North Tyne drain south, while Tweed tributaries drain north. A valuable breed of sheep, the Cheviot, pastures on the smooth slopes and takes its fame from these hills. Border warfare marked the range in earlier days, and its name lives in the ballad of Chevy Chase. Ruins of castles and peel towers stand on the English side, and the geology runs from Silurian rocks to volcanic lavas and granite.
britannica-1911-chiltern-hills:
Chiltern Hills, or the Chilterns, are a range of chalk hills in England running through parts of Oxfordshire, Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire. They run from south-west to north-east, forming a sharp escarpment to the north-west and a long slope to the south-east. The name covers the hills between the Thames near Goring and the headwaters of the Lea between Dunstable and Hitchin. That crest line runs about 55 miles in length.

Heights of 800 to 850 feet are frequent in the centre, from Watlington to Tring, and the line continues east as the East Anglian ridge. Passes near Tring, Wendover and Prince's Risborough carry main roads and railways converging on London. The floors of those passes hold gravels of former rivers, the entry notes. Beech forest once covered the hills, and local beech still supplies chair making and other work near Wycombe.
britannica-1911-chin-hills:
Chin Hills is a mountainous district of Upper Burma on the border between the Lushai districts of Bengal and Assam and the plains of Burma. Its area is 8,000 square miles, bounded by Assam and Manipur, Arakan, Burma, Tippera and the Chittagong hill tracts. In 1895 the district was declared part of Burma and is now run by a political officer with headquarters at Falam. Broken ranges run mostly north to south, from 5,000 to 9,000 feet.

The Chins, Lushais and Kukis are said to share one stock, perhaps from Tibet, with like customs, speech habits and clan feeling. Sudden raids and fast retreats to their strongholds marked their warfare, with marches of two days and nights without cooking or sleep. British rule from both sides brought roads, bridges and new crops in the entry's closing account. The Chin Hills held 87,189 people in 1901, while Chins in all Burma totalled 179,292.
britannica-1911-cotteswold-hills:
Cotteswold Hills, also called the Cotswolds, form a range in the west midlands of England in this 1911 Britannica entry. Most of the hills lie in Gloucestershire, with parts in five more shires. They run from north east to south west as part of a long belt of lime rich rock. On the west they drop in a steep face to the Severn vale. On the east they slope down to the Thames and Avon basins.

Soft farm scenes fill much of the text, with high bare wolds and deep wooded vales. Cleeve Cloud tops the range at more than eleven hundred feet. Lime in the soil means crops need much feed, but poor land feeds sheep well. The herb sainfoin grows wild and yields well when sown.
britannica-1911-credentials:
Credentials, in French lettres de créance, are the formal papers an envoy hands to the government that receives him. Ambassadors, ministers plenipotentiary, and chargés d'affaires all present them on arrival. Their chief purpose is to state the envoy's diplomatic rank to the receiving state. They also ask that full credence be given to his official statements. Until the papers are presented and found in proper order, the envoy has no official standing.

The signature on the papers follows the envoy's rank. A head of state signs for an ambassador or a minister plenipotentiary. A foreign minister signs for a chargé d'affaires. Between presentation and acceptance the envoy waits without official recognition. Once the papers are found in proper order, his statements carry the full weight his rank allows.
britannica-1911-cresols:
Cresols, also called methyl phenols, are the subject of a chemist's article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. They come in three forms that are much alike. All three are found in the tar drawn from coal, beech wood, and pine. The raw mix from tar cannot be split by heat, since the three forms boil at points too close to part.

Pure forms are best made by fusing matched sulphur acids with potash. The ortho form is a solid that melts at thirty degrees. The meta form stays liquid till well below the frost point. The para form sets in prisms and melts at thirty-six degrees. Each form is tracked through the tests it gives, such as the blue tint it shows with iron salts.
britannica-1911-daphla-hills:
The Daphla Hills are a tract of hilly country on the border of eastern Bengal and Assam, held by an independent tribe called the Daphla. The hills lie north of the Tezpur and North Lakhimpur subdivisions. The Aka Hills bound them west and the Abor range east. They have a name for cowardice and, being disunited, lie at the mercy of the Akas.

A cane cap fringed with bearskin or feathers marks Daphla dress, fixed by a long skewer to hair coiled in a ball on the forehead. In 1872 a party of free Daphlas raided a settled colony of their own people and carried off forty-four captives. The Daphla expedition of 1874, with 1,000 troops, freed the prisoners and brought the tribe to submission. In British territory the census of 1901 counted 954 Daphlas. The tribal country itself was not counted.
britannica-1911-decretals:
Decretals are letters of the pope that state decisions in church law, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines them for students of canon law. Most decretals were sent in answer to questions put to Rome. Some came from the free initiative of the popes themselves. With the canons of the councils, they form the chief source of church law.

Decretals make up the greater part of the Corpus Juris, the body of canon law. A special interest hangs on one set, the False Decretals. That famed collection holds at least as many council canons as decretals. Not all the decretals in it are forgeries, the entry notes. The mix of true and false matter is part of what makes the collection a puzzle. Readers are sent to the canon law article for the full treatment.
britannica-1911-feasts-and-festivals:
Feasts and festivals are days, or runs of days, set apart publicly for religious observance. A day counts as a festival, grave or gay, while it is held in the name of religion. The entry argues that tracing the world's festivals would mean tracing the whole history of religion and civilization together. Where there is no religion there can be no feasts, and as religion grows, festivals grow in number, ritual richness and fixed order.

The survey that follows ranges widely across peoples and ages. It notes rare reports of tribes with no ceremonies at all, set against the strong religiosity found in most observed peoples. From such beginnings the long article follows festival forms through ancient and later religion, treating their seasons, rites and social weight. It is a general study of sacred days as a mirror of human belief and of the civilizations that keep them.
britannica-1911-foundling-hospitals:
Foundling hospitals were institutions for receiving foundlings: children abandoned or exposed, and left for the public to find and save. Their early history is bound up with the practice of infanticide. In western Europe, amid disorder and frequent famine, exposure and the sale of children were common evils. Against them the church set a rough relief. Children were laid in marble shells at church doors and tended by male nurses, then by foster-parents found for them by the parish.

Set institutions arose in the seventh and eighth centuries at Treves, Milan and Montpellier. St Vincent de Paul later rescued the foundlings of Paris with the help of devout ladies. The long article then surveys foundling hospitals country by country. The hosted file opens with the end of the Founding article.
britannica-1911-galashiels:
Galashiels is a burgh of Selkirkshire in Scotland, standing on Gala Water near its junction with the Tweed, 33 miles south-south-east of Edinburgh. Its people numbered 13,615 in 1901, down from 17,367 in 1891. The town runs more than two miles along both banks, mills and factories in the valley, villas on the high ground either side. Its woollen manufacture, dating from the close of the 16th century, is the most important in Scotland and now works mainly in tweeds. Hosiery, tanning, dyeing and boot-making also employ the town.

Galashiels began as a village for pilgrims to Melrose Abbey, became an occasional seat of the Douglases as keepers of Ettrick Forest, and was made a burgh of barony in 1599. Ashestiel, some miles west, was Scott's home from 1804 to 1812, where he wrote his most famous poems and began Waverley.
britannica-1911-garo-hills:
Garo Hills, a district of British India, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It lies in the hills division of Eastern Bengal and Assam. It takes its name from the Garos, the tribe who live there. Their origins are in doubt, and their customs are called peculiar in the text.

The Garos, the article says, are most likely a branch of the great Bodo tribe. That tribe once held a large part of Assam. In the census of 1901 the Garos numbered over a hundred and twenty-eight thousand. In the eighteenth century they often clashed with the folk of the plains below. In 1790 the British government first tried to subdue them. No lasting success was won. Raids in 1852 brought a blockade of the hills. In 1856 the Garos rose again in revolt. The piece records a frontier the empire could not easily hold.
britannica-1911-hoosick-falls:
Hoosick Falls is the subject of a village entry in the 1911 Britannica. The village lies in New York in Rensselaer county. It stands on the Hoosick river north east of Troy. Counts are given for the village across four census years. The count in 1910 was just over five thousand souls. A rail line and an electric line served the place. Falls on the river gave power for mills.

Farm machines were the chief goods made there. One firm dated from 1866 in that trade. Its founder had served in Congress for two terms. Knit goods, shirts, and paper mill gear were also made. Dutch settlers founded the place about 1688. More settlers came from New England after 1763. The fight at Bennington in 1777 took place near by. That fight is noted at the close of the entry.
britannica-1911-infant-schools:
Infant schools give planned training to children below the normal age for elementary school, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces their growth. The line starts with a village school at Waldbach founded by Jean Frederic Oberlin in 1774. Robert Owen opened such a school at New Lanark in 1800.

The entry notes a British society formed in 1836 to train infant school teachers, and the strong push given by Froebel and his play-school, the kindergarten, for children aged three to six. It also records a reaction in England, as health officers warned of infection risks and of the harm of formal lessons before age six or seven.
britannica-1911-ingram-john-kells:
John Kells Ingram is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Ingram was an Irish scholar and economist who lived from 1823 to 1907. He was born in County Donegal and schooled at Newry and at Trinity College in Dublin. He became a fellow of his college in 1846. He taught speech and English writing at Dublin from 1852 to 1866, then became professor of Greek.

The article stresses his wide range of work. In his student days he wrote a famed poem on the rising of 1798. He wrote papers for maths societies on geometry. He also did valued work on the roots of Greek and Latin words. His books treat the history of religion, human nature, and practical morals. He wrote a long article on political economy for an earlier edition of the Britannica. It was translated into nearly every European language.
britannica-1911-juel-niels:
Niels Juel (1629–1697) was a Danish admiral, brother of the statesman Jens Juel, born on the 8th of May 1629 at Christiania. He learned his trade at sea under Van Tromp and De Ruyter, and fought in the chief battles of the war of 1652 to 1654 between England and Holland. A long illness at Amsterdam gave him a deep knowledge of ship building.

Back in Denmark in 1656, he served with credit in the wars with Sweden of 1658 to 1660 and helped defend Copenhagen against Charles X. Through fifteen years of peace he worked to build up the Danish navy, though he chafed at the placing of Cort Adelaar over him in 1663. When Adelaar died in November 1675, during the Scanian War, Juel took the chief command. He then won fame. His method, later perfected by Nelson, was to cut off part of the foe's fleet and throw the whole attack on that part.
britannica-1911-kells:
Kells is a market town of county Meath, Ireland, on the Blackwater, on a branch of the Great Northern railway. Its urban district held 2428 people in 1901. The prosperity of the town rests chiefly on its ancient remains. The most notable is St Columbkille's house, first an oratory and later made a church.

The present church is modern, save for its bell tower, rebuilt in 1578. Near the church stands a fine though imperfect round tower, 99 feet high, and there are several ancient crosses, the finest now set up in the market place. Kells was first a royal seat. Its old name Ceanannus means the circular northern fort where the king lived, and its later name Kenlis means head fort. Conn of the Hundred Fights lived here in the 2nd century, and Dermot, king of Ireland, had a palace on the spot.
britannica-1911-leadhills:
Leadhills is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a village of Lanarkshire, Scotland. A count from 1901 gives the village 835 people. It is the highest village in all Scotland. It lies 1301 feet above the level of the sea. It stands near the source of Glengonner Water. A light railway serves the village for travel. Lead and silver have long been mined there.

The mines at Leadhills and Wanlockhead run back for centuries. Gold was discovered there in the reign of James the Fourth. That gold once gave work to three hundred persons, it is said. Its mining has long ceased to be profitable. The village is neat and well built in its streets. It contains a masonic hall and a library. The miners founded that library in the mid 1700s. The poet Allan Ramsay was born in the village.
britannica-1911-llanwrtyd-wells:
Llanwrtyd Wells, an urban district of Breconshire in south Wales, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands amid wild mountain scenery on the river Irfon, a branch of the Wye. A rail station on the central Wales line links it to London. The place is chiefly noted for its sulphur and chalybeate springs, the former the strongest of their kind in Wales.

The healing power of the sulphur water was found, or found again, in 1732 by Theophilus Evans. He was a famed Welsh writer and vicar of the parish to which Llanwrtyd then belonged. Saline water is brought in daily in the season from Builth Wells for drinkers. The Irfon is famed as a trout stream for miles of its course. Welsh is the main tongue of the district, and the parish held just 854 souls in 1901.
britannica-1911-mendip-hills:
The Mendip Hills of Somerset are ranged out in a land entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The range runs north-west for some twenty-three miles in length. It stands about six miles wide and covers near one hundred and thirty square miles. Marshy moors lie at its south-west foot, drained by the Axe. Axbridge, Cheddar, and Wells sit in a row at that foot.

A high flat top crowns the range, swelling to over a thousand feet. The hills are built chiefly of a hard carbon rock, limestone. Fine cliffs scar the flanks, as in the gorge of Cheddar. Rain water has carved a famed run of caves below. Sink holes on the top, called swallets, swallow whole streams down.
britannica-1911-oels:
Oels is a town of Germany in the Prussian province of Silesia, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was once the capital of a small principality of its own name. It lies in a sandy plain on the Oelsbach stream, twenty miles north-east of Breslau by rail. Its people numbered 10,940 in 1905.

The princely castle, then held by the crown prince of Prussia, dates from 1558 and was restored in the early eighteen nineties. It holds a good library and a stock of pictures. Of the town's three churches, one dates from the thirteenth century and one from the fourteenth. The folk work chiefly at shoe making and at growing vegetables for the Breslau market. Oels was founded about the year 940 and became a town in 1255. Its principality passed through many hands and lapsed to the Prussian crown in 1884.
britannica-1911-parallels:
Parallels, in siegecraft, are trenches dug by a besieging army. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains their zigzag advance. They run in a rough line with the fort front under attack. Along with zigzag approaches they form the formal attack of a siege.

Each short length is set so its line clears the fort works. That skew keeps the trench safe from fire along its length. The first parallel opens at a set range under cover of night. Great digging parties throw it up in one stretch of work. Zigzag cuts then link it to the rear for safe passage. New zigzags push out to a second parallel, then a third. Each line stands stronger and closer than the last. From the last line troops can rush across open ground.
britannica-1911-seals:
Seals are stamps used to mark a deed or thing as truly coming from a named person. The 1911 Britannica article opens with the root idea. A seal print stands in for the presence or act of its owner at a set moment. In the East, seals have long been pressed in ink or paint, much as a signature works in the West. In the West, seals were pressed in relief into wax, clay, or soft metal.

The word seal names both the print and, in loose speech, the tool that makes it. Strictly, the tool is called the matrix, and the print alone is the seal. The oldest finds come from Egypt, Babylonia, and Assyria. Prints on clay jar stoppers there go back before the first pharaohs. The article goes on to trace the craft through later ages.
britannica-1911-stanhope-earls:
Stanhope is the subject of a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The article centres on James Stanhope, first Earl Stanhope, who lived from about 1673 to 1721. He was an English statesman and soldier. He was schooled at Eton and at Oxford. He went to Spain with his father in 1690 and learned the country well.

The article follows his service as a volunteer in Italy and Flanders. He gained an army post in 1695 and entered the Commons in 1701. He fought in Spain in the War of the Spanish Succession. He took Port Mahon and helped win two battles in 1710. At Brihuega he was overwhelmed and held prisoner for over a year. Back in England he left the army for politics and led the Whigs in the Commons.
britannica-1911-state-trials:
State trials, in English law, are trials touching offences against the state, and this 1911 Britannica entry is a history of the printed collections of them. In practice the name also covers cases that throw light on state officers and on points of national or church law. The first collection of accounts came out in 1719 in four volumes, the work, it seems, of the writer Thomas Salmon.

The entry walks through edition after edition as the set kept growing. A second edition of 1730 ran to six volumes, and a third of 1742 to eight. The best known is the fifth, begun by William Cobbett and edited by Thomas Bayly Howell, issued from 1809 to 1826 in thirty-three volumes. A new series under a parliamentary committee began in 1885 and reached eight volumes by 1898, bringing the trials down to 1858.
britannica-1911-strength-of-materials:
Strength of materials is the part of engineering study that deals with stress in built parts, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Its chief aim is to find the right size and shape for pieces that must bear set loads. It can also work the other way, to find safe loads for pieces already sized.

The field also treats how loads change the form of a piece. It joins tests of how strong and springy each material is with maths on ties, struts, and beams. Stress is defined as a shared action between two bodies or two parts of one body. Each side pushes the other with equal force, as a stone pushes the ground and is pushed back.
britannica-1911-suliman-hills:
The 1911 Britannica article on the Suliman Hills describes a mountain system in India. The range lies on the north-west frontier. It runs south from the Gomal river. It forms a hard barrier between the plains of the Indus and Afghanistan. At last it merges into the hills of Baluchistan.

The account centres on the chief mass of the range. It is called Takht-i-Suliman, or Solomon's throne. From Dera Ismail Khan it looks like a grey rampart. The article tells the legend of Solomon's throne. The throne was hollowed from the rock. The spot is now a place of pilgrimage. A survey in 1883 mapped the whole mountain. It found two parallel ridges over 11,000 feet high. A high tableland with pine forests joins them.
britannica-1911-tamils:
The Tamils are the subject of a language and peoples entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry opens by linking the word Tamil to Dravida, a Sanskrit name for south Indian peoples and tongues. The stages by which the word changed form are traced in detail. Bishop Caldwell's grammar of the Dravidian tongues is cited as the key discussion.

Earlier scholars who first proposed that link are named and dated. Their books on travel, handbooks, and word lists are given in full. One scholar is noted as holding a distinct view on how the word Tamil arose. The entry shows how scholars of the day built their case from printed sources.
britannica-1911-tunbridge-wells:
Tunbridge Wells, a town and inland watering place in Kent, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands about thirty-four and a half miles south-east of London, on two rail lines. The census of 1901 counted 33,375 people there. Part of the town spills over the county line into Sussex.

The article credits its fame to an iron-rich spring and a hilly, wooded setting. The wells stand by the Pantiles, a paved walk tied to fashion since the days of Queen Anne. Nearby sights get their share of space as well. They include the odd sandstone mass called the Toad Rock and the crags known as the High Rocks. Ruined Bayham Abbey, founded in 1200, lies five miles to the south-east.
britannica-1911-wells:
Wells, a city and market town in Somerset, England, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It lies in a hollow under the Mendip Hills, twenty miles south of Bristol. Its count in 1901 was 4,849 people. The city is said to take its name from springs called Saint Andrew's Wells, once thought to heal.

In Saxon times Wells was a chief town of Wessex, and in 905 it was made a bishop's seat. The see was moved to Bath near 1091, then a shared plan was set in 1139. The bishop would bear the title of Bath and Wells and be picked by both houses. The town's weight is near all church based, the piece says. Its cathedral ranks among the finest in England.
britannica-1911-wels:
Wels is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Wels is a town of Upper Austria, standing on the River Traun. It lies south-west of Linz on the railway. Its population in 1900 was 12,187.

The parish church draws the entry's first notice. It is a Gothic building, rebuilt in the fifteenth century, with parts said to date from the ninth. The town draws natural gas from deep wells first bored in 1891. That gas serves for lighting, heat, and power. Trade in corn, timber, cattle, pigs, and horses was brisk. Makers produced machinery, iron goods, calico, gunpowder, paper, and leather. A short history closes the piece: the Roman town Ovilaba stood on the site. Dukes held court there in the eighth century, and the present town dates from the eleventh.
britannica-1911-wilde-oscar-o-flahertie-:
Wilde, Oscar, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of the English author. Born in Dublin on the 15th of October 1856, he was son of a famed Irish surgeon. His mother wrote verse and prose under the pen name Speranza. He shone in classics at Trinity College in Dublin.

In 1874 he went to Magdalen College at Oxford on a scholarship. He won the Newdigate prize in 1878 with his poem Ravenna. He also took first class marks in his classics work. But his fame at Oxford came from a new cult of art for art's sake. Long hair, lilies, and blue china marked his pose. The cult spread in spite of mockery and a ducking in the Cherwell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acquaviva-car:
Acquaviva is the name of several Italian cardinals, and this entry sketches seven of them. Francesco, born at Naples in 1665 of the Dukes of Atri, served under four popes, was made cardinal and Bishop of Sabina by Clement XI, and died in 1723. Giovanni Vincenzo, Bishop of Melfi and Rapolla, became cardinal-priest in 1542 and died in 1566. Giulio, nuncio of Pius V to Philip II of Spain, was made cardinal by that pope and attended him on his deathbed.

Ottavio the elder, Archbishop of Naples in 1605, helped convert Henri IV. Ottavio the younger, made cardinal in 1654, served as legate in Viterbo and Romagna, curbing the banditti there. Troiano, made cardinal in 1732, represented the Spanish kings in the Curia and influenced the conclave electing Benedict XIV in 1740. Pasquale, made cardinal in 1773, closes the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-vessels:
Altar vessels centre on the chalice, holding the Eucharistic wine and water. It should be gold, or silver gilt inside, or a silver cup gilt inside with base and stem of any solid, clean, becoming metal. Stannum, a tin-lead alloy, is also allowed with a gilt interior. The paten, holding the altar bread, matches the chalice's material, gilt on its concave side if not gold, its edge thin and sharp to gather particles from the corporal.

The ciborium keeps consecrated particles for the laity's Communion, of any solid decent material, even gilt copper. The ostensorium, a glass-framed shrine of gold, silver, brass, or gilt copper, exposes the Blessed Sacrament publicly. A chalice loses consecration when unfit for use, as when the slightest break appears near the cup's bottom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angels:
Angel, from Latin angelus and Greek aggelos, from Hebrew for one going or one sent, means messenger. The Hebrew word means a divine or human messenger, rendered aggelos by the Septuagint, with both meanings. The Latin version distinguishes the spirit-messenger from humans, using angelus for the one and legatus or nuntius for the other. In a few passages the Latin version misleads, using angelus where nuntius would fit better, as in Isaiah 18:2.

Only the spirit-messenger concerns this article. It discusses the term's meaning, the angels' offices and names, good and evil spirits, the choirs, and appearances. Districts are allotted to angels termed their princes, as in the Apocalyptic angels of the seven churches. De Coelesti Hierarchia, ascribed to Saint Denis the Areopagite, treats of the hierarchies and orders of angels, though it dates centuries later. Its doctrine of the choirs has been received with extraordinary unanimity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-sch:
Apostolic schools are schools that train boys for the foreign missions, where the church is not yet normally organized. In settled lands, junior seminaries begin the training of diocesan clergy and theological seminaries complete it. Mission lands, by contrast, depend on foreign mission colleges and on apostolic schools to supply priests. Their object is to foster vocations, or calls to mission work, among youths who might otherwise never reach a seminary.

As distinct from junior seminaries, apostolic schools trace their origin to Father Alberic de Foresta, a Jesuit who lived from 1818 to 1876. He found many fine societies for prayer and mission funds, yet judged them weak without a supply of men to preach and give the sacraments. Experience in guiding souls convinced him that pious youths, held back by poverty or other bars, could still become missionaries if a school took them in hand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-appeals:
Appeals gives a comprehensive view of the church's positive law on appeals within the church court system. It leaves the nature of that court and the pope's right to receive appeals to other articles. An appeal is defined as a legal application to a superior authority for redress against an injury from a lower authority's act. The lower authority is called the judge from whom appeal is made, the higher the appellate judge or court. Appeals divide into judicial and extrajudicial kinds.

A judicial appeal attacks acts of the lower authority in its official role as judge at any stage of proceedings. It covers not only a final sentence but also an interlocutory sentence, one given during the case. The long article then works through kinds, effects, time limits, and procedure, giving canon lawyers and historians the full framework by which church judgments could be challenged and corrected.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bath-and-well:
Bath and Wells is an ancient diocese coextensive with Somerset, England, though its first bishop under that exact title came only in 1244. Æthelhelm, later Archbishop of Canterbury, first ruled there from 909 to 914, choosing Wells's secular church as cathedral. Rivalry followed between Wells's secular canons and the monks of Glastonbury and Bath, with Wells struggling.

Bishop Gisa (1060-88) found Wells small and poor, its canons begging bread, and rebuilt it with lands from Edward, Harold, and William the Conqueror. His successor John de Villula undid much by moving the see to Bath in 1088, using its abbey as cathedral. Robert of Lewes (1136-66) rebuilt Wells's cathedral and arranged a settlement, and the diocese held three archdeaconries: Bath, Wells, and Taunton.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bells:
Bells get a wide-ranging survey in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, treated in five parts that move from origins to law. The entry opens with ancient and early Christian uses of bells and sounding instruments, then turns to the rite of blessing them. That blessing, with its prayers and anointing, gives a bell its place in church life.

Later sections cover daily uses, from calling worshippers to marking deaths and alarms, and then inscriptions and old examples that survive. A closing part sets out points of canon law on who may bless, ring, and remove bells. The entry joins liturgy, craft, and church rule in one reference piece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-kells:
The Book of Kells, an Irish manuscript of the Four Gospels, ranks as the choicest relic of Irish art. Also called the Book of Columba, it likely comes from Iona, and the Annals of Ulster record the theft of Columba's Gospel in 1006, probably this book. Tradition makes it Columba's own work, but its script and ornament place it no earlier than the late seventh or early eighth century.

Gerald of Wales saw it at Kildare in the twelfth century and praised it warmly. It later rested at Kells in Meath until 1541, and Archbishop Ussher gave it to Trinity College, Dublin, where it remains the library's treasure. Two unknown scribes seem to have written and painted it in black, red, purple, and yellow ink. Its spirals, trumpet patterns, beast interlacements, and ribbon plaits show Irish design at its inventive peak, though some ornaments stay unfinished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brussels:
Brussels, capital of Belgium, held 612,041 people at the end of 1905 with its eight suburban communes. It grew on the little Senne, now arched over by inner boulevards, and rose on the inland trade road between the Low Countries and Cologne. Canals link it to the Sambre and the Scheldt, and it has borne the title of seaport since 1895.

Tradition credits Saint Gery, Bishop of Cambrai, with a village and chapel on a Senne island late in the sixth century. First named Brosella, marsh dwelling, near the ninth century's end, it passed through Gerberga's dower to Lorraine's dukes. Charles of Lorraine made it his home and brought Saint Gudule's bones from Mortzelle in 979, making her the town's patron. On his son Otto's death in 1004, Lambert Balderic took Brussels, Vilvorde, and Louvain, seed of the duchy of Brabant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carolingian-s:
Carolingian schools grew from a Merovingian palace school, the scola palatina, that trained young Frankish nobles in war and court ceremony rather than letters. Literary teaching in those days belonged to monastic and cathedral schools.
