With Charlemagne's accession in 768, reform began in the palace school itself and spread by imperial decree to schools across his vast empire.

The palace school changed from tactics and manners to learning from 780, once victories over Lombards, Saxons, and Saracens allowed it. Real success came only with Alcuin's arrival at Aachen in 782. Alcuin headed the emperor's palace school and joined his council on all educational matters, becoming Charlemagne's prime minister of education and bringing York's learning tradition. Monastic, episcopal, and village schools carried the revival forward, despite war and pillage, to the dawn of university teaching in the thirteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-summ:
A Catholic summer school gathers clergy and laity in the summer months for lectures and special courses, fostering intellectual culture in harmony with Christian faith along university-extension lines. The movement began with the Champlain Summer School. It was founded at New London, Connecticut, in 1892. In 1893 it settled permanently at Cliff Haven, New York.

Other schools followed. The Columbian Summer School opened at Madison, Wisconsin, in 1895, later moving to Milwaukee. A winter school began at New Orleans in 1896, and the Maryland Summer School in 1900. The article traces the roots of the movement in reading circles, university extension, and summer institutes, including Isaac Hecker's library work and the young men's lyceums.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-mathi:
An entry on Charles Mathieu Schols, a Dutch civil engineer and geodesist, a measurer of the earth's surface, born at Maastricht in 1849. He trained at the Delft polytechnic, taught at the Royal Military Academy at Breda, and published a textbook on surveying in 1879. Offered the Delft chair of geodesy and surveying in 1878, he was elected to the Royal Academy of Sciences in 1880 and published a stream of papers on the mathematics of mapping.

Schols wrote on computing distance and direction from latitude and longitude, on joining small survey triangles to larger nets, and on map projections, the ways of flattening the curved earth onto paper. He also worked on error theory, pure mathematics, and bridge stresses, and he helped write a textbook on hydraulic architecture, the building of waterworks. He prepared and supervised the new national survey of Holland begun in 1886. He died at Delft in 1897.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerks-regula:
The Clerks Regular of the Pious Schools, also called Piarists and Scolopi, are a religious order founded at Rome in 1597 by Saint Joseph Calasanctius. A Confraternity of Christian Doctrine member, he taught country people and saw the need for early religious instruction of poor children. Antonio Brendoni, Santa Dorotea in Trastevere's pastor, gave him two rooms, soon joined by two other priests.

As attendance grew, Calasanctius moved the school into the city and lived there with companions. A later move to the Vestri Palace began community life, and Clement the Eighth approved the work with a yearly allowance for rent. Inspection by Cardinals Antoniani and Baronius satisfied critics, and Paul the Fifth approved still more warmly. On 25 March 1617 Calasanctius and his companions took the religious habit. Gregory the Fifteenth made the congregation a religious order on 18 November 1621.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cruelty-to-an:
A moral entry surveys attitudes to cruelty toward animals from pagan antiquity to Catholic doctrine. Pythagoras and Empedocles first urged kindness, holding that human souls pass into animal bodies after death, so animals share human rights. Cicero condemned that error, while Roman law still protected useful beasts.

The Old Testament forbade muzzling the treading ox and yoking ox and ass together. The New Testament is nearly silent, and the Fathers say little. Scholastics, above all St. Thomas, condemned needless suffering chiefly for its harm to the doer's character. Catholic doctrine, the entry argues, grants animals no rights yet denounces cruelty vigorously. Excessive fondness, it warns, is no sure index of moral worth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cure-of-souls:
A canon law entry defines the cure of souls, in Latin cura animarum, as a clerical office with a set district. Its holder teaches the faithful by sermons and warnings, and makes them holy through the sacraments, by lawful appointment. The pope holds it for the whole Church, bishops in their dioceses, and parish priests in their parishes.

Others share it under these leaders. Missionaries in lands without sees share the pope's care for those regions, and parish curates serve parts of a parish under their pastor. Its object is the salvation of souls, carrying on Christ's mission on earth. A priest's mission comes from the Church alone. It flows through apostolic succession in two forms: holy orders, passed on by bishops, and jurisdiction, passed on by the living teaching office headed by the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-devotional-me:
A survey of devotional medals, pieces of metal struck or cast like coins but never used as money, bearing an image, device, or inscription for memory's sake. Religious medals outdo secular ones in variety. They mark persons, shrines, and events, first Communions and ordinations, and mysteries of faith. They teach piety, badge associations, protect the wearer, and carry indulgences.

Early Christian examples were long doubted. De Rossi's 1869 article settled some as genuine. The Middle Ages left little trace, and the Renaissance brought medals proper into popular post-Reformation use. Classes follow. Plague medals show Sebastian, Roch, and shrine views. Other medals mark Eucharistic miracles such as Seefeld, and private medals mark baptisms and weddings. Legend medals close the list, led by the cross said to have reached Saint Ulrich before battle in 955.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-early-christi:
Angels were seldom shown in Christian art before Constantine. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry names the oldest angel fresco, an Annunciation of the second century in the cemetery of Saint Priscilla. In the cemetery of Saints Peter and Marcellinus, Wilpert found a third-century Annunciation, where Gabriel likewise appears as a human figure, robed in tunic and pallium. The Good Angel of a fourth-century fresco of the judgment of Vibia also wears human dress, as a sacred personage.

The winged angel, though Scripture offers ample warrant, does not appear before Constantine, likely because wings would recall favorite subjects of classical art. The entry then traces angels in litanies and churches, with Michael and Gabriel invoked just after the Trinity. Umbria was famed for angel churches, and the East raised many to Saint Michael.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Ecclesiastical annals belong to the historical writing of the Middle Ages, classed with chronicles and lives of saints. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that chronicles began in Greece, while annals first appear among Romans. In the Middle Ages chronicle covered every form of history, though at first it meant only a chronological table. Pagan history no longer appealed to Christian writers, who sought a history centered on the kingdom of God.

To the new generation the heart of history lay in the misfortunes of the Jewish nation, a theme Roman historians ignored. Christians needed a general history in tune with their ideal. The entry follows the annal form from its Roman roots through Carolingian writers such as Einhard, with Kurze and Waitz among its guides.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-episcopal-san:
Episcopal sandals are low shoes, more like slippers, worn with liturgical stockings at pontifical solemn Mass. Unlike ancient sandals, mere soles tied by straps, they have a leather sole and an upper of silk or velvet, often embroidered. No cross is required on them, since at Rome that mark is a papal privilege alone. The stockings, called caligae, are silk, knitted or sewn.

Only bishops may wear sandals and caligae by right; abbots and other prelates need a special papal privilege. They are used only at pontifical Mass and ordinations, never at Confirmations or solemn Vespers. Their colour follows the day, but there are no black sandals or stockings, since they are not used at Masses for the dead or on Good Friday. They belong to the Latin rite alone and are unknown in Eastern rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernst-of-hess:
Ernst of Hesse-Rheinfels, a landgrave, was born on 9 December 1623 at Cassel and died on 12 May 1693 at Cologne. Moritz, Landgrave of Hesse-Cassel, was his father, and Ernst was his sixth son. Ernst and his brother Hermann founded the collateral lines of Hesse-Rheinfels and Hesse-Rotenburg after Moritz resigned the government in 1627 to his son Wilhelm V. His conversion to the Catholic Faith stirred controversial literature, and that is why he figures prominently in his country's religious history.

His mother raised him under strict discipline, and his instruction in the Reformed Church received the utmost attention. In 1642 he joined the Hessian army, where he proved an able commander of troops fighting on Sweden's side in the Thirty Years' War. While visiting the Hessian General Geyso, imprisoned at Gesecke, he was himself arrested and taken prisoner to Paderborn. Talk there with the royal army chaplain began his conversion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-espousals:
An espousal is a contract of future marriage between a man and a woman, who are thereby affianced. The law governing this contract was amended by the decree Ne Temere, published 2 August 1907 and effective 19 April 1908. For the old legislation see Betrothal; the present article is confined to the new. The decree enacts that only written espousals, signed by both parties and by the parish priest, the ordinary, or two witnesses, are valid and beget canonical effects.

If a party cannot write, this is noted, and another witness signs with the priest, the ordinary, or the two witnesses. Until Easter 1908 no written document was prescribed for espousals, except for Spain. Before, the promise of marriage bound the parties according to prevailing law or custom. That caused difficulties which necessitated this law. Private, clandestine espousals are henceforth of no value in the eyes of the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evangelical-c:
The Evangelical Counsels, also called the Counsels of Perfection, are Gospel counsels for those who would do more than the bare minimum for heaven. Christ laid down precepts binding on all, above all the Ten Commandments, as the needful condition of eternal life. Beside them he taught counsels, not binding on all, for those aiming at Christian perfection as far as it can be reached on earth. Christ told the rich young man first to keep the commandments, then, if he would be perfect, to sell all and give to the poor.

The three chief counsels answer the three great goods of this world: riches, pleasures of the flesh, and honors. Poverty frees the soul from riches, chastity from fleshly pleasure, and obedience from self-love and rank. A soul may be saved without them, but reaches heaven more surely with them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-false-decreta:
The False Decretals are a forged set of papal letters from the ninth century. They circulated under the name of Isidore Mercator, or Pseudo-Isidore. The collection mixes genuine texts with about a hundred forged letters. Its three parts cover early popes, councils, and later decretal law.

Scholars exposed the forgery through anachronisms in dates, language, and law. Blondel's critique of 1628 proved decisive against the collection. The Ballerini brothers and Hinschius later produced critical editions of the texts. The article traces the forgery's spread and its effect on church law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-fool:
The Feast of Fools was a licensed medieval revel held near New Year's Day. It grew from the subdeacons' festival on the Circumcision feast. Deacons, priests, and choristers each had their own December days. The subdeacons' day became a feast of the lower clergy and fools' guilds.

Its license echoed the pagan Saturnalia, when slaves stood equal to masters. Church authorities condemned its excesses again and again, often in vain. At Paris in 1199 the bishop curbed, but did not ban, the revel. The feast's core idea was brief reversal, with the lowly raised high.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-guar:
The Feast of Guardian Angels honours the angels assigned to each individual person. Local at first, it reached Cordova in 1579 and Toledo and Valencia soon after. Paul V placed it in the general calendar in 1608. Clement X later made it obligatory for the whole Church on 2 October.

The belief itself is ancient, though the feast is comparatively recent. Early liturgies already praised angelic protection and intercession for mortal men. The Mass texts stress the angels' threefold office of praise and guidance. In Germany the feast is kept on the first Sunday of September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-general-counc:
General Councils are lawfully convened assemblies of church leaders and theologians to settle doctrine and discipline by common deliberation. Council and synod mean the same, though mere worship meetings and diocesan synods fall short of the name, and unlawful gatherings earn the titles of robber synods. The entry defines the thing before it sorts its kinds.

Its heads run from classification and history through the pope's share in calling, guiding, and confirming councils, to who may sit, how many must come, and how business moves. The deepest questions close the work: whether councils err, how papal and conciliar infallibility fit, whether a council stands above the pope, and whether it can depose him. Definition, facts, and theory each get their turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gospel-and-go:
Gospel and Gospels is a general article on the word Gospel, usually a written record of Christ's words and deeds. It likely comes from the Anglo-Saxon god, good, and spell, to tell. It matches the Greek euangelion, good tidings, and the Latin Evangelium. A Catholic Encyclopedia article sets out the other meanings of euangelion in the body of the piece.

The first four historical books of the New Testament carry titles such as Euangelion kata Matthaion, which, however ancient, do not go back to the authors themselves. The Muratorian Canon, Clement of Alexandria, and Irenaeus witness to the headings in the latter part of the second century. Their early currency suggests they were prefixed in the first part of that century, once the four narratives were collected.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grace-at-meal:
Grace at Meals is an article on prayer at table from apostolic times, when Paul counseled doing all to the glory of God. Clement of Alexandria held it fitting to praise the Creator before nourishment and to sing his praises over the things created. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the ancient formulae behind the Roman Benedicite and Graces.

Tertullian shows third-century Christians signing the cross at table, praying before reclining, and closing the feast with prayer. Archaeology has found cup-bases reading Drink in Christ and Drink piously. One ancient formula, in a fourth-century treatise wrongly ascribed to Athanasius, thanks the Father for the Resurrection. It prays the scattered Church be gathered as bread is made one. In the Roman liturgy the Benedicite and Graces use Psalms 149 and 33, with Psalm 1 at midday and Psalm 116 in the evening.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grace-before-:
Grace before Meals is an article on thanksgiving over food, where grace in pre-Elizabethan English always took the plural graces and means nothing but thanksgiving. Gratitude for bounty is not exclusively Christian, yet following the Saviour's own example the obligation was emphasized from the beginning. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces the practice from Paul and Aristides to the Breviary.

Paul gave thanks before eating in the sight of all. About 123 Aristides declared Christians render God thanks over food and drink. Tertullian wrote that prayer is tasted before the banquet and ends the feast, and Prudentius composed hymns Before Food and After Food. In religious orders the custom was much insisted on, with a section in Chapter 43 of Benedict's Rule, and schools and colleges kept their own metrical forms, some surviving today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-great-falls:
Great Falls is a diocese created by Pius X on 18 May 1904, covering eleven counties in eastern Montana over 94,158 square miles. Its titular city takes its name from the Missouri's falls, 533 feet in cascades yielding 340,000 horsepower, ranking next to Niagara in beauty and mechanical value. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a mission land turned manufacturing centre.

Father De Smet and companions first celebrated Mass in the territory at Fort Benton in 1850. Jesuits founded Indian missions as early as 1841. At Saint Peter's Mission, now the Ursuline mother-house of Montana, 2732 baptisms of Indians were recorded from 1855 to 1879. Cheap power feeds flour, plaster, and iron works and a smelter turning out over one hundred million pounds of copper a year, and the city ranks next to Butte in population.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guardian-ange:
Catholic teaching on guardian angels holds that each soul has an angel charged with guarding it from birth. Yet the entry stresses that this has never been defined as an article of faith. It is, in St. Jerome's phrase, the mind of the Church. The belief itself runs through pagan antiquity, Babylonian monuments, and the writings of Menander, Plutarch, and Plotinus.

Scripture carries the doctrine from Old Testament guides and protectors, in Genesis, Exodus, Tobias, and Daniel, to the New Testament's sharper statements in Matthew and Hebrews. St. Thomas holds that only the lowest angelic orders serve as guardians, acting on senses and imagination but not on the will, while Scotus and Durandus allow any angel that rank. The guardians stay with us even after death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-nails:
The Holy Nails raise a long-debated question: was Christ crucified with three nails or four? Early medieval art strongly supports four nails, and some historical writers favour that view, though none earlier than Gregory of Tours. In the thirteenth century, western art began to show the feet placed one over the other and pierced by a single nail.

That three-nail view matches Nonnus, Socrates, and a poem attributed to Gregory Nazianzen. More recent criticism notes that the two earliest Crucifixion images show no nails in the feet at all. Ambrose and other early writers imply only two nails, and Ambrose says Helena had one nail made into a bridle for Constantine. The entry sifts art, texts, and relic claims with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-oils:
Holy oils, or olea sacra, are blessed oils whose symbolic meaning matches their natural uses. They sweeten, strengthen, and make supple, and the church uses them so in its rites. Liturgical blessing of oil is very ancient. Serapion's fourth-century Prayer Book and the Apostolic Constitutions show it, as does a Syriac document from the fifth or sixth century.

Serapion's book gives a formula for blessing oil and chrism for the newly baptized, when baptism and confirmation formed one ceremony. It gives separate blessings for oil of the sick, water, and bread. The prayer asks Christ to grant his creatures power for curing the sick, purifying souls, driving away impure spirits, and wiping out sins. Old Testament oil consecrated priests, kings, and altars, and served in sacrifices and purifications.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hospitals:
Hospitals began as places where strangers or visitors were received, from the Latin hospes, a guest. Only over time did the word narrow to institutions for the care of the sick. That change tracks a long development under religious, political, economic, social, and scientific influences. The modern hospital, in this view, joins natural human care for suffering with Christian charity and medical skill.

Pagan antiquity already shows humane practice among civilized peoples, though some tribes killed the feeble. Princess Macha founded an early Irish hospital in 300 BC, and the Buddhist king Asoka set up hospitals for men and animals in 252 BC. The entry follows hospitals from those beginnings through Christian foundations, medieval houses, and modern scientific institutions across the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-infidels:
Those who have not been baptized are the people this entry calls infidels, from a Latin root meaning lack of faith. The name covers pagans who do not know the true God, and also Jews and Muslims, who worship God yet do not recognize Jesus Christ. Catechumens, still preparing for baptism, fall under the term in strict use, though early ages often called them Christians instead.

Baptized Christians outside the Catholic Church are not infidels in this language but non-Catholics. Baptism already makes a person a subject and child of the Church, even a rebellious one. The entry then maps how each group stands toward the Church and her laws. That distinction shaped mission policy, marriage rules, and the Church's claim over baptized persons everywhere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-hessels:
Jean Hessels, a Louvain theologian born in 1522 and dead in 1566, taught eight years at Parc before taking the university theology chair. Like his senior colleague Baius, he drew theology from the Fathers, above all Augustine, rather than the Schoolmen, yet never strayed from received doctrine.

In 1559 Hessels went with Jansen and Baius to Trent, helped draft the decree on invoking saints, relics, and images, and faced Scholastic critics for leaving beaten paths. Back home he turned his energy against Protestants, defended the Immaculate Conception against Baius himself. He argued for papal infallibility in a work appended to his 1565 refutation of a new faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jocelin-of-we:
Jocelin of Wells, bishop of Bath and Wells, died on 19 November 1242. Probably a Wells native, he acted as royal justiciar at Westminster in 1203, guarded vacant Lincoln, and held Wells canonry with two Herefordshire benefices. Sent by Savaric to force Glastonbury monks to drop a papal appeal, he later succeeded Savaric himself.

Elected bishop in February 1206 and consecrated at Reading that May, Jocelin fled the interdict in 1208, saw his estates seized, and regained them when John submitted in 1213. In 1215 he helped Langton win Magna Carta and stands named in it as royal counsellor. With Winchester's bishop he crowned boy-king Henry III, backed Hubert de Burgh against French forces, and served as travelling justice in the southwest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lateran-counc:
The Lateran Councils were five important councils meeting at Rome between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries. From Constantine's reign until the papal court moved to Avignon, Rome's bishops lived in the Lateran palace and worshipped in its basilica.

Popes chose council cities to spare travelling bishops long and costly absences. Five general councils met in the Lateran itself: the First in 1123, Second in 1139, Third in 1179, Fourth in 1215, and Fifth in the sixteenth century. Other Lateran councils, not ecumenical, include those of 649 against Monothelitism and of 823, 864, and 900. In 1725 Benedict XIII gathered Rome's directly subject bishops there to fight Jansenism and confirm the bull Unigenitus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthias-kess:
Maastricht sculptor Matthias Kessels (1784-1836) learned goldsmithing at Venloo, studied at the Paris Beaux-Arts, and spent eight years at St. Petersburg making silver and wax models and sculpture. Back in Paris he worked under Girodet, then joined Thorvaldsen's studio at Rome. There he helped carve the famed Day and Night reliefs of 1819. A Canova competition prize for his St. Sebastian pierced with arrows launched his name.

Commissions followed from the Duke of Alba, the Prince of Orange, and the Duke of Devonshire. They include reclining and active Discus-throwers, a Cupid whetting his darts, and a colossal Paris resting at Laeken. Religious work was his strength: Christ at the Column, busts of Christ and Mary, the Four Evangelists in terra-cotta, and a Pieta. A St. Michael for Brussels was still unfinished when he died at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ordeals:
Ordeals, or judgments of God, settled guilt or innocence by trial when ordinary proof failed, trusting God to shield the innocent. The practice rested on belief that a just and all-knowing God would intervene, by miracle if need be, rather than let an innocent person suffer.

Imposed by a judge or chosen by the parties, ordeals took two forms. Tests borne by the accused alone included hot iron or cold water, and tests shared by both sides included oath-helpers or combat. The entry traces them through Germanic law, church councils, and their slow abolition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-fria:
The Conventual Franciscans form one of three bodies, with Friars Minor and Capuchins, that make up the First Order of Saint Francis. All three follow Francis's rule, but Conventuals observe it with dispensations lawfully granted, chiefly on poverty, while the others profess it pure and simple.

Innocent IV's 1250 bull let Franciscan churches with convents be called conventual, and the name marked large-convent friars against hermit-like brothers. After 1431, and sharply after 1517, Conventual came to name the branch accepting dispensations, and the entry traces its houses and rule. The term conventual marked no distinct section officially before 1431.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-decreta:
Papal decretals are pontifical letters carrying a papal decision. In a wide sense any decretal letter counts. In a narrower sense only rulings on discipline count. In the strictest sense a decretal is a rescript, an answer when the pope is appealed to or asked for counsel on discipline. Decretals are not always general church laws. Popes often ordered recipients to share the answer with district authorities. Those authorities then followed it in like cases.

The oldest commonly cited decretal is Siricius's letter of 385 to Himerius of Tarragona, though a fourth-century letter of Damasus to Gaul's bishops may be older. Decretals differ from council canons, from dogmatic letters, and from constitutions issued on the pope's own motion. Later pages trace their gathering into collections, their sway in canon law, and their use in courts and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacramentals:
In instituting the sacraments Christ did not fix matter and form down to the slightest detail, leaving the Church to determine suitable rites. These rites, called Sacramentalia, manifest respect for the sacrament and secure the faithful's sanctification. They span many categories: substance in mixing water with wine, quantity in triple effusion, and quality in unleavened bread. Relation appears in the minister's capacity, time and place in churches, habit in vestments, and posture in genuflection.

Many external conditions link sacramentals with the virtue of religion. Trent says ceremonies, blessings, lights, and incense enhance the Holy Sacrifice's dignity and arouse the faithful's piety. Sacramentals also distinguish Church members from heretics, who abolished them or use them arbitrarily. Sacramental rites depend on the establishing Church, which alone may maintain, develop, modify, or abrogate them. The Church, through its visible head, alone legislates them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-kel:
Kells, Gaelic Cenannus, was the chief Irish monastery of Columba's order. Founded most probably in 554, nine years before Columba founded Iona, it lived in Iona's shadow during the saint's lifetime. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia tours monuments that tradition ties to Columba's stay.

Most interesting is Columba's House, a tall, steep-roofed building. Its ground floor served as an oratory, while the croft between the oratory's curved arch and the roof gave the saint his sleeping chamber. Two fine crosses, probably ninth-century, date from when Kells held primacy over all Columban houses in Ireland and Scotland. One stands in the market-place, the other in the churchyard, bearing on its plinth the words Cross of Patrick and Columba.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schools:
Schools, in this vast entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, are treated first as the Church's own task. By her divine charter, Going, teach all nations, the Church is essentially a teaching body, founded to dispense salvation's means and teach truths needed for salvation. Her earliest catechumenal schools taught those spiritual and moral truths. The entry then asks where other learning fits.

Truths of science, history, and culture, called profane learning, do not belong intrinsically to the Church's programme. Yet they enter her work by circumstance, when Christian youth cannot learn them without danger to faith or morals. They enter also by a teaching principle she has always practised: religion coordinates all education as it coordinates life. The entry surveys church schools from antiquity to modern states.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sioux-falls:
The diocese of Sioux Falls, suffragan to Saint Paul, covers all of South Dakota east of the Missouri River, 34,861 square miles. The first Mass in South Dakota was said in 1842 in Brown County by Monsignor Ravoux of Saint Paul, and the first church rose in 1867 at Jefferson through Father Pierre Boucher.

In August 1879 the Vicariate Apostolic of Dakota was set up, and Martin Marty, Abbot of Saint Meinrad's in Indiana, became vicar apostolic. Consecrated in February 1880, he faced an immense district of 149,112 square miles with scarcely any travel but ox or mule teams. Thirty-one years on, where one bishop and twelve priests had stood, the entry counts four bishops and 284 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-th:
Founded in Paris in 1856 by Eugénie Smet, in religion Mary of Providence, the Society of the Helpers of the Holy Souls assists the souls in purgatory. Smet, born at Lille in 1825 and educated at the Sacred Heart convent there, reached Paris on 19 January 1856 and won Archbishop Sibour's permission three days later. Her community took possession of 16 Rue de la Barouillère on 1 July 1856, still the mother-house.

Besides the three usual vows the Helpers take a fourth obligation to pray, suffer, and labour for souls in purgatory. Choir nuns and lay sisters share the same vows, rule, and privileges, and their chief mercy work is visiting and caring for the sick poor at home. Houses spread from Nantes and Shanghai to Brussels, Rome, and New York, and the Helpers nursed wounded of both nations in the Franco-Prussian War.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spirituals:
The Spirituals were groups of Friars Minor in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries who broke with the main body of the Franciscan order over how strictly St. Francis's Rule should be kept. Claiming to hold the Rule in its first severity, they took a name drawn from homo spiritualis, the deeply religious and ascetic man of medieval speech and of Paul's letters.

Some derive the name from the Rule's own clause about brothers unable to observe it spiritually. While a recent scholar traces it to the language of Joachimism, the prophetic movement that coloured Franciscan hopes. The entry follows the Spirituals through their quarrels, condemnations, and scattered survival, a chapter of reforming zeal turned schism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paul-witho:
St Paul Outside the Walls, the great basilica on the Via Ostia, guards the apostle's burial place beyond Rome's ancient boundary. By the year 200 a memorial chapel marked the grave, near the catacomb of Commodilla. Constantine raised it into a basilica, and Theodosius began a far larger church in 386, finished with mosaics under Leo the Great.

Prudentius sang its splendours, and a frieze of papal portraits ringed its nave. Fire in 1823, begun by a workman repairing roof lead, destroyed the ancient church, sparing only part of the apse, the triumphal arch, and some mosaics. Rebuilt on the old plan, it keeps its rank as an abbey nullius and a patriarchal basilica. The entry traces architecture, art, and rebuilding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stalls:
Stalls, the enclosed choir seats of clergy, trace a history from stone benches to carved wooden masterpieces. Mentioned from the eleventh century, stalls began as subsellia, usually stone, placed right and left of the bishop's cathedra in the basilica apse. As clergy numbers grew, they stood during choir service, as Chrodegang's Rule and Aachen's statutes of 816 show.

Even in the eleventh century Peter Damian wrote against sitting in choir. The weak leaned on a T-shaped crutch called a reclinatorium, sometimes censured, sometimes allowed. Then came formae, seats with backs, and actual stalli, connected seats divided only by arms, seeking architectural effect. Once movable, stalls became fixed, with higher sides and backs, and ornament turned from pictorial to carved. The entry surveys famous examples across Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanley-falls:
Stanley Falls, a vicariate apostolic in the Belgian Congo, covered about ninety thousand square miles of river country. Its bounds ran east to the 30th meridian and south from Lake Albert Edward to the Elila-Congo confluence and Bena-Kamba. West lay the Lomami and Congo, and north the Ilimbiri, Welle, and Arwimi watersheds. Together they framed a vast mission field.

Sacred Heart Fathers founded the mission in 1897. They sailed from Antwerp on 6 July. They settled on Christmas Day at a spot four miles below Stanleyville on the Congo's right bank. Their first foundation, an orphanage, took the name St Gabriel. At first part of the Belgian Congo vicariate, the mission became a prefecture apostolic on 3 August 1904 and a vicariate apostolic on 10 March 1908. The entry maps boundaries, stations, and staff.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-angelical:
Milan in about 1530 saw the birth of this congregation of women, founded by Countess Luigia Torelli of Guastalla to shelter and reclaim girls in need. Working under Saint Antonio Zaccaria, founder of the Barnabites, the women took the Rule of Saint Augustine and won approval from Paul III in 1534. Each was called Angelica rather than Sister or Mother, and their dress followed Dominican custom.

Uncloistered at first, they helped the Barnabites on missions until scandal struck, when one member set herself up as a prophetess. Cloister followed in 1557, statutes were revised by Saint Charles Borromeo and confirmed in 1625, and political upheaval early in the nineteenth century finally destroyed their houses. A sister institute founded by the same countess still survived.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-universals:
Universals are the ideas by which different things can be represented by a single thought applied to all in the same way. The name points two ways: to the shared likeness in things themselves, and to the one idea that gathers them. Universals are ideas that set aside what makes things of one genus or species differ, and keep what is needful to their being, essential, and common to all, fixed through every change.

The entry places universals among the divine ideas that ground them, distinguishing universals before things, in things, and after things, in the scholastic phrases. It contrasts universal ideas with sense impressions, which catch only what is fleeting and particular. It then reviews the great medieval debate over whether universals are real things, mere names, or concepts of the mind, a debate that shaped logic and metaphysics for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vandals:
The Vandals were a Germanic people of the East German family, first settled, by Tacitus's account, between the Elbe and Vistula. At the Marcomannic War of 166 to 181 they lived in what is now Silesia, and about 271 Emperor Aurelian had to guard the Danube's middle course against them. About 330 Constantine the Great granted them lands in Pannonia on the Danube's right bank.

Under Emperor Valens they accepted Arian Christianity, though scattered orthodox Vandals existed, among them Stilicho, minister of Honorius. In 406 the Vandals crossed from Pannonia through a devastated Gaul into Spain, settling there in 411. From 427 their king was Genseric, who in 429 landed in North Africa with about 80,000 followers and founded a kingdom that sacked Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-george-ni:
George Nichols, also called Nicolls, was an English martyr born at Oxford about 1550 and executed at Oxford on 19 October 1589. He entered Brasenose College in 1564 or 1565, was readmitted on 20 August 1567, and supplicated for his Bachelor of Arts degree in 1570-71. He later served as an usher at St Paul's School in London. He reached Reims with Thomas Pilchard on 20 November 1581 but went on to Rome, returning on 21 July 1582.

Ordained subdeacon and deacon at Laon in April 1583, and priest at Reims by Cardinal Archbishop Louis de Guise on 24 September, he was sent on the mission the same year. After converting many, including a convicted highwayman in Oxford Castle, he was seized at Oxford's Catherine Wheel Inn, across from St Mary Magdalen's Church, alongside Humphrey Prichard, a Welsh servant. Tried for his priesthood, he suffered at Oxford.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-swithin-w:
Swithin Wells was a Hampshire gentleman who became one of the English martyrs of Elizabeth's reign. Born at Brambridge about 1536, he first conformed to the established church and ran a school for young gentlemen at Monkton Farleigh. Reconciled to Rome in the early 1580s, he later kept a house in Gray's Inn Lane, London.

His home became the scene of a raid on 1 November 1591, when priest Edmund Gennings was caught saying Mass there. Wells, returning afterward, was arrested too, tried at Westminster, and condemned under the statute against priests. He was hanged in Gray's Inn Lane, opposite his own house, on 10 December 1591. His wife was reprieved and died in prison in 1602. At his death he forgave his persecutor, Richard Topcliffe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vessels-for-h:
Vessels for holy oils surveys the containers, chiefly small flasks called ampullae or pittacia, in which Christians carried blessed oil from pilgrimage shrines. Made of wood, metal, ivory, and most often earthenware, they took flat shapes like a bulla, or the form of a thimble or little flagon. Most numerous today are the ampullae of St Menas.

Scarcely a pilgrimage place lacked its beneficial or miraculous oil, carried far to satisfy devotion or relieve the sick. Since oil was believed to share the virtues of saints it had touched, whether from lamps burning before their tombs or issuing from the tombs or images themselves. The entry's prized document is Gregory the Great's list of holy oils sent to Queen Theodelinde, accompanied by ampullae still preserved at Monza. It closes with bishops reserving the blessing of oils to Holy Thursday from the late sixth century.
cave-regions-of-the-ozarks-and-black-hil:
Luella Agnes Owen, a fellow of the American Geographical Society, published her cave study at Cincinnati in 1898. She treats cave study, geology, and geography as three branches of one science. Southern Missouri and the Black Hills of South Dakota, she argues, reward that combined approach better than almost anywhere.

Sixteen chapters move from a general view to Marble Cave, Fairy Cave, and the smaller Stone and Oregon County caves of the Ozarks. The Grand Gulf follows. Attention then shifts north to Wind Cave, given four chapters, and to the onyx and crystal caves. Photographs by several named photographers record entrances, formations, and famous chambers such as the Fairies' Palace.
christmas-in-legend-and-story-a-book-for:
Elva S. Smith of Carnegie Library, Pittsburgh, and Alice I. Hazeltine of the St. Louis public library compiled an illustrated Christmas book for young readers in 1915. Luke's account of the shepherds opens it, under a Shakespeare epigraph about the gracious season. Famous paintings illustrate the whole.

Carols, hymns, and legends then alternate. Milton, Browning, Longfellow, and Eugene Field supply the verse. Lagerlöf contributes the flight into Egypt and a Christmas rose legend. Tolstoy's tale Where Love Is, There God Is Also stands among the prose. Babouscka, St. Christopher, Good King Wenceslas, and St. Francis at Greccio widen the map beyond Bethlehem. A prince bishop learns rest from an ox-team's bird in one middle tale. Librarians built the book as a season's treasury, story by story.
clear-crystals:
Clear Crystals, by Clara Frances McKee Beede, is a book of verse whose contents run from page 51 to page 98 in the printing shown. Titles include More Brown Plumes, Sunshine and Rain, Only Pebbles, Golden Leaves, and Sail High Above. The title poem, Clear Crystals, appears as a second printing within the volume.

A Mother's Prayer signed Kay McKee opens the selections. It gives thanks for a new day and prays for soldier boys, that none be lost from the way in his search for the light. Let There Be Peace follows, wishing clouds and storm past and hatreds cast away. Faith, home, and seasons supply the book's steady themes.
common-diseases-of-farm-animals:
Common Diseases of Farm Animals, by Robert Alexander Craig, is a veterinary textbook in six parts. An introductory part treats disease in general: its discussion, diagnosis and symptoms, and treatment. Non-specific diseases follow by system: digestive, liver, urinary, generative, respiratory, circulatory, nervous, skin, and eye.

The horse's limbs get five chapters of their own, from structure and unsoundnesses to diseases of the foot. Teeth, surgery, and parasites have parts to themselves. Infectious diseases close the book: hog cholera, tuberculosis, and the infections of horse, cattle, and poultry species by species. Photographs teach as well as text; the frontispiece shows an insanitary dairy stable and yards. Study questions end the chapters, asking what a broken knee is and how wind-galls are treated.
condensed-novels:
Bret Harte's first Condensed Novels squeezed famous fiction into a few pages each, and the joke made his early reputation. Handsome Is as Handsome Does mocks Charles Reade's manner, disposing of whole families in numbered lists. Muck-a-Muck travesties James Fenimore Cooper's frontier novels, Miss Mix sends up Charlotte Brontë, and The Ninety-Nine Guardsmen reduces Dumas's musketeers to manageable absurdity.

Wilkie Collins, Bret Harte's contemporaries, and a southern novel after Belle Boyd all get the treatment, names dashed out in the contents and styles copied to the life. Harte wrote these as a young California editor. They remain funny because the imitation is exact: every tic of plot, diction, and sentiment stands exposed in miniature.
courts-and-criminals:
Arthur Train's Courts and Criminals gathers essays written between 1905 and 1910, reprinted, he notes, without revision. Train served as a New York prosecutor, and the first essay attacks the pleasant fiction of the presumption of innocence. A young man named Duffy, photographed and measured by police without charge, opens the argument. The mayor, a judge, and a commissioner fight over his treatment.

Chapters move through the courts as Train worked them: police methods, juries, lawyers, and the machinery of prosecution. He writes with a practitioner's impatience for legal pieties and a storyteller's eye for the case that proves the rule. The essays argue for common sense against both brutality and sentimentality. Train later created Mr. Ephraim Tutt, fiction's beloved old lawyer. Here the material is real, and the insider's candour still startles: an American district attorney explaining, in public, how justice actually worked.
crooked-trails:
Western tales and sketches by Frederic Remington fill Crooked Trails, first published in 1898 with the author's own pictures. Remington had made his name with Pony Tracks. The contents name eleven pieces, from Texas to Florida.

How the Law Got into the Chaparral opens with Colonel 'Rip' Ford of the old Texas Rangers, telling tales at San Antonio. Massai's Crooked Trail follows an Apache raider. Cracker Cowboys of Florida moves the scene far east. Other pieces treat a sergeant of an orphan troop, blue quail in the cactus, and the girls of Soledad. Remington writes the West he rode and drew, in short, vivid scenes of men, horses, and guns.
danger-signals:
Tales of brave railroad men fill Danger Signals, by John A. Hill and Jasper Ewing Brady. Jamieson-Higgins Company of Chicago issued it in 1902, with parts under copyright from 1898 to 1900. The subtitle praises the daring and stoicism of train dispatchers and engineers.

Part one holds stories such as Jim Wainright's Kid and An Engineer's Christmas Story. Part two turns to memoir: learning the business, a first office, train robbers, and a wreck. A woman operator who saved a train gets her own chapter. One tale blames a brakeman's neglect for a tail-end collision and his flight. The book sells the romance of the rails, and the nerve it took to run them.
dead-souls:
Nikolai Gogol's Dead Souls, translated by D J Hogarth with an introduction by John Cournos, follows the smiling traveler Chichikov buying dead serfs, souls still listed on census rolls, from provincial landowners. The file contains the complete first part and the surviving fragment of the second, which Gogol partly burned. His preparer's note explains the missing pages honestly.

Manilov, the box-like Korobochka, the liar Nozdrev, and the miser Plyushkin, who read every book with equal empty attention, form a gallery of Russian provincial types. Chichikov's scheme is both fraud and mirror. Gogol meant a Dante-like trilogy of fall and redemption; what survives is the funniest and saddest portrait of his Russia ever written.
different-girls:
Eleven tales of girls and women fill this Harper's Novelettes volume, edited by William Dean Howells and Henry Mills Alden. Harper and Brothers of New York and London issued it under dates from 1895 to 1906. Each tale is by a named hand, and the contents page is a roll of the period's magazine writers.

Richard Le Gallienne opens with The Little Joys of Margaret, whose five sisters have left the nest one by one to marry. Elizabeth Jordan, Alice Brown, and Octave Thanet follow. Howells's own Editha stands in the list, beside The Stout Miss Hopkins's Bicycle and The Marrying of Esther. Margaret's slow fate, watched by kind spectators, sets the key: quiet lives, plain towns, and the turns of love and duty.
doe-osti-17038113-testing-machine-learni:
Graeme Sutcliffe and M. Jones of Lawrence Livermore tested machine learning physics models of fusion implosion performance in this September 2026 report. Three dimensional unevenness in an implosion can cut yield, yet full modeling is slow and costly. Their framework mixes fast, simplified rocket piston simulations with real measurements, such as neutron images.

From sparse data the framework rebuilds implosion conditions, estimates values no instrument measured, and states its own uncertainty. The team then removed single neutron imaging views and energy channels one at a time. That test showed which measurements best pin down each kind of unevenness. Results can guide which diagnostics future fusion facilities should pay for.
doe-osti-2997807-engineered-colloidal-he:
A project summary by Krishna Acharya covers engineered nanocrystals that make hydrogen from sunlight and water. Hydrogen supplies under 1 percent of world energy because steam reforming and electrolysis cost so much energy. Photocatalytic particles could split water directly, but common oxide materials absorb only ultraviolet light, under 5 percent of sunlight, while broader absorbers often carry cadmium or lead.

The team built layered particles from less toxic III-V and II-VI semiconductors. Products include indium phosphide cores shelled with zinc selenide and zinc sulfide, as quantum dots about 10 nanometers across, plus two kinds of nanorods. Magnetic dopants such as neodymium and nickel were added during shell growth to help pull charges apart. Light emission lifetime tests under varied excitation power tracked that separation. The summary states the designs and the reasoning behind each layer.
doe-osti-2998668-slia-reference-architec:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2012387, by Alexandra Karpilow, Brady McBride and Brian Kelley, dated October 2025, documents the SLIA Reference Architecture Models project. The project ran from October 2024 to September 2025 under an Energy Department cyber program for the power sector. It built computer models of grid equipment so cyber risks could be ranked before testing.

Work centred on PySCES, a Livermore simulation tool, and on matching it to the CyTRICS PIRA reference designs for transmission substations. The team reviewed parts, added a transformer tap controller model, and tested how an attack on that controller would play out. Code changes cut clutter, moved the tool to Python 3.11, and added a schema database for checks. Gaps remain in model validation and in full device criticality scoring, and more development is advised.
doe-osti-2999153-education-for-pv-modeli:
Clifford Hansen of Sandia National Laboratories reports survey findings in SAND2025-13099, printed October 2025, from the 2025 PVPMC workshop, a gathering for solar power modelling specialists. Photovoltaic modelling predicts how solar plants will perform, yet few formal courses teach it deeply. Hansen asked working professionals five questions about the skills they wish they had, the skills that proved valuable, and how they learned the trade.

Programming and Python topped the wished-for list with 44 votes, trailed by data analysis at 17 and model assumptions at 14. Most learning turns out to be self-taught, through public media and software. Existing courses and certificates miss the mark, respondents said, either skimping on the detail behind performance models or teaching one software platform instead of core methods. Tables sort answers on hiring needs and skill checks. The report is a small but direct guide for anyone building training for this field.
doe-osti-3004386-tunable-few-layer-van-d:
Peter Sutter and Eli Sutter of the University of Nebraska-Lincoln give the final technical report for DOE project DE-SC0023437. The project studied few-layer van der Waals crystals: semiconductors built from weakly bound sheets, stacked into layered crystals and mixed stacks called heterostructures. Most earlier work stopped at single monolayers of a few famous materials. Thicker, tunable stacks were the open territory here.

The partnership paired the university with a national laboratory under the EPSCoR program. Goals centered on making high-quality layered crystals and probing their structure and optoelectronic behavior near the atomic scale with electron microscopy. New microscopy and spectroscopy methods were a deliverable in themselves. The report also records workforce training for students and postdocs, and collaborations formed along the way. Applications point at energy conversion and quantum information devices.
doe-osti-3006643-properties-of-electroni:
Final report for DOE grant DE-SC0002623 closes a 16-year project at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute led by Shengbai Zhang with Damien West. The period ran from September 1, 2009 to May 31, 2025, and the report was submitted November 30, 2025. Using first-principles computation, the team studied the structural, electronic, and dynamic properties of electronic materials for energy, optoelectronics, and data storage.

Chapters cover topological insulators, phase change materials and memory, graphene and 2D materials, and photovoltaics and solar materials, with further work on defect engineering, kagome lattices, and ultrafast carrier dynamics. The grant produced 115 journal publications. The summary ties the findings to better energy use, lead-free solar cells, and high-speed data processing. The group also enhanced VASP and other DFT codes for defect and dynamics simulations, and trained students through doctoral and master's theses at RPI.
doe-osti-3377975-nuclear-security-risks-:
Nuclear Security Risks for HALEU Fuels, Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/LTR-2026/4451 from June 2026, comes from the Office of International Nuclear Security. Four Oak Ridge authors are printed, A. Smith, S. Nelson, J. Karcz, and M. Feldstein, with J. Bland of Sandia National Laboratories. HALEU, high-assay low-enriched uranium, is the fuel many advanced reactor designs depend on.

The report walks the HALEU fuel cycle step by step, from enrichment through fuel fabrication and beyond, and sets the security risk of each stage against the regulatory frameworks that govern it. Background sections explain what HALEU is and why its higher enrichment, still below weapons grade, changes the security picture compared with the low-enriched fuel of today's fleet. Objectives and scope are stated up front, and the analysis follows the fuel.
doe-osti-3453386-education-for-pv-modeli:
Sandia report SAND2026-24968, by Clifford W. Hansen and Marios Theristis and printed August 2026, surveys educators who teach solar system modeling. The field needs trained modelers as solar fleets grow. Most current instructors taught themselves, the survey finds.

Mechanical engineering departments sponsor many of the courses found. Electrical and materials programs also host modeling classes. The report argues future instructors need deep modeling training themselves. A shared curriculum could raise course quality across schools. Program planners get a clear map of who teaches modeling now and what support they lack. Survey answers came from instructors across many university departments and multi-disciplinary programs.
doe-osti-3625672-semi-transparent-perovs:
CRADA CRD-19-00810 with Tandem PV, Inc. closes in National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5F00-99345, dated August 2026. Joey Luther, Bryon Larson, and Kyle Reiter were the lab contacts. The report date is February 17, 2026, and the work ran from June 2019 to June 2025. Its subject is semi-transparent perovskite solar cells that can stand alone or stack on top of other cells.

Scale-up work covered perovskite inks, coating and heating steps, clear electrodes, and anti-reflection layers. Joining cells into modules was also in scope, as was recycling. Later changes added microwave conductivity checks for steady module output. Another change tuned atomic layer barrier steps so the top contact sticks better and modules last longer. Perovskite films react to oxygen and water, so ageing tests compared barrier coatings under light soaking. Modules shown pair ten perovskite cells in series with a silicon cell behind them.
edward-macdowell-his-work-and-ideals:
Elizabeth Fry Page writes on Edward MacDowell in a short New York volume that joins a prose study to poems of her own. The book is dedicated to Mrs. Aline Reese Blondner, founder of the MacDowell Club of Nashville. Page opens with Sidney Lanier's saying: music means harmony, harmony means love, and love means God.

Her essay argues that music and poetry are near inseparable. A great song without words, she writes, will in time draw a poet to supply them. Great music, in turn, often springs from a single stanza. The second half gives her poetical interpretations of MacDowell's pieces. Titles include A. D. 1620, To a Wild Rose, In Deep Woods, and A Deserted Farm. Page writes as a devotee, and the book is a fan's tribute as much as a study. One odd stretch of the hosted file, a kitchen scene, seems to stray from another work.
english-literature-for-boys-and-girls:
English Literature for Boys and Girls, by H E Marshall, tells the story of English writing as a chain of tales young readers can follow. Marshall opens in what she calls the listening time, before books, with the Irish cattle raid of Cooley and the sorrows of storytelling. Chapters move through King Arthur, Beowulf, and Caedmon, the father of English song, then to Bede, the father of English history.

Alfred the Great fights with his pen, Chaucer appears as bread and milk for children, and the Canterbury Tales get three chapters of inn and pilgrims. Later headings promise the first English guide book, the Bruce in Scotland, a poet king, the mystery plays, and Everyman. Marshall writes literary history as biography and adventure, trusting story to carry fact. Generations of children first met their national literature through her voice.
esther-a-book-for-girls:
Rosa Nouchette Carey's Esther is a book for girls, told in the first person by its heroine. Esther begins by confessing that she was always sorry her name was Esther, a small vexation that opens a long story of home, school and growing up.

Chapters follow her last day at Redmayne House, her arrival at Combe Manor, the old house at Milnthorpe, and life at the Brambles. Dot, Uncle Geoffrey, Miss Ruth, smugglers' caves, a long night and a brave deed carry the plot toward its sunset close. Carey writes with the warmth and moral steadiness that made her a favourite with Victorian girls, and modern readers will find Esther an engaging period heroine.
explanation-of-catholic-morals:
Stapleton's Explanation of Catholic Morals offers a concise, reasoned, popular account of Catholic moral teaching. John H. Stapleton was a priest writing for general readers. The copy carries a 1904 copyright and a 1913 printing by Benzinger Brothers. It bears the imprimatur of Archbishop John M. Farley of New York.

The contents run to dozens of short chapters. Early ones cover conscience, law, and sin, then the capital sins in turn. Pride, covetousness, lust, anger, gluttony, envy, and sloth each get a chapter. Middle chapters treat faith, hope, love, and prayer. Later ones address oaths, vows, blasphemy, and the religious life. Stapleton aims to join what Catholics believe with how they should act.
familiar-spanish-travels:
William Dean Howells's Familiar Spanish Travels records his travels in Spain, illustrated and published by Harper and Brothers in 1913. Howells begins with autobiographical approaches, recalling how a train toward Granada on a November evening in 1911 brought back an Ohio village of the 1850s.

Chapters follow San Sebastian and Biscay, Burgos and its bitter cold, Valladolid, Madrid, a night and day in Toledo, Cordova, Seville, Granada, Ronda, Algeciras and Tarifa. Howells writes as a familiar, companionable traveller, noting manners, buildings and daily life rather than Baedeker facts. Readers planning a Spanish journey, or revisiting one, will find his account warm and observant.
fifty-two-story-talks-to-boys-and-girls:
Chidley preaches to the young in Fifty-Two Story Talks to Boys and Girls. Howard J. Chidley was pastor of Trinity Congregational Church in East Orange, New Jersey. The book, dated 1914, gives one talk for each week of the year. Its titles mix Bible tales with plain morals: Habits, A Lesson in Courtesy, Little Foxes, and Ulysses and the Sirens.

Each talk hangs a lesson on a small tale. The sampled pages tell of Zaccheus, who gave his money back after Christ dined with him. Chidley draws the rule: if we wish people to be good, we must look for the good in them. He adds a Chicago jailer who gives each freed man a letter of praise, so the man is ashamed to fall again. The talks are short, warm, and built to be read aloud.
fundamental-principles-of-the-metaphysic:
Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, by Immanuel Kant and translated by Thomas Kingsmill Abbott, lays out Kant's account of duty. Kant dates the work 1785 and begins by sorting philosophy into physics, ethics, and logic. Ethics, the science of the laws of freedom, is his ground here: what a rational person ought to do, apart from what custom or reward suggests.

Across its sections Kant moves from ordinary moral judgment to his central test. An act has true moral worth, he argues, when it is done from duty, not from liking or gain. The rule for action must be one the actor could will as a law for everyone, the test later called the categorical imperative, meaning an unconditional command of reason. Abbott's English made this short, hard book a standard text for students of philosophy in Britain and America.
gems-gathered-in-haste-a-new-year-s-gift:
A friend signing only T.B.F. put this small gift book together fast, as a New Year's present for four Sunday schools. The preface jokes that haste is a fault, yet work done in haste beats no work at all. Short tales, poems, and dialogues fill the pages, each sized for young readers and for reading aloud.

Pieces praise neat habits, kind deeds, and brave women. One tale tells of a heroine of Pillau in Prussia, held up beside Grace Darling. Verses mark a tidy girl by her clean books and ordered toys. A closing note tells children to ask parents or teachers about any hard parts. The book shows how Sunday schools taught faith and conduct through short, bright reading.
general-history-for-colleges-and-high-sc:
P. V. N. Myers's General History for Colleges and High Schools compresses the story of the world into a single school volume. Myers bases the book on his earlier Ancient History and his Mediaeval and Modern History, changing the perspective and proportions where a one-volume survey required it.

The narrative runs from the ancient East through Greece and Rome, the Middle Ages and modern Europe, with the frontispiece showing the Attic plains and the Acropolis of Athens. Myers says he took the greatest care to verify facts and to report the newest finds and judgments of scholars, while admitting that so wide a range invites error. Teachers and students will find it a solid, old-fashioned survey, built for classroom use.
glenloch-girls:
Grace M. Remick's Glenloch Girls opens its series with a pleasant winter, says the introduction, in the lives of everyday girls and boys. Ruth Shirley expects to be very forlorn; instead, a new home in Glenloch welcomes her. The kindest of friends make her a Glenloch girl in heart and name. Ruth's Father, the first chapter, starts her story.

Three chums, a newcomer, and a new club follow: the Social Six is formed. Caps and aprons, Charlotte's problems, and Christmas presents fill the winter's small events. A boy among them learns patience when what he most prizes is taken away. Remick lists the sequels on her title page — Abroad, the Girls' Club, and Camp West — as promises. The book is wholesome series fiction of its period: friendship as curriculum, faults confessed, and good times earned. Glenloch's snow is the setting; the girls' loyalty is the plot.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Pistols_Pistols: Special Agent Jack A. French of the FBI's Dallas office wrote this memorandum about a telephone tip. The caller was Tony Jackson of Fort Worth. His tip concerned Lee Harvey Oswald. Tips flooded the Dallas office after the assassination, and each one was written up whether it led anywhere or not. The file gives the agent, the caller, and the subject. It does not preserve what Jackson reported, so the tip itself cannot be described.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Referrals_Refer:
Harold Weisberg wrote this memorandum about a withheld record. The FBI had referred material elsewhere and withheld Orest Pena's passport information from headquarters file 105-82555. Weisberg's point is sharp: the same information was already in the public domain, printed by the Warren Commission.

Pena was a New Orleans bar owner whose name runs through the Oswald inquiry. A passport detail about him, public in one place and withheld in another, was the kind of absurdity Weisberg collected. The memo argues that referral withholding had become a habit, not a judgment. It preserves the file number, the man's name, and the contradiction, a small clean example of secrecy outliving its reason.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WLS_WLS: Harold Weisberg wrote to Merrill Mazuer at WLS-TV in Chicago on April 30, 1970. Letters to television staff were a steady part of Weisberg's campaign against the Warren Commission report. He pressed broadcasters to cover his findings and answer his charges. The WLS letter shows that campaign reaching a major Chicago station, in Weisberg's direct and persistent style.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Le:
A car bomb in Washington, D.C. killed former Chilean ambassador Orlando Letelier and Ronni Moffitt on September 21, 1976. In the months after the attack, four State Department officers used a formal Dissent Channel memo to push their own government. This briefing book, posted in September 2019, publishes that declassified memo.

The officers wrote that President Augusto Pinochet probably ordered the assassination himself. They urged an aggressive policy to end normal relations with Chile and force him from power. Their protest failed at the time, but the memo shows dissent inside the State Department in plain, official language.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
Signals intelligence, the interception of communications, caused turf wars inside American spying for decades. Jeffrey T. Richelson compiled this briefing book, number 506, published in March 2015. Its core is a formerly top-secret, multi-volume CIA history of that fight.

The history details CIA conflicts with the National Security Agency and the military over who owned the signals mission. Added documents describe CIA signals work at home and abroad, often in direct competition with NSA. Later cooperation between the rivals made possible the exploits that Edward Snowden exposed. Few sets trace one bureaucratic rivalry from its roots to its modern results.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig: Soviet transmitters beamed microwave signals at the American embassy in Moscow for years, exposing staff including, as this page's title notes, President Richard Nixon during his visits. This briefing-book page presents the declassified Moscow Signals record. A fuller Archive series on the signals, covering projects PANDORA and BIZARRE, supplies the detailed documents. The evidence here is the title alone. The page marks the strange fact at the story's center: a president was irradiated in his host's capital, and Washington kept the matter quiet.
great-englishwomen-an-historical-reading:
M. B. Synge wrote Great Englishwomen as a reading book for schools, published in 1911 in Bell's series. Its lives run in time order, each with dates on the contents page. Queen Bertha, who died in 606, comes first, followed by Maude the Good and Eleanor of Aquitaine. Philippa of Hainault and Margaret of Anjou carry the tale through the Middle Ages.

Later lives include Lady Jane Grey, the painter Angelica Kauffmann, Hannah More, and the prison reformer Elizabeth Fry. Mary Somerville, Elizabeth Barrett Browning, and Florence Nightingale close the book. Bertha's life sets the tone: quiet influence praised above public acts. The prose is plain and clear, made for young readers. The book shows which women a school of 1911 thought girls should know, and in what order of honor.
h-g-wells:
J. D. Beresford published the first book-length study of H. G. Wells in 1915, while Wells was at the height of his powers. The contents set the plan: an introduction, then the romances, the novels, and the sociology, with a bibliography and an American bibliography at the end. A portrait of Wells leads the book. Beresford was himself a novelist, and a friend of his subject.

He treats the scientific romances, The Time Machine and its kin, as Wells's most original work. Then come the novels of English life, and the books of social prophecy in which Wells preached a planned world. Beresford writes with sympathy, yet keeps a critic's rights. The study is now a period piece in itself: it shows how the first readers sorted the work of a writer who seemed to be inventing the future in public.
half-a-dozen-girls:
Half a Dozen Girls, by Anna Chapin Ray, opens its contents in a country town's visiting season. Polly arrives first, in the opening chapter. The Adams family receives her. A round of calls follows, and then a frank exchange of confidences. The six girls of the title form a circle of cousins and friends. Callers, she calls them tartly in one chapter heading. How They Managed It gives the plot away.

Ray writes the girls' novel of manners for the 1890s. Small economies, small vanities, and small kindnesses fill her chapters. A strawberry festival, a day in the country, and a Christmas of last words and last gifts close the year. Nothing enormous happens, by design. Ray's subject is how nice girls actually behave to one another when adults are not watching. The circle holds, and holding is the happy ending.
herzegovina-or-omer-pacha-and-the-christ:
Lieutenant G Arbuthnot published this travel and war account at London in 1862. He rode through Herzegovina while Omer Pacha put down a Christian revolt. Arbuthnot admits his stay was short and his grasp of the tongue slight. He offers what his own eyes saw, checked by men who knew the land.

Marches, bivouacs, and rough stony roads fill the tale. He meets troops under rival pachas and notes the strain of the war. A brief account of Servia, its state and funds, closes the book. Readers get a British officer's plain view of a tense Balkan land.
his-life-a-complete-story-in-the-words-o:
William E Barton, Theodore G Soares, and Sydney Strong prepared this life of Jesus. They wove the four Gospels into one complete story. Their text is the American Standard Revised Bible, used by leave. The book first came out in 1906, in cheap paper and cloth forms.

The editors sort Christ's words and deeds into one smooth order. No words of their own are added to the sacred text. Readers can follow the whole life, from birth to rising, without turning between four books. The plain aim is to let the Gospels speak as a single, clear narrative.
his-sombre-rivals:
His Sombre Rivals, by Edward Payson Roe, appears as the thirteenth volume of his works, illustrated and dated 1883. Roe's preface explains that the story had taken form in his mind for years. A Northern man, he asks his Southern readers to trust his fairness. He argues that surviving soldiers of both armies now respect each other. Confederate and Union veterans, he says, were sincere Americans. Their patriotism matched, whatever their cause.

He promises to show Bull Run through the eyes of the men who stood in it. Reconciliation between North and South is his stated purpose throughout. The contents move through Warren Hilland, supreme moments, and a revelation. An ordeal and a flight to nature follow. Roe uses the late war as the sombre rival of his title's love story. Every character must out argue, out suffer, or out forgive that past.
in-a-hollow-of-the-hills:
Bret Harte opens In a Hollow of the Hills on a night so dark that three lost horsemen can see nothing but a match flame. Then a square of light appears where no house should stand, on Galloper's Ridge, fifteen miles from anywhere, and a face crosses the lit window. The riders have stumbled on a hidden household in the California hills, and the novel grows from that glimpse.

Secrecy rules the hollow: a concealed home, a guarded woman, and a past that the mountains are meant to bury. Harte spins a frontier mystery of love, shame, and rescue around the hidden valley. The tale is melodrama in his best manner, short, scenic, and driven by the question of who lives behind that window.
let-s-collect-rocks-and-shells:
Shell Union Oil issued Let's Collect Rocks and Shells as a hobby booklet. Its introduction notes that millions collect rocks or shells for pleasure. Collecting can grow into a career or stay a satisfying hobby, it says.

Sections explain how rocks are made of minerals. The main kinds of rocks receive simple treatment. Gem collecting gets a chapter for the lucky few, the title jokes. The booklet aims to arouse curiosity, not to teach everything. Its plain approach suits young beginners with a beach or quarry nearby. Shell collecting receives equal space with rock hunting. Bright pictures in the original help young collectors start.
letters-to-a-daughter-and-a-little-sermo:
Helen Ekin Starrett published Letters to a Daughter with Jansen, McClurg in Chicago in 1886. A Little Sermon to School Girls shares the volume. Starrett had written The Future of Educated Women.

Nine letters treat behavior, self-control, and aims in life. Personal habits, society, conversation, and friends follow in order. Tact and religious culture close the mother's counsel. Starrett writes as a guide for girls entering wider life. Her advice reflects the hopes and limits placed on educated young women then. Starrett championed women's higher education in her career. Her counsel balances ambition with the era's expectations.
levels-of-living-essays-on-everyday-idea:
Henry Frederick Cope published Levels of Living with Fleming Revell in 1908. Its subtitle calls the pieces essays on everyday ideals. Cope dedicated the book to his wife, Elizabeth.

The dedication calls her God's best gift and his inspiration. The essays first ran under the title A Sermon for To-day. They treat the art of everyday living in short chapters. Home, work, and character supply their plain themes. Cope writes as a minister for readers seeking a higher daily standard. Revell published much religious and self-help writing then. Cope's essays fit that list with their sermon roots.
life-of-lord-byron-vol-1-with-his-letter:
Thomas Moore edited Byron's letters and journals across six volumes. John Murray published this first volume in London in 1854. Its contents run to Byron's return from the Continent in July 1811. Moore dedicated the volumes to Sir Walter Scott.

Notices of Byron's life frame the letters and journal extracts. Readers follow the young lord through his early travels abroad. Moore, himself a poet and friend, arranged the materials. The set became the standard early source for Byron's own voice. Transcriber links point readers to the other five volumes' etexts. Murray's Albemarle Street house published Moore's edition in London.
life-of-lord-byron-vol-2-with-his-letter:
Volume Two of Moore's Byron covers July 1811 to January 1814. Murray's new edition appeared in London in 1854. Moore pauses to judge how travel changed Byron's mind and disposition. Two years of adventure followed a childhood among mountain scenery.

He doubts scenery alone forms a poet, however romantic. The poet feeds later on recollections of such scenes, perhaps. Byron's homecoming scenes now await him in England. Letters and journals carry the narrative through his rising fame. A childhood among mountains may implant poetic feeling, Moore concedes. Whether such scenes actually form poets remains, for him, questionable.
life-of-lord-byron-vol-3-with-his-letter:
Moore's third Byron volume spans February 1814 to April 1817. Byron's journal for February 1814 opens this portion. He had spent a busy, pleasant month away from London. Newspapers greeted his return with hysterics over two republished stanzas.

The stanzas concerned Princess Charlotte weeping at the Regent's speech. Talk of a motion in the Lords amused and annoyed him. Hobhouse, newly returned, earns praise as his best friend. Journals and letters together show Byron at fame's uneasy height. The Morning Post paragraph on Byron stretched as long as his pedigree. Vituperative abuse, he notes dryly, arrived as usual that morning.
life-of-lord-byron-vol-4-with-his-letter:
Volume Four of Moore's Byron runs from April 1817 to October 1820. Letter 272 finds Byron in Venice, recovering from a slow fever. He credits his recovery to avoiding medicine and doctors alike. Rome tempts him next, though he expects to change plans often.

Letters should still be directed to Venice, he instructs Murray. Forwarding will follow him if he actually travels. Moore's notices link the correspondence into a continuous life. Exile in Italy shapes every page of this middle volume. A slow fever's rise, progress, decline, and fall fill his medical report. Nocturnal burnings and morning perspirations marked its final quickening.
life-of-lord-byron-vol-5-with-his-letter:
Moore's fifth volume covers October 1820 to November 1822. Letter 394, from Ravenna, demands two letters Moore owes him. Byron asks after Moore's poem and reports a French translation received. He calls the travesty abominable but knows railing is useless.

He has begun a continuation of his memoir for Moore. Italy news stays unspoken here because government watches travelers. The letters show Byron restless between Ravenna and new ventures. Moore's notices bind these fragments into Byron's unfolding story. Sophia Gay, not Gail, was corrected as his Paris correspondent. Byron asks whether Moore received his copied memoir safely.
life-of-lord-byron-vol-6-with-his-letter:
The final Byron volume runs from February 1823 to April 1824. Letter 508 opens from Genoa in February 1823. An appendix gathers Byron's miscellaneous prose pieces. Reviews, parliamentary speeches, and his Pope controversy letters appear there.

His 1807 review of Wordsworth's poems leads the appendix. Speeches from 1812 and 1813 show the lord in Parliament. The narrative ends with Byron's death in April 1824. Moore thus closes the life in Byron's own words. A fragment from 1816 and Bowles controversy letters fill the appendix. His second Bowles letter answers observations on Pope's character. Genoa was Byron's last Italian home before he left for Greece.
maria-mitchell-life-letters-and-journals:
Maria Mitchell: Life, Letters, and Journals was compiled by Phebe Mitchell Kendall in 1896. Its first chapter tells of her Nantucket home and schooling. The young Maria watched a solar eclipse in 1831 and learned the heavens. She became librarian of the Nantucket Atheneum while still young.

Chapter two tells how she swept the skies and found her comet in 1847. King Frederick VI of Denmark honored that discovery with a medal. Letters from famous men of science crowd these pages. Diary extracts show her wit, faith, and love of teaching. Mitchell became America's first great woman astronomer. Her life still encourages girls who look at the stars.
memoirs-of-the-union-s-three-great-civil:
Memoirs of the Union's Three Great Civil War Generals joins three lives. Ulysses S. Grant, William T. Sherman, and Philip H. Sheridan stand in the contents. Grant's personal memoirs lead the set in full.

Grant says he had vowed never to write his memoirs at all. A fall at sixty two, and a partner's fraud, changed his mind. The Century Magazine asked for pieces, and he wrote for the pay. He vows to do no injustice to either side in the war. Hero deeds by the thousand go unnamed, he admits with regret. Commanders' own reports must hold the full tale of those acts.
nasa-tm-19650022516-the-lunar-rills:
Lunar rills are long, winding grooves cut into the Moon's surface, and this survey sorts them into at least four groups. The first rill was noted in 1787, near the crater Hyginus, and it still bears that name in the text as scanned. Many rills lie in the lunar highlands. Some have edges or banks that look scalloped along their length.
